questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: General Pharmacology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Healthy adult volunteers are enrolled in a phase I clinical trial investigating the properties of a newly developed oral antimicrobial agent. While reviewing the data, the researchers note that the drug's half-life seems to vary amongst the study participants. An increase in which of the following pharmacologic parameters is most likely responsible for the longer half-life seen in certain individuals?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Volume of distribution

Drug half-life is determined by the equation t½ = 0.693 × (Volume of distribution / Clearance). An increased volume of distribution (Vd) means the drug is more extensively distributed into tissues rather than remaining in plasma. This creates a larger drug reservoir, from which the drug returns slowly to the circulation for elimination, thereby prolonging the half-life even if clearance remains unchanged. Interindividual differences in body composition or tissue binding commonly explain such variability.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Drug glucuronidation: Increases clearance → shortens half-life.

B. Glomerular filtration rate: Higher GFR increases elimination → shorter half-life.

C. Oral bioavailability: Affects amount absorbed, not half-life.
questions.learning: Volume of distribution Drug half-life is determined by the equation t½ = 0.693 × (Volume of distribution / Clearance). An increased volume of distribution (Vd) means the drug is more extensively distributed into tissues rather than remaining in plasma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Hormone responsible?
questions.explanation: Breastfeeding and lactation are regulated by two primary hormones: prolactin and oxytocin. Prolactin is responsible for milk production within the breast. Oxytocin, however, is the hormone responsible for the "milk ejection reflex" or "let-down reflex". When an infant suckles, it triggers the release of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which causes the myoepithelial cells surrounding the breast alveoli to contract, forcing milk into the ducts for the baby. TSH (Option B) regulates the thyroid gland and has no role in lactation. Growth Hormone (GH) (Option C) promotes general growth but does not influence milk release. FSH (Option D) regulates the development of ovarian follicles and is not involved in breastfeeding. Thus, oxytocin is the hormone directly responsible for facilitating the flow of milk during feeding
questions.learning: Breastfeeding and lactation are regulated by two primary hormones: prolactin and oxytocin. Prolactin is responsible for milk production within the breast.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A thalassemia patient has received multiple blood transfusions. Aplastic crisis can occur in this patient due to infection from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Parvovirus

Aplastic crisis in this patient is triggered by parvovirus infection.

Parvovirus infects and kills the red cell precursors. This creates a transient arrest of erythropoiesis i.e. aplastic crisis as the life span of RBCs is shortened. The immune response clears the virus in 1-2 weeks. It may be seen in patients with underlying chronic hemolytic anaemia like sickle-cell disease, thalassemia, hereditary spherocytosis, and RBC enzyme deficiencies like pyruvate kinase deficiency. Patients with aplastic crisis appear ill with fever, malaise, and paleness with tachycardia and tachypnea due to profound anaemia. The rash may or may not be present.

Parvovirus B19 infection occurs usually in children 5–10 years causing erythema infectiosum. It is also known as the fifth disease. It begins as a prominent erythema of the cheeks- slapped cheek disease, spreading to the trunk and limbs, followed by lymphadenopathy and arthralgia. Fever and mild constitutional symptoms may accompany the rash.

Other options:

Option B: Epstein Barr virus affects adolescents and younger adults more frequently but may occur from childhood to old age. It is transmitted primarily through close contact with oropharyngeal secretions. The incubation period of EBV infectious mononucleosis is 4-6 weeks. Clinically, patients may present with, fever, malaise, nausea, anorexia, lymphadenopathy- bilateral and symmetrical, pharyngitis, tonsillar enlargement, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. A drug-induced rash may develop on using beta-lactam. antibiotics.

Option C: Cytomegalovirus causes mononucleosis in healthy individuals and disseminated diseases like leukopenia, hepatitis, colitis, pneumonitis, esophagitis, gastritis, and retinitis in immunocompromised patients.

Option D: Herpes simplex virus type 1 which belongs to the subfamily alpha viruses causes Herpes labialis (also known as cold sores). HSV type 1 (human herpes virus type 1 or HHY type 1) is isolated from lesions in and around the mouth and is transmitted by direct contact or droplet spread from cases or carriers. The most common site is the face- around the mouth, on the cheeks, chin, or the forehead.
questions.learning: Parvovirus Aplastic crisis in this patient is triggered by parvovirus infection. Parvovirus infects and kills the red cell precursors.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is classified under Biosafety level -3 infections?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. XDR-TB

Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3) is required for pathogens that cause serious or potentially lethal infections via airborne transmission.

• Transmitted by aerosols
• Can cause severe disease
• Require controlled laboratory access, negative pressure rooms, and respiratory protection

Correct example:

• Mycobacterium tuberculosis (including XDR-TB) → airborne infection → BSL-3

Differentiation:

• Salmonella → BSL-2 (fecal-oral transmission)
• Ebola virus → BSL-4 (highly lethal, no effective treatment, high risk)
• Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever → BSL-4

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a contraindication to the procedure shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primigravida

The procedure shown in the image is the external cephalic version (ECV). Being a primigravida (first pregnancy) is not a contraindication to ECV. The procedure can be performed in both primigravida and multigravida patients as long as other contraindications are not present.

ECV is recommended to manage transverse lie when the membranes are intact.

Prerequisites for ECV - Women who have reached 370/7 weeks of gestation. Multiparity, unengaged presenting part, nonanterior placenta, nonobese patient, and abundant amnionic fluid improve the chances of ECV.

Absolute contraindications - When vaginal delivery is contraindicated, e.g. placenta previa

Relative contraindications - Early labor, oligohydramnios or ruptured membranes, known nuchal cord, structural uterine abnormalities, fetal growth restriction, multifetal gestation, and prior abruption of the placenta
questions.learning: Primigravida — The procedure shown in the image is the external cephalic version (ECV). Being a primigravida (first pregnancy) is not a contraindication to ECV.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a patient, after administration of Noradrenaline injection, the heart rate started to decrease. What is the reason behind it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stimulation of baroreceptors

The decrease in heart rate (bradycardia) after noradrenaline (norepinephrine) injection is due to the stimulation of baroreceptors (baroreceptor reflex, also known as the baroreflex).

When noradrenaline is administered, it causes vasoconstriction via alpha-1 receptors, leading to an increase in blood pressure. This increase in blood pressure activates the baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch, which through the baroreflex mechanism, leads to increased vagal tone and decreased sympathetic outflow to the heart, resulting in a compensatory decrease in heart rate (reflex bradycardia).

Baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the walls of the heart and blood vessels. Baroreceptors are stimulated by the stretching of the walls of the respective vessels when there is an increased volume or pressure in the vessel. They are important in the immediate management of blood pressure.

The afferents from the baroreceptors activate the Nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) which in turn activates the caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM). The CVLM, on activation, releases gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) which is inhibitory to the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM). The RVLM is the major excitatory source of the sympathetic nervous system. As it is inhibited, there is sympathetic inhibition thus reducing the blood pressure.

The NTS also simultaneously activates the vagal motor neurons causing bradycardia.

Other options:

Option A: (Stimulation of alpha-2 receptors): While alpha-2 receptor stimulation can cause a decrease in sympathetic outflow, this is not the primary mechanism for the heart rate decrease seen with noradrenaline administration. Alpha-2 effects are more relevant for drugs like clonidine.

Option B: (Stimulation of beta-1 receptors): Beta-1 stimulation would actually cause an increase in heart rate (tachycardia), not a decrease. While noradrenaline does have some beta-1 activity, its alpha effects predominate.

Option D: (Inhibition of Baroreceptor): The baroreceptors are stimulated, not inhibited, by the increase in blood pressure. Inhibition of baroreceptors would actually lead to an increase in heart rate.

Pearl PF0543: Factors Affecting Heart Rate

Heart rate is accelerated by

• Decreased activity of arterial baroreceptors
• Increased activity of atrial stretch receptors
• Inspiration
• Excitement
• Anger
• Pain
• Hypoxia
• Exercise
• Thyroid hormones
• Fever

The Heart is slowed by

• Increased activity of arterial baroreceptors
• Expiration
• Grief
• Stimulation of pain fibers in trigeminal nerve
• Increased intracranial pressure
questions.learning: Stimulation of baroreceptors — The decrease in heart rate (bradycardia) after noradrenaline (norepinephrine) injection is due to the stimulation of baroreceptors (baroreceptor reflex, also known as the baroreflex).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: When quarantine was introduced in the 14th century for plague, how many days were people who were suspected to have the infection quarantined for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 40 days

In the 14th century, quarantine was used for plague and the suspects were quarantined for 40 days.

The idea of quarantine when it was initially introduced was that, the disease would remain dormant in the quarantine period and die out. But the 40 day period caused inconveniences and was based on a lack of scientific knowledge regarding the causation and spread of the disease.

Quarantine is the restriction on the movement of people, animals, and goods that may have been exposed to a communicable disease. It is intended to prevent the spread of communicable diseases.

Quarantine is distinct from medical isolation, in which those confirmed to be infected with a communicable disease are isolated from the healthy population.

It is a primary level of prevention and falls under specific protection measures. The various types of quarantine are:

* Absolute - Complete limitation of movement

* Modified - Selective partial limitation of movement

* Segregation - Observation of a group of persons in a population after separation

Note:

With respect to the COVID-19 pandemic, home quarantine is advised when a person comes in contact with a COVID-19 positive patient.
questions.learning: 40 days In the 14th century, quarantine was used for plague and the suspects were quarantined for 40 days. The idea of quarantine when it was initially introduced was that, the disease would remain dormant in the quarantine period and die out.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old gravida 2 with previous LSCS develops suprapubic pain during contractions with maternal tachycardia and fetal bradycardia at 8 cm dilation. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediate cesarean section

These findings strongly suggest Uterine scar dehiscence (or uterine window), a life-threatening obstetric emergency. Uterine rupture occurs when the uterine wall tears partly, often at the previous cesarean scar.

This leads to:

• Massive hemorrhage
• Fetal hypoxia
• Maternal shock

Classic Clinical Signs

| Sign | Explanation

| ---- | -----------

| Severe abdominal/suprapubic pain | Scar tearing

| Maternal tachycardia | Blood loss

| Fetal bradycardia | Fetal hypoxia

| Loss of fetal station | Indicates complete rupture

Fetal bradycardia is the most common early sign of uterine dehiscence/ rupture.

Suspected uterine dehiscence

↓

Immediate resuscitation

↓

Emergency laparotomy

↓

Cesarean delivery

↓

Repair uterus or hysterectomy

The goal is rapid delivery to save the fetus and prevent maternal hemorrhage.
questions.learning: Immediate cesarean section — These findings strongly suggest Uterine scar dehiscence (or uterine window), a life-threatening obstetric emergency. Uterine rupture occurs when the uterine wall tears partly, often at the previous cesarean scar.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 62-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease presents for routine follow-up. His blood glucose and lipid profile are normal, but laboratory testing reveals an elevated homocysteine level above the normal range. Based on these findings, deficiency of which enzyme is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: A elevated homocysteine level is a significant risk factor for cardiovascular disease and premature atherosclerosis. The most common enzyme deficiency leading to hyperhomocysteinemia is Cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS). CBS is responsible for the conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine in the transsulfuration pathway; its lack causes homocysteine to accumulate in the blood. Homogentisate oxidase (Option A) deficiency causes Alkaptonuria (dark urine/ochronosis). Cystathionine gamma-synthase (Option C) is not a primary human enzyme defect associated with this clinical presentation. HGPRTase (Option D) deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, which results in hyperuricemia and self-mutilation, not homocysteinemia. Patients with homocystinuria often present with early-onset CAD, lens subluxation, and tall stature. While vitamin deficiencies (B6, B12, folate) are common causes of mild elevation, a primary genetic enzyme defect like CBS deficiency is the most probable cause for significant, unexplained hyperhomocysteinemia in a patient with established vascular disease
questions.learning: A elevated homocysteine level is a significant risk factor for cardiovascular disease and premature atherosclerosis. The most common enzyme deficiency leading to hyperhomocysteinemia is Cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A female patient presents with ambiguous genitalia and rapid virilization. She also complains of excessive facial hair growth, voice deepening, and an enlarged clitoris over the past few months. CT scan is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

The presented clinical scenario, along with the CT scan findings of bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands with nodules in the adrenal cortex, suggests a likely diagnosis of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH).

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a disorder of cortisol synthesis. It has an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. Cortisol deficiency increases the secretion of the adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), causing adrenal hyperplasia with the overproduction of intermediate metabolites. This child has clitoromegaly due to increased androgen synthesis. The enzyme 21-hydroxylase helps in the downstream synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone. A deficiency of aldosterone causes salt wasting that presents as low blood pressure.

The presentation depends on the enzyme that is deficient, which could result in mineralocorticoid deficiency or excess, incomplete virilization or precocious puberty in affected males, and virilization or sexual infantilism in affected females.

Given below is the pathway and enzymes involved in adrenal steroid synthesis:

Other options:

Option B: Adrenocortical carcinoma might appear as a large, irregular mass within the adrenal gland. The mass could have areas of necrosis or hemorrhage, contributing to its irregular appearance.

Option C: A pheochromocytoma typically presents as a well-defined, solid mass within the adrenal gland. It might be associated with areas of hemorrhage, leading to a heterogeneous appearance.

Option D: The adrenal glands may appear normal in size or slightly enlarged on a CT scan in case of primary hyperaldosteronism. There might not be distinct masses or nodules in the adrenal glands.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The government pasted public awareness posters in public places. What type of communication method does this approach represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mass approach

The type of communication method used when the government pastes public awareness posters in public places is called the mass approach.

The mass approach in communication refers to the dissemination of information to a large audience through various mediums, such as posters, television, radio, and social media. It is typically used for public awareness campaigns or to promote a message to the general population.

The goal of this approach is to reach as many people as possible, often with a focus on important social, health, or safety issues. By using mass communication tools, governments and organisations can efficiently spread vital information to create awareness, educate, and encourage positive behaviour among the public.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 35-year- old man who presents with scant, foul-smelling blood-stained discharge, associated hearing loss, and a persistent fever that does not subside?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of chronic ear discharge (likely due to cholesteatoma in an atticoantral type of CSOM) followed by a high, swinging "picket-fence" fever are characteristic of lateral sinus thrombophlebitis. This is a serious intracranial complication of ear infection where the infection spreads to the sigmoid or transverse dural sinuses. Hearing loss is common in CSOM. Meningitis (Option A) would present with severe neck stiffness and photophobia. A brain abscess (Option C) typically presents with signs of raised intracranial pressure and focal neurological deficits. An extradural abscess (Option D) is often asymptomatic or presents with a persistent deep-seated headache. The "foul-smelling blood-mixed discharge" indicates local tissue destruction. The characteristic "swinging" nature of the fever, caused by the periodic release of bacteria into the bloodstream from the thrombus, is the hallmark of lateral sinus involvement. Urgent surgical intervention and IV antibiotics are necessary
questions.learning: The symptoms of chronic ear discharge (likely due to cholesteatoma in an atticoantral type of CSOM) followed by a high, swinging "picket-fence" fever are characteristic of lateral sinus thrombophlebitis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman has cramps in her legs. What will you suggest her to relieve the pain?
options: Extend knee and plantar flex foot
Flex knee and plantar flex foot
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extend knee and dorsiflex foot

Extension at the knee joint and dorsiflexion at the ankle joint helps in stretching the calf muscles which relieves the pain.

Leg cramps are minor ailments during pregnancy mostly due to a deficiency of diffusible serum calcium or elevation of serum phosphorus. Management includes massaging the leg, stretching exercises, application of local heat, and supplementation of vitamin B1 and calcium.
questions.learning: Extend knee and dorsiflex foot Extension at the knee joint and dorsiflexion at the ankle joint helps in stretching the calf muscles which relieves the pain.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with a history of a fall presents to the emergency department and undergoes a CT scan of the brain (shown below). What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: The CT scan shows a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection along the cerebral convexity, consistent with a subdural hematoma (SDH), typically caused by rupture of bridging veins following trauma. In this case, the most appropriate treatment depends on the underlying cause and severity. Here, the question implies conservative management, likely in a patient with coagulopathy (e.g., on anticoagulants). Therefore, Vitamin K is administered to reverse anticoagulation and promote clotting, helping to control further bleeding. Key concept: 1. Small or stable SDH → conservative management 2. Correct coagulopathy → Vitamin K (if warfarin-related) Why other options are incorrect: (A) Alteplase & (B) Reteplase: Thrombolytic drugs; would worsen intracranial bleeding (D) Surgery: Indicated only in large hematoma or significant mass effect, not in stable cases Thus, in a stable SDH with bleeding tendency, Vitamin K is the appropriate treatment
questions.learning: The CT scan shows a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection along the cerebral convexity, consistent with a subdural hematoma (SDH), typically caused by rupture of bridging veins following trauma.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-week-old infant presents with a cough and sore throat. The mother reports that the infant develops a paroxysm of cough followed by apnea. The total leucocyte count is >50,000 cells/μL. Which of the following drugs will you prescribe for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Azithromycin

The given clinical scenario of paroxysm of cough, apnea, and leukocytosis (>50,000 cells/μL) in a neonate is suggestive of pertussis. Azithromycin is the recommended drug of choice for the treatment of pertussis in neonates (< 1 month of age).

Macrolides are recommended for the treatment of pertussis. Azithromycin is the drug of choice in all age groups, for treatment or postexposure prophylaxis. Post-exposure prophylaxis is given to household close contacts and high-risk contacts (infants, immunocompromised, pregnancy).

Other options:

Option B: Amoxicillin is not used for the treatment of pertussis due to its inefficiency in the nasopharynx.

Option C: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (cotrimoxazole) is recommended as an alternative for infants >2 months old and children who are allergic to macrolides.

Option D: Clarithromycin is an alternative drug that can be used in infants aged >2 months. In children less than 2 months of age, it is contraindicated due to the risk of kernicterus.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Inhalational agent of choice for cardiac patients is______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Isoflurane

The inhalational agent of choice for cardiac patients is Isoflurane as the cardiac output is best preserved by it.

Isoflurane has myocardial protective properties, limiting infarct size (ischaemic preconditioning).

Isoflurane has also been implicated in the coronary steal phenomenon as it dilates coronary arteries. But, as long as coronary perfusion pressure is maintained, this phenomenon does not occur.

Other Options :

* Halothane is associated with a higher incidence of cardiac dysrhythmias and myocardial depression.

* Desflurane is a sympathomimetic. This is the use-limiting disadvantage of desflurane.

* Sevoflurane can decrease sympathetic nervous activity.

Note: There is a controversy between Desflurane and Isoflurane as to which is the most preferred one in cardiac patients. The standard references do not mention if desflurane is more preferred. So isoflurane remains the answer.
questions.learning: Isoflurane — The inhalational agent of choice for cardiac patients is Isoflurane as the cardiac output is best preserved by it. Isoflurane has myocardial protective properties, limiting infarct size (ischaemic preconditioning).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the location of the Bartholin cyst?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior ⅓ of the vulva

Bartholin cysts are located in the posterior 1/3 of the vulva.

The Bartholin glands are known as the greater vestibular glands in females. These glands are located in the posterior part of the vestibule and open through a duct into the vaginal orifice at approximately 5 and 7 o’clock positions. They secrete mucus during sexual arousal for lubrication. They are the homologs of the male bulbourethral or Cowper glands.

Bartholin cyst is caused by obstruction of the duct due to infection, trauma, mucus changes, and congenitally narrowed ducts. If the cyst gets infected, it leads to the formation of a Bartholin abscess. Escherichia coli is the most common causative agent, however, other gram-positive and gram-negative organisms can also cause the same.

Clinical features:

* If the size is big, it might cause abdominal and vaginal discomfort with dyspareunia.

* A vulval cleft of 'S' shape is usually noted on inspection.

* It is fluctuant swelling and transillumination can be positive as the fluid collected is generally clear.

Treatment:

* Analgesics for pain

* Antibiotic for combating infections.

* Specific treatment:

* Drainage under anesthesia: Generally conservative method, chances of re-infection and formation of granulation tissue can happen.

* Marsupialization Complete excision of sac and cyst along with drainage of the substance. The edges are also clearly approximated. This is the ideal management.  The advantages of marsupialization over other methods include:

* Simple procedure

* Can be done even under local anesthesia.

* Shorter hospital stay (24 hours).

* The postoperative complication is almost nil.

* Gland function (moisture) remains intact.

* Incision and drainage with word catheter placement: A deflated word catheter is used to tuck the vagina here and prevent it from damage that can happen during movement of the perineum and thus avert re-infection and granulation tissue formation. Alternatively, a 14 F foley catheter can also be used.

* Bartholinectomy: This is a very invasive surgery and carries a greater morbidity profile. This is also associated with loss of lubricant function.

Notes:

In any woman above the age of forty with recurrent Bartholin cyst, a suspicion of Bartholin gland cancer should arise and the cyst wall should be sent for biopsy.
questions.learning: Posterior ⅓ of the vulva Bartholin cysts are located in the posterior 1/3 of the vulva. The Bartholin glands are known as the greater vestibular glands in females.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The characteristic appearance of oesophagus on barium swallow, as shown in the image below, is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diffuse esophageal spasm

The corkscrew appearance of the esophagus is seen in diffuse esophageal spasm.

* Diffuse/distal esophageal spasm (DES) is a motility disorder of the esophagus.

* On barium swallow, DES may appear as a corkscrew or rosary bead esophagus, but this is uncommon.

* Manometry is the gold-standard diagnostic test.

Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterised by the absence of esophageal peristalsis and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) in response to swallowing.

In achalasia single contrast esophagogram shows, dilatation of the esophagus with a bird beak deformity near the gastroesophageal junction.

In esophageal carcinoma barium study will show irregular narrowing, mucosal destruction and shouldered margins.

Double-contrast esophagram shows a large, flat ulceration (arrow) in the distal esophagus in a patient with CMV esophagitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is evaluated and found to have a refractive error of −2 diopters in the right eye and +1 diopter in the left eye. The fundus examination and visual acuity are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: Anisometropia is defined as a significant difference in refractive power between the two eyes, regardless of whether the refractive error is myopia, hyperopia, or astigmatism. Clinically, a difference of ≥2 diopters (commonly ≥2–2.5 D) between the eyes is considered significant. In this child, the right eye has myopia (−2 D) and the left eye has hyperopia (+1 D). The interocular difference is 3 diopters, which clearly fulfills the diagnostic criteria for anisometropia. While the child does have myopia (Option A) in one eye and hyperopia (Option B) in the other, these terms describe individual refractive errors and do not explain the bilateral imbalance. Amblyopia (Option D) is a possible complication of untreated anisometropia due to unequal visual input to the brain, but it is not the diagnosis here, especially since the child currently has normal visual acuity and fundus findings. Therefore, the most accurate and comprehensive diagnosis explaining the refractive discrepancy is anisometropia
questions.learning: Anisometropia is defined as a significant difference in refractive power between the two eyes, regardless of whether the refractive error is myopia, hyperopia, or astigmatism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which type of mutation results in the reversal to wild type of phenotype when the mutant gene is suppressed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mutations in tRNA

Mutations in tRNA are known to suppress the mutant gene and cause reversal to wild phenotype. Such mutations are called suppressor mutations.

Suppressor mutations are secondary mutations that alter the phenotypes caused by an existing mutation. This is not to be confused with reversion mutations in which the original mutation has been lost. Instead, suppressor mutations return the phenotype caused by the original mutation to a more wild-type phenotype despite the presence of the original mutation. The suppressor mutation’s effect on the phenotype can vary from partial restoration to full restoration of the wild-type phenotype.

In prokaryotic and lower eukaryotic organisms, abnormally functioning tRNA molecules have been discovered that are themselves the results of mutations. Some of these abnormal tRNA molecules are capable of binding to and decoding altered codons, thereby suppressing the effects of mutations in the structural genes.

These suppressor tRNA molecules, usually formed as a result of alterations in their anticodon regions, are capable of suppressing certain missense mutations, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations. An example of suppressor mutation is illustrated below.

A primary mutation occurs changing the original codon sequence from UGG (Trp) to UAG (Stop). A secondary mutation occurs in the gene for a glutamine tRNA leading to the anticodon switch from a GUC to AUC. This mutant tRNA can recognize the UAG stop codon and insert glutamine in place of the stop, allowing translation to continue past the stop and suppressing the original mutation.

In the laboratory context, such suppressor tRNAs, coupled with mutated variants of aminoacyl- tRNA synthetases, can be utilized to incorporate unnatural amino acids into defined locations within altered genes that carry engineered nonsense mutations. The resulting labeled proteins can be used for in vivo and in vitro cross-linking and biophysical studies.
questions.learning: Mutations in tRNA Mutations in tRNA are known to suppress the mutant gene and cause reversal to wild phenotype. Such mutations are called suppressor mutations.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient comes with complaints of progressive weakness as the day progresses. He is found to have antibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Which is the most common ocular finding in this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ptosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of myasthenia gravis and ptosis is the most common ocular feature of the disease.

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction most commonly caused by anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. The disorder is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles where the weakness increases during repeated use and may improve following rest.

Ptosis and diplopia are common initial complaints due to early involvement of the lids and extraocular muscles (EOMs). Of them, Ptosis is a more common manifestation than diplopia. Ptosis in myasthenia gravis is insidious, bilateral, and frequently asymmetrical.

Investigations of myasthenia gravis include:

1. Ice pack test -This tests for a transient improvement of the ptotic eyelid on placing an ice pack for 2 minutes, as  the cold inhibits the breakdown of acetylcholine by acetylcholinesterase.
2. Tensilon (Edrophonium) test - This tests for a transient improvement in the weakness on administration of a short-acting anticholinesterase such as edrophonium.
3. Antibody testing - for Acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies, MuSK protein antibodies helps support a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a part of a Primary Health Centre?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Physiotherapist

A Primary Health Centre (PHC) is the first point of contact between the community and a medical officer in the public health system. As per the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS), the core PHC staff include a Medical Officer, Pharmacist, and Laboratory Technician. A Physiotherapist is not a routine member of the PHC team.

A Physiotherapist is generally posted at higher-level health facilities such as Community Health Centres (CHCs), Sub-District Hospitals, or District Hospitals, not at a standard PHC.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pharmacist: Essential PHC staff responsible for dispensing medicines.
• B. Laboratory Technician: Performs basic laboratory investigations at the PHC.
• C. Medical Officer: In-charge of the PHC and provides clinical and public health services.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with thalassemia has a history of multiple blood transfusions, iron overload, and cardiac arrhythmia. She has now come for blood transfusion and during the process, complains of backache and looks very anxious. What would you do next?
options: Continue the transfusion but do an ECG
Stop the transfusion. Wait for patient to become normal and then start it again
Do clerical check and get ECG
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stop the blood transfusion

The patient is being transfused blood and has complaints of backache, this is suggestive of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.

The first step is to stop transfusion immediately and then collect blood samples for testing.

Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions typically occur within the first 24 hours following a blood transfusion, primarily due to ABO incompatibility.

It presents with symptoms such as hypotension, tachypnea, tachycardia, fever (1-2°C increase in temperature), chills, chest and back pain, hemoglobinuria, and hemoglobinemia. In severe cases, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), acute renal failure, shock, and death can occur.

Management of immune-mediated acute hemolytic transfusion reactions is to provide supportive care, administer vigorous hydration with isotonic saline and use diuretics to maintain urine output.
questions.learning: Stop the blood transfusion — The patient is being transfused blood and has complaints of backache, this is suggestive of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the defect in the given image:
questions.explanation: The provided clinical image depicts a severe form of spina bifida known as rachischisis or myeloschisis, which is a type of open neural tube defect. This condition occurs due to the failure of the neural tube and covering ectoderm to close properly, leaving neural tissue exposed to the environment without any skin or meningeal covering. In contrast, occult spina bifida (Option C) is a closed defect where the vertebral arch fails to fuse, but the skin remains intact, often marked only by a tuft of hair or a dimple. A meningoencephalocele (Option B) involves a sac-like protrusion of both meninges and brain tissue through a skull defect. An encephalocele (Option D) specifically refers to a protrusion of brain tissue through a cranial opening. Because the image shows a contiguous spinal defect with exposed neural elements, it is definitively classified as an open neural tube defect

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about the condition shown in the image below?
options: It can be seen on the dorsal and volar aspect of wrist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Less chances of recurrence

Image A shows a ganglion cyst of the wrist and image B shows the surgical excision of the cyst. Image B shows a swelling that is cystic, translucent, and filled with a fluid which is suggestive of a ganglion cyst. It has high rates of recurrence and thus , option A is false.

Ganglion cyst:

* It arises from the leakage of synovial fluid from a joint or tendon sheath and thus contains a glary, viscous fluid.

* It can appear anywhere in the wrist but the most common area is the dorsal surface of the scapholunate ligament.

* Usually appears as a painless, well-defined, cystic, transillumination positive, and non-tender swelling. If there is an impingement on a nearby nerve or structure it can cause pain.

* It disappears spontaneously, but the aspiration of the swelling or operative removal can be done for reassurance or when there is pressure on the nerve.

* If the swelling is near the radial artery or nerves then removal is done under ultrasound guidance.

* Even if treatment is done, the rates of recurrence are high.

Note:

A lipoma can be a differential here but it is not a transilluminant swelling and has a positive slip sign, i.e when palpated, the edge of the swelling slips under the finger.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following steps of a planning cycle: 1. Assigning priorities among the problems 2. Evaluation 3. Selecting best programme 4. Operating the programme Which among the following is the correct sequence of steps?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 → 3 → 4 → 2

Health planning is a systematic process of identifying health problems, setting priorities, selecting the best interventions, implementing them, and evaluating outcomes. The planning cycle ensures that health programs are evidence-based, efficient, and continuously improved.

The correct sequence of the given steps is: 1 → 3 → 4 → 2

• 1. Assigning priorities among the problems ✓

• After identifying health problems, priorities are set based on magnitude, severity, feasibility, and available resources.

• 3. Selecting best programme ✓

• Alternative strategies are evaluated, and the most appropriate intervention/programme is selected.

• 4. Operating the programme ✓

• The selected programme is implemented.

• 2. Evaluation ✓

• The programme is monitored and evaluated to determine whether the objectives have been achieved and to guide future planning.
questions.learning: 1 → 3 → 4 → 2 Health planning is a systematic process of identifying health problems, setting priorities, selecting the best interventions, implementing them, and evaluating outcomes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the statements below accurately describes p53?
options: It increases telomere length in the liver.
It is stable by preventing genome mutation.
It retains the telomerase enzyme in the nucleus
questions.explanation: The p53 protein is widely known as the "guardian of the genome." Its primary function is to maintain cellular and genetic stability by preventing genome mutation. When DNA damage is detected, p53 halts the cell cycle at the G1/S checkpoint to allow for repair. If the damage is too severe, p53 triggers apoptosis (programmed cell death) to prevent the propagation of mutated cells. Loss or mutation of the TP53 gene is found in more than 50% of all human cancers. Options A and D refer to the function of telomerase, which maintains the ends of chromosomes. Option B is incorrect as p53 is a transcription factor that regulates gene expression rather than a polymerase that synthesizes RNA directly. By acting as a critical tumor suppressor, p53 ensures that cells with damaged DNA do not divide. Understanding the p53 pathway is fundamental to modern oncology and the study of cellular responses to stress and carcinogens
questions.learning: The p53 protein is widely known as the "guardian of the genome." Its primary function is to maintain cellular and genetic stability by preventing genome mutation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old asymptomatic woman on USG shows a unilocular cyst in the ovary of 6 cm with negative serology. Treatment involves:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Follow-up after 1-2 cycles of OCPs

Follow up after 1-2 cycles of oral combined pills (conservative management) is the best treatment modality in the given scenario as it is most likely to be a functional cyst.

For conservative management of ovarian cysts, the following criteria should usually be met:

* Asymptomatic

* Unilocular

* Unilateral

* No solid areas

* Normal CA 125

* Less than 7cm

* Ultrasound re-examination after 3-6 months (no signs of increase in size or malignancy)

Features of a functional cyst:

* Related to temporary hormonal disorders

* Benign and rarely become complicated

* Usually 6-8cm in diameter

* Usually asymptomatic

* Unilocular

* Contains clear fluid, unless haemorrhage occurs

* Lining epithelium corresponds to the functional epithelium of the unit from which they arise

* Spontaneous regression occurs within 4-6 months

Treatment of functional cysts:

* Usually conservative; spontaneous regression occurs after 4-6months.

* Oral combined pills to hasten the regression of cyst.

* Laparotomy for tumours more than 7 cm to prevent complications or malignant transformation.
questions.learning: Follow-up after 1-2 cycles of OCPs Follow up after 1-2 cycles of oral combined pills (conservative management) is the best treatment modality in the given scenario as it is most likely to be a functional cyst.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A student had his jaw locked while yawning. Which of the following muscles is attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lateral pterygoid

The muscle that is attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint is the lateral pterygoid.

Lateral pterygoid muscle:

• Origin - Upper head arises from the infratemporal surface and infratemporal crest of the greater wing of the sphenoid bone. The lower head arises from the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate.
• Insertion - It is inserted into the pterygoid fovea, the capsule of the temporomandibular joint, and the articular disc.

The action of lateral pterygoid muscle is depression, protrusion, and side-to-side movement of the jaw.

questions.text: All of the following are true regarding the urban primary health center staff except _____.

An urban primary health center will be staffed with two doctors (one regular and one on a part-time basis): 3 staff nurses, 1 pharmacist, 1 lab technician, 1 lady health visitor, and 4–5 ANMs (depending upon the population covered.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following structures is responsible for balance and hearing?
questions.explanation: The inner ear, also known as the labyrinth, houses the sensory organs for two distinct special senses. The vestibule (Option C) is the central part of the bony labyrinth and acts as a common chamber. It contains the utricle and saccule, which detect linear balance, and it communicates directly with the semicircular canals (Option A), which detect angular balance. The vestibule also connects to the cochlea (Option B), the structure responsible for hearing. While the cochlea is solely for hearing and the canals are solely for balance, the vestibule is the anatomical region associated with the housing of components for both functions. The Organ of Corti (Option D) is the specific sensory neuroepithelium for hearing located within the cochlea. Therefore, in a general anatomical context, the vestibule is the most appropriate collective answer for the site of both these senses. Damage to the labyrinth often causes concurrent vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss
questions.learning: The inner ear, also known as the labyrinth, houses the sensory organs for two distinct special senses. The vestibule (Option C) is the central part of the bony labyrinth and acts as a common chamber.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What nerve fibers are responsible for the transmission of proprioception?
questions.explanation: The Erlanger-Gasser classification categorizes nerve fibers based on their diameter and conduction velocity. Proprioception—the sense of self-movement and body position—is transmitted by the largest and fastest myelinated fibers, categorized as A alpha fibers (or Group Ia/Ib). These fibers carry signals from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs to the central nervous system with speeds up to 120 m/s. A beta fibers (Option B) are slightly smaller and slower, primarily responsible for carrying sensations of touch, pressure, and vibration. A gamma fibers (Option C) are motor fibers that innervate the contractile ends of muscle spindles to regulate their sensitivity. A delta fibers (Option D) are thin, myelinated fibers that transmit "fast" pain and cold temperature. C fibers (not listed) are unmyelinated and carry "slow" burning pain and warmth. High-speed proprioceptive feedback is essential for maintaining balance, coordinating complex motor tasks, and protecting joints from overextension during movement

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old primigravida at 18 weeks of gestation presents for her antenatal check-up. Her random plasma glucose level was 243 mg/dL and thus she was asked to undergo further tests. The fasting blood glucose levels were 146mg/dL and HbA1c was 7.6%. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
options: Maturity onset Diabetes of the young
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Overt diabetes

A fasting blood sugar > 126 mg/dL , random blood sugar > 200mg/dL and HbA1c> 6.5% is suggestive of overt diabetes or pregestational diabetes.

The following are the lab results that would be suggestive of overt diabetes in a mother.

* Fasting blood sugar at least 126 mg/dL

* A random blood sugar of at least 200 mg/dL

* HbA1c of at least 6.5%

Cardiac anomalies are most commonly seen in the fetuses of overt-diabetic mothers. Musculoskeletal, urogenital, and CNS anomalies are also seen,

Congenital malformations occur at a higher rate, in overt diabetes than in gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). This is because GDM manifests in the second trimester and by then organogenesis would be complete.

Threshold values for gestational diabetes (75 g OGTT):

Plasma glucose
Glucose concentration threshold

Fasting
92 mg/dl

1 hr OGTT
180 mg/dl

2 hr OGTT
153 mg/dl

According to WHO and ADA guidelines, the one-step approach omits the screening test and simplifies diagnostic testing for gestational diabetes mellitus by performing only a 75-gram, two-hour oral GTT.

Diagnostic criteria or cut-off values with a 75 g OGTT are as follows:

* Fasting: 92 mg/dl

* 1 hour: 180 mg/dl

* 2 hours: 153 mg/dl

Two-step approach :

* The first step (screening) is a 50-gram one-hour glucose challenge test (GCT) at 24-28 weeks of gestation who are not previously diagnosed with diabetes.

* If the plasma glucose level measured 1 h after the load is ≥130, a 100-gram, three-hour oral glucose tolerance test (GTT) is done, which is the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus.

At least 2 of the following 4 values should be raised for a diagnosis to be made:

* Fasting: 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L)

* 1 h: 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L)

* 2 h: 155 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L)

* 3 h: 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L)

Other options:

Option A: MODY or maturity-onset diabetes of the young is a monogenic form of diabetes that occurs < 25 years. There is impaired insulin secretion, but no antibodies.

Option D: LADA  is a form of diabetes mellitus affecting lean and thin adults less than 50 years with a positive family history. It is insulin-dependent and associated with autoantibodies.

Pearl PF0141: Types of Diabetes mellitus

I. Type 1 diabetes: Beta cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency

* Immune-mediated

* Idiopathic

II. Type 2 diabetes: Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency

III. Other specific types of diabetes

* Genetic defects of beta cell development or function

* MODY – Maturity Onset Diabetes of Young

* Genetic defects in insulin action

* Type A insulin resistance

* Leprechaunism

* Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome Lipodystrophy syndromes

* Diseases of the exocrine pancreas

* Pancreatitis

* Neoplasia

* Cystic fibrosis

* Hemochromatosis

* Endocrinopathies

* Acromegaly

* Cushing’s syndrome

* Glucagonoma

* Pheochromocytoma

* Hyperthyroidism

* Infections

* Congenital rubella

* Cytomegalovirus

* Coxsackievirus

* Uncommon forms of immune-mediated diabetes

* “Stiff-person” syndrome

* Anti-insulin receptor antibodies

* Genetic syndromes sometimes associated with diabetes

* Wolfram’s syndrome

* Down’s syndrome, Klinefelter’s syndrome, Turner’s syndrome

IV. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the type of necrosis seen in the vessel wall of a patient with polyarteritis nodosa?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fibrinoid necrosis

Immune reactions involving blood vessels, as seen in the case of polyarteritis nodosa, usually show fibrinoid necrosis. Fibrinoid means fibrin-like.

In some immune disorders, the antigen-antibody complexes get deposited in the blood vessels. These complexes result in complement activation (type III hypersensitivity) leading to cell injury. This leads to leakage of fibrin out of the blood vessel, giving a pinkish appearance around the blood vessels.

Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in the following conditions:

• SLE
• Libman-sacks endocarditis
• Arthus reaction
• Serum sickness
• Polyarteritis nodosa
• Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
• Malignant hypertension
questions.learning: Fibrinoid necrosis Immune reactions involving blood vessels, as seen in the case of polyarteritis nodosa, usually show fibrinoid necrosis. In some immune disorders, the antigen-antibody complexes get deposited in the blood vessels.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The production of which of the following hormones is increased in obesity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Insulin

Insulin levels are increased in obesity. It stimulates the synthesis of fatty acids and TAG and decreases the rate of lipolysis. Thyroxine, growth hormone, and adiponectin have lipolytic effects, hence their levels are reduced in obesity.

Hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance are consistent features of obesity. Insulin resistance is more strongly linked to intra-abdominal fat than to fat in other areas.

Adiponectin (Option D) is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that is produced by adipocytes. It performs vital functions that are reduced in obesity - like, increasing insulin sensitivity and the inhibition of gluconeogenic enzymes. It also enhances fatty acid oxidation.

Insulin resistance in obesity occurs as a result of the following:

• Insulin receptor downregulation
• Increased FFA (free fatty acids) and capable of impairing insulin action
• Intracellular lipid accumulation
• Circulating peptides produced by adipocytes such as TNF-α, IL-6, RBP4, and resistin modify insulin action.
questions.learning: Insulin Insulin levels are increased in obesity. It stimulates the synthesis of fatty acids and TAG and decreases the rate of lipolysis.

questions.text: If a simple muscle twitch has a latent period of 10 milliseconds, a contraction period of 40 milliseconds, and a relaxation period of 50 milliseconds, what is the tetanizing frequency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 25HZ

Tetanizing frequency = frequency at which next stimulus arrives before relaxation completes → sustained contraction (tetanus).

• Latent period = 10 ms
• Contraction period = 40 ms
• Relaxation period = 50 ms
• 1 / contraction period = 1 / 40 ms = 1 / 0.040 s = 25 Hz ✔
• The latent period (10 ms) and relaxation period (50 ms) are pure distractor data here

| Phase | Duration | Event

| ----- | -------- | -----

| Latent | 10 ms | Excitation–contraction coupling

| Contraction | 40 ms | Cross-bridge cycling

| Relaxation | 50 ms | Ca²⁺ reuptake

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency can lead to lactic acidosis?
questions.explanation: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) serves as an essential cofactor for the enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase. This enzyme is responsible for converting pyruvate into acetyl-CoA to enter the Krebs cycle. In states of thiamine deficiency, this conversion is blocked, causing pyruvate to accumulate and shunt toward the production of lactate. This metabolic shift results in lactic acidosis, which is commonly seen in severe thiamine deficiency syndromes like beriberi and Wernicke's encephalopathy. Riboflavin (Option B) is involved in the electron transport chain but its deficiency does not typically drive lactic acid production. Niacin (Option C) is a precursor for NAD, and its deficiency leads to pellagra. Biotin (Option D) is a cofactor for carboxylases; while its absence causes metabolic issues, it is not the primary cause of lactic acidosis. Thus, thiamine is the specific vitamin required to prevent the toxic buildup of lactate
questions.learning: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) serves as an essential cofactor for the enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase. This enzyme is responsible for converting pyruvate into acetyl-CoA to enter the Krebs cycle.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Marshall’s triad of abrasion, bruise & punctate laceration is seen in which phase of bomb blast injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secondary

Marshall’s triad (abrasion, bruise, punctate lacerations).

Characteristic of secondary blast injury --> caused by flying debris and shrapnel.

• Secondary blast injury:

• Due to projectiles (glass, metal, fragments)
• Produces multiple external injuries:

• Abrasions
• Contusions (bruises)
• Punctate lacerations (small penetrating wounds)

Blast injury classification:

• Primary: Pressure wave → affects air-filled organs (lungs, ear, bowel)
• Secondary: Shrapnel → Marshall’s triad
• Tertiary: Body thrown → blunt trauma, fractures
• Quaternary: Burns, inhalational injuries, toxins

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with an intense urge to urinate but is unable to void. He has a history of perineal trauma, and examination reveals blood at the external urethral meatus. Which anatomical structure is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: In a young male with a history of perineal trauma (such as a straddle injury), the bulbar urethra is the most commonly injured segment of the anterior urethra. The classic clinical presentation includes an inability to void despite a full bladder and the presence of blood at the external urethral meatus. Regarding the distractors, a posterior urethral valve (Option B) is a congenital anomaly found in male infants, not healthy young adults. Intraperitoneal bladder rupture (Option C) occurs during blunt abdominal trauma and presents with peritonitis and urinary ascites rather than meatal blood. The membranous urethra (Option D) is part of the posterior urethra and is typically injured during pelvic fractures rather than isolated perineal trauma. Therefore, based on the mechanism of injury (perineal) and meatal bleeding, the bulbar urethra is the anatomical site of damage
questions.learning: In a young male with a history of perineal trauma (such as a straddle injury), the bulbar urethra is the most commonly injured segment of the anterior urethra.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old female presented with dyspnea and chest pain. Which of the following proves that she has aortic stenosis rather than aortic regurgitation?
options: Increase in myocardial oxygen consumption is seen with increased pressure work than volume
Aortic stenosis causes reduced pressure at the aortic valve
Workload has nothing to do with myocardial oxygen consumption
Increased pressure - Increase in preload more than afterload
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase in myocardial oxygen consumption is seen with increased pressure work than volume

Valvular diseases affect the heart in two major ways:

| Type | Example | Cardiac Work

| ---- | ------- | ------------

| Pressure overload | Aortic stenosis | Pressure work

| Volume overload | Aortic regurgitation | Volume work

Pressure overload requires more myocardial oxygen consumption (MVO₂).

Thus, this helps differentiate AS from AR.

Aortic stenosis causes a pressure overload, requiring the left ventricle to generate high systolic pressures.

Myocardial oxygen consumption correlates more with pressure work than volume work, favoring a diagnosis of aortic stenosis.

In contrast, aortic regurgitation produces volume overload with relatively lower pressure work.

Thus, increased oxygen demand due to pressure overload distinguishes aortic stenosis.

B) Aortic stenosis causes reduced pressure at the aortic valve

Incorrect.

In AS: LV pressure increases, creating a pressure gradient across the valve.

C) Workload has nothing to do with oxygen consumption

Myocardial oxygen consumption is directly related to cardiac workload.

D) Increased pressure → increase in preload more than afterload

Pressure overload mainly increases afterload, not preload.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child went to an ophthalmologist and is found to have a power of -1 D spherical and -2 D cylindrical at 180 degrees. What kind of astigmatism does the child have?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. With the rule astigmatism

The child with a power of -1 D spherical and -2 D cylindrical at 180 degrees has with the rule astigmatism, as the vertical meridian is greater and more curved than the horizontal meridian.
Step 1 : - 1 D spherical would mean a power of -1 on vertical and horizontal axes.

| (-1)

--------|------- (-1)

Step 2 : - 2 D cylindrical at 180 degrees, would mean a power of -2 D at 90 degrees (perpendicular to 180).

| (-1 - 2 = -3)

--------|------- (-1)

Hence, as the vertical meridian (-3D) is greater than horizontal meridian (-1D), this would be with the rule astigmatism.
Astigmatism refers to the condition where there is different refractory power in both the principal meridians of the eye. Astigmatism is classified into two broad varieties - regular and irregular astigmatism.

• Regular astigmatism: there are two principal meridians.

• With the rule -  principal meridians are vertical and horizontal; both meridians at 90°; and the vertical meridian is more curved than horizontal.
• Against the rule (Option C) -  principal meridians are vertical and horizontal; both meridians at 90°; and the horizontal meridian is more curved than vertical.
• Oblique - the principal meridians are not vertical and horizontal, but they are at 90° to each other; e.g., at 45° and 135°.
• Bi-oblique -  the two principal meridians are not vertical and horizontal, and they are not at 90° each other; e.g., at 40° and 100°.

• Irregular astigmatism: there are multiple meridians.

Clinical presentation of astigmatism include asthenopia (tiredness of eyes relieved by closing the eyes), blurred vision and defective vision, elongation of objects, keeping reading material closer, and half closure of the lid.
Tilted or oval optic disc is seen on ophthalmoscopy. Retinoscopy shows different power on the two meridians. Other investigations include keratometry, astigmatic fan test, and Jackson’s cross-cylinder test.

Prescription in astigmatism: There are 3 components.

1) Power of the spherical component: Convex (+) or concave (-) dioptre sphere (DS)

2) Power of the cylinder: Convex (+) or concave (-) dioptre cylinder (DC)

3) Axis (orientation) of the cylinder

Other options :

Option A : In simple astigmatism, one of the meridia focuses on the retina. The other meridian focuses either in front of the retina (simple myopic) or behind the retina (simple hyperopic). Example, -1.00 DC × 180 degree.

Option D : Mixed astigmatism: Light rays in one meridian are focused in front of the retina and those in the other meridian are focused behind the retina. Example, -1DS with +2DC at 180 degree.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with fluctuating muscle weakness predominantly involving speech and swallowing. Repetitive nerve stimulation demonstrates a decremental response. Serological testing is negative for acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies. Which other antibody is most likely responsible for her symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms—fluctuating weakness in speech and swallowing (bulbar symptoms) and a decremental response on nerve stimulation—are typical of Myasthenia Gravis. In patients who are seronegative for AChR antibodies, the Anti-MuSK (Muscle-Specific Kinase) antibody is the most likely culprit. MuSK is essential for clustering AChRs at the neuromuscular junction; its inhibition disrupts signal transmission. Regarding the distractors, Anti-dsDNA (Option A) is a marker for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Anti-TPO (Option C) is associated with autoimmune thyroiditis. Anti-Ro (Option D) is found in Sjogren's syndrome. Because MuSK-positive patients often present with severe bulbar involvement and are negative for the standard AChR test, this antibody specifically matches the patient's clinical and laboratory profile
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms—fluctuating weakness in speech and swallowing (bulbar symptoms) and a decremental response on nerve stimulation—are typical of Myasthenia Gravis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome is defined as failure to achieve remission after _________ weeks when on a daily corticosteroid therapy regimen.
questions.explanation: The definition of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) varies slightly between pediatric and adult guidelines, but for clinical examinations based on standard pediatric protocols, it is generally defined as the failure to achieve complete remission (reduction of proteinuria to trace or negative levels) after a minimum of 4 to 6 weeks of daily corticosteroid therapy. Specifically, many international groups define resistance at 4 weeks, while some extend the evaluation to 6 weeks to ensure the patient is truly unresponsive before switching to more toxic second-line agents like calcineurin inhibitors or cyclophosphamide. Options B, C, and D do not represent the standard diagnostic window. Most children with minimal change disease (the most common cause) are "steroid-sensitive" and show response within the first 2 weeks. Recognizing steroid resistance is a critical clinical step because it often correlates with a higher risk of progressing to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and eventual chronic kidney disease

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with progressively unsteady gait since age 2, along with recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Examination reveals telangiectatic vessels over the conjunctivae and skin. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is markedly elevated, and the child shows an exaggerated tissue reaction following a diagnostic chest X-ray. A defect in which DNA repair pathway is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. dsDNA break repair

• This presentation is classic for Ataxia telangiectasia, caused by mutation of the ATM gene, a key sensor and signaling kinase in the homologous recombination pathway that repairs double-strand DNA breaks.
• Because ionizing radiation predominantly causes double-strand breaks, defective homologous recombination explains the child's exaggerated, radiosensitive reaction to a routine chest X-ray, along with the progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, recurrent sinopulmonary infections (from combined immunodeficiency), and elevated alpha-fetoprotein that together characterize this disorder.
• A. Nucleotide excision repair defects instead cause disorders of UV-induced bulky adduct/pyrimidine dimer repair (xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome), presenting with photosensitivity rather than radiosensitivity or ataxia.
• B. Base excision repair defects cause MUTYH-associated polyposis (colorectal polyps/cancer), and C. mismatch repair defects cause HNPCC with microsatellite instability — neither fits this neurological and immunological picture.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 54-year-old farmer from Ohio who presents with a chronic cough, a chest X-ray showing a mass lesion with hilar lymphadenopathy, and biopsy findings (lactophenol cotton blue stain) demonstrating multiple yeast forms within macrophages?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is supported by both geographic exposure and microscopic findings. Ohio lies in the Ohio–Mississippi River Valley, an endemic area for histoplasmosis, caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. The characteristic histopathological feature is the presence of small yeast forms clustered within macrophages, reflecting the organism’s intracellular nature. Other options are less likely: coccidioidomycosis occurs in the Southwestern United States and shows large spherules with endospores; cryptococcosis demonstrates encapsulated yeasts and has no specific association with Ohio farmers; blastomycosis shows large yeasts with broad-based budding. Exposure to soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings is a common risk factor for histoplasmosis. Clinically, it may mimic lung cancer or tuberculosis by presenting as a lung mass with hilar lymphadenopathy. Hence, the combination of Ohio exposure and yeasts within macrophages is pathognomonic for histoplasmosis
questions.learning: The diagnosis is supported by both geographic exposure and microscopic findings. Ohio lies in the Ohio–Mississippi River Valley, an endemic area for histoplasmosis, caused by Histoplasma capsulatum.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl presents with cyclical lower abdominal pain and has not yet attained menarche. On pelvic examination, a hypogastric mass along with a bluish bulge is noted. What is the most likely underlying cause of this presentation?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of primary amenorrhea (no menarche) and cyclic abdominal pain in an adolescent girl is highly suggestive of an outflow tract obstruction. The findings of a hypogastric lump (hematometra) and a bluish swelling at the introitus are characteristic of an imperforate hymen. The blue color results from the dark, old blood trapped behind the hymenal membrane (hematocolpos) reflecting through it. A transverse vaginal septum (Option B) can also cause primary amenorrhea and cyclic pain but would not show the distinct bulging bluish membrane at the vulva. Bartholin cyst (Option A) presents as a vulvar mass but not with amenorrhea. Endometrioma (Option D) is common in older women and would not explain primary amenorrhea. Treatment involves a simple cruciate incision of the hymen to allow the trapped blood to drain. Therefore, the physical findings confirm imperforate hymen as the diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of primary amenorrhea (no menarche) and cyclic abdominal pain in an adolescent girl is highly suggestive of an outflow tract obstruction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
All are true regarding heart failure except:

HFpEF- Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction; HFrPF- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
options: Regardless of ejection fraction and the type of heart failure, the 5 year mortality rate is around 50%
Non-cardiovascular death is more in HFrEF -30-40% as compared to HFpEF -15%
Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors cause cough in 15% and angioedema in 1%
Atrial fibrillation is common in elderly and is the cause of stroke in quarter of the stroke cases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Non-cardiovascular death is more in HFrEF -30-40% as compared to HFpEF -15%

Non-cardiovascular deaths are more in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) as compared to heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).

Non-cardiac causes accounted for 62% of deaths in HFpEF, 54% in HFmrEF (heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction), and 35% in HFrEF. Cancer was twice as frequent as a cause of death in HFpEF and HFmrEF versus HFrEF.

Heart failure is divided according to the ejection fraction:

• Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF): Left ventricular ejection fraction is >40-50%
• Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrPF): Left ventricular ejection fraction is <40%

Patients with a left ventricular ejection fraction between 40% and 50% are considered to have borderline or mid-range EF.

Other options:

Option A: 'Regardless of the EF and the type of heart failure, the 5-year mortality rate is around 50%' is a true statement. The development of symptomatic heart failure has a poor prognosis. 30-40% of patients die within 1 year of diagnosis. More than 50% (60-70%) die within 5 years.

Option C: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors cause cough in 15% and rashes and angioedema in 1%. ACE inhibitors inhibit the angiotensin-converting enzyme and inhibit the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. ACE also splits bradykinin, substance P, enkephalins, etc. The bradykinin and substance P which are not broken down lead to cough, urticaria, and rarely angioedema.

Option D: The prevalence of atrial fibrillation increases with age, and >95% of AF patients are >60 years of age. Atrial fibrillation increases the risk of stroke by five-fold and is estimated to be the cause of 25% of strokes.
questions.learning: Non-cardiovascular death is more in HFrEF -30-40% as compared to HFpEF -15% Non-cardiovascular deaths are more in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) as compared to heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which is not a branch of the vessel known as the Anesthetist’s artery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mental

The “Anesthetist’s artery” refers to the facial artery because it is commonly encountered and sometimes compressed during regional anesthesia and facial procedures.

Branches of the facial artery (in the face):

• Inferior labial artery → supplies the lower lip
• Superior labial artery → supplies the upper lip and nasal septum
• Lateral nasal artery → supplies the side of the nose
• Angular artery → terminal branch at the medial angle of the eye

Mental artery is not a branch of the facial artery. It arises from the inferior alveolar artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, and emerges through the mental foramen to supply the chin and lower lip.
questions.learning: Mental — The “Anesthetist’s artery” refers to the facial artery because it is commonly encountered and sometimes compressed during regional anesthesia and facial procedures.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young male presents to the emergency department after a road traffic accident as he had sustained a fracture of mid shaft of the right femur. After 72 hours, he developed altered sensorium, shortness of breath, and petechial rash over the upper chest and conjunctiva. He had saturation of 85% and chest X-ray shows bilateral patchy infiltrates. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of his current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fat embolism

The patient has classic features of fat embolism syndrome following long bone fracture. Fat globules from bone marrow enter circulation and lodge in pulmonary microvasculature.

This causes respiratory distress, hypoxemia, neurological symptoms, and petechial rash.

The onset typically occurs 24–72 hours after trauma, distinguishing it from air embolism or shock.
questions.learning: Fat embolism — The patient has classic features of fat embolism syndrome following long bone fracture. Fat globules from bone marrow enter circulation and lodge in pulmonary microvasculature.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During the court proceedings, the defense lawyer asks a leading question, which the prosecutor appeals against. The judge grants the appeal. Leading questions are not allowed in all of the following except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cross examination

Leading questions are not allowed in all of the given options except cross-examination, i.e leading questions are allowed during cross-examination.

As per section 141 of the Indian Evidence Act, a leading question is one which is suggestive of the answer that is desired or one which includes a fact and leads to the admitting of a conclusive answer, such as yes or no.

Cross-examination is one wherein the witness is questioned by the opposite party's lawyer, i.e the lawyer for the accused or the defense lawyer. It is undertaken with the objective to demonstrate favorable facts to their case, to test the accuracy of the witness statements, to unearth new or old facts, and to discredit the witness.

The sequence of examination while recording evidence is as follows:

1. Examination-in-Chief/direct examination by the party that summoned the witness to elicit all the facts from the witness. Leading questions are not allowed (option C). The only exception is if the judge is satisfied that the witness is hostile.
2. Cross-examination is done by the defence lawyer.
3. Re-examination is done by the party that summoned the witness to correct or clarify or detail the statements made by the witness during cross-examination. Leading questions are not allowed (option A).

Other options:

Option D: A dying declaration is an oral or written statement made by a person who is dying. The doctor should certify that the person is conscious and with normal mental faculties before the declaration is recorded. It is recorded by the executive magistrate, or a doctor in the presence of two witnesses, if there is no time for the magistrate to come. Leading questions should not be asked.
questions.learning: Cross examination Leading questions are not allowed in all of the given options except cross-examination, i.e leading questions are allowed during cross-examination.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Two doctors examined 100 chest X - Rays of patients. The kappa statistic was found to be 0.71. What does it mean?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Good agreement

A kappa statistic of 0.71 indicates a good agreement between the two doctors who collected the data.

The strength of agreement varies with the kappa coefficient as follows:

0.81 to 1: perfect agreement between the two tests/methods
0.61 to 0.80: substantial agreement/ good agreement
0.41 to 0.60: moderate agreement
0.21 to 0.40: fair agreement
0.10 to 0.20: slight agreement

Most of the studies test the association between an exposure variable and the disease. In certain cases, it is anticipated that there will be a correlation between the variables, and the challenge is to determine the extent of this correlation or association. This assertion holds special significance in the realm of reliability studies, wherein the researcher seeks to quantitatively assess the extent to which a given variable (such as a particular finding on a chest X-ray ) can be reproduced through several measurements which is the utility of the kappa statistic. It is also important to note that a chi-square test can also be used but would only qualitatively assess the data and not quantitatively which of course is accomplished by the use of kappa statistic.

Kappa statistic can be calculated as:

where pO is observed agreement and pE is expected agreement.
