questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: During rounds, your senior was discussing the given image. The following is an image of which of the following investigations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT scan

The image in the question is a CT scan as it shows the bone as a high-intensity structure (white appearance).

In CT study X-rays are applied in a circular motion and body tissue slices are recreated mathematically. Different tissues are seen with different intensities depending on the proportion of attenuation of the X-rays that pass through them.

• Air and water are displayed as low intensities (dark appearance) because they produce only little attenuation.
• Bone is displayed as a high-intensity structure (bright appearance) because of its significant attenuation.
• High density is seen with hyperemia, freshly clotted blood, and when contrast is used.
• Edema and necrosis are seen as low-intensity lesions.

Other options:

Contrast dye study: In this imaging study, a special dye or contrast is given to evaluate structures that are not identified by conventional imaging. The contrast added would be visible in the image depending on the type of contrast and tissues targeted. Intravenous pyelogram, barium studies, angiography, etc are all examples of contrast studies.

X-ray: It shows different parts of the body in varying shades of black and white. The difference in the appearance of various tissues is due to the differences in the amount of radiation absorbed by them.

• Bone appears white because calcium has high x-ray absorption.
• Fat and soft tissues appear grey due to less x-ray absorption.
• The least absorption is seen with air which appears black.

Angiography: Here a special dye or contrast is injected to highlight the blood vessels are they are not clearly identified in normal imaging. Hence vessels would be highlighted in an angiogram.

Note: A contrast study is different from a contrast-enhanced CT scan, Intravenous pyelogram, barium studies, angiography, etc are all examples of contrast studies.
questions.learning: CT scan — The image in the question is a CT scan as it shows the bone as a high-intensity structure (white appearance). In CT study X-rays are applied in a circular motion and body tissue slices are recreated mathematically.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 23-year-old woman presents with malodorous discharge and positive whiff test. Which of the following is likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bacterial vaginosis

Malodorous vaginal discharge with a positive whiff test (fishy odor on adding KOH) is characteristic of bacterial vaginosis (BV).

• Cause: Polymicrobial overgrowth, most commonly Gardnerella vaginalis
•

Key diagnostic features (Amsel criteria):

•

Thin, homogeneous discharge

• Positive whiff test (amine odor with KOH)
• Clue cells on microscopy
• Vaginal pH > 4.5

Why not others:

• Candidiasis → thick curdy discharge, no fishy odor, pH normal
• Trichomoniasis → frothy discharge, strawberry cervix, motile organisms
• Neisseria → purulent discharge, no whiff test positivity

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old female presents to the hospital with an episode of acute cholecystitis. Symptoms are controlled with medical management. On ultrasound, there is a solitary gallstone of 1.5 cm. What is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient? (NEET PG 2015)
options: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the next available elective list
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the next available elective list

• The patient presented with acute cholecystitis, and her symptoms have settled with medical management (IV fluids, antibiotics, analgesics, NPO).
• Once the acute attack has settled, the standard of care is laparoscopic cholecystectomy, since gallstone disease is a surgical condition and recurrence/complications (empyema, perforation, gangrene, recurrent cholecystitis) are common if left untreated.
• The key nuance is timing:

• Early cholecystectomy (within 72–96 hours of symptom onset) is preferred during the same admission if the patient presents early and is a good surgical candidate — this is now increasingly favored by most contemporary guidelines (e.g., Tokyo Guidelines) as it reduces overall hospital stay without increasing complication rates.

• Why not other options (commonly given as distractors in this question):

• Emergency cholecystectomy — not ideal once the acute attack has already settled; higher operative risk due to friable, edematous tissue.
• Conservative management only — inadequate, as gallstones with a prior attack of cholecystitis have a high risk of recurrent symptoms/complications.
• ERCP — not indicated here; there's no mention of choledocholithiasis, jaundice, or biliary obstruction — this is isolated gallbladder stone disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident (RTA) presents with signs of seat belt abdominal trauma on the anterior abdominal wall. What should be the primary concern in terms of potential injuries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hollow viscus injury

The clinical scenario of a seat belt injury most likely indicates a hollow viscus injury. In cases of blunt abdominal trauma, particularly those involving seat belt injuries, there is a risk of sustaining injuries to the hollow viscera, which includes organs such as the stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and bladder.

Seat belt injuries can lead to compression forces against the abdomen, potentially causing shearing or tearing injuries to these structures.

Hollow viscus injuries can be challenging to diagnose clinically and may require imaging studies such as CT scans or exploratory surgery for confirmation.

Other Options:

Options A & B: While liver and spleen injuries are also common in blunt abdominal trauma, especially in cases of seat belt injuries, the question specifies signs of seat belt abdominal trauma on the anterior abdominal wall, which suggests a concern beyond these solid organs.

Option C: While the pancreas can be injured in cases of blunt abdominal trauma, the primary concern in this scenario, given the history of RTA and signs of seat belt abdominal trauma, should be focused on potential injuries to hollow viscera rather than the pancreas specifically.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs, when given with erythromycin, can cause QT prolongation and Torsades de pointes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Astemizole

Astemizole is a second-generation antihistamine metabolized by CYP3A4.

Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, leading to elevated astemizole levels.

Astemizole is a second-generation antihistamine.

It can block: Delayed rectifier potassium channels (IKr)

This causes:

• Delayed repolarization
• QT interval prolongation

Because of this risk, astemizole has been withdrawn in many countries.

This causes QT prolongation and predisposes to torsades de pointes.

Cetirizine, loratadine, and promethazine have minimal QT risk with erythromycin.
questions.learning: Astemizole Astemizole is a second-generation antihistamine metabolized by CYP3A4. Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, leading to elevated astemizole levels.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The screening method for GDM recommended in India is done between:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 24-28 weeks of gestation

Universal screening for GDM is done for all pregnant women. The first testing should be done during the first antenatal contact as early as possible in pregnancy. The second testing should be done during 24-28 weeks of pregnancy if the first test is negative.

The screening method for GDM recommended in India is a 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) irrespective of the last meal timing. A value of ≥140 mg/dL after 2 hours is considered a positive test, indicating GDM.

Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) refers to any degree of glucose intolerance having its onset or first recognition during pregnancy.

For IADPSG criteria, an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is done in the fasting state using 75 g of glucose, and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is diagnosed if any one of the following cut-offs is met i.e.

* Fasting: >92 mg/dl

* 1 hour: >180 mg/dl

* 2 hour: >153 mg/dl

Earlier, a two-step approach was being used to diagnose GDM. In this, the first step (screening) is a 50-gram one-hour glucose challenge test (GCT). The patients having a positive result of >140mg/dl, are candidates for the OGTT. A 100-gram, three-hour oral glucose tolerance test (GTT), is the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus. GDM is diagnosed if two or more values are positive.

Diabetes in Pregnancy Societies of India(DIPSI) recommends a 1-step procedure with 75 g oral glucose without regard to the time of the last meal. A venous plasma glucose value at 2 hours >140 mg/dL is diagnosed as GDM.

Some complications of GDM include:

* Maternal

* Hypertension, preeclampsia

* Hydramnios

* Increased operative interventions

* Future development of diabetes mellitus

* Fetal and neonatal

* Fetal macrosomia

* Congenital anomalies

* Metabolic abnormalities such as hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.

* Respiratory distress syndrome

* Subsequent childhood and adolescent obesity

Screening is usually done at 24-28 weeks of gestation. Early diagnosis and treatment are important to prevent complications.
questions.learning: 24-28 weeks of gestation Universal screening for GDM is done for all pregnant women. The first testing should be done during the first antenatal contact as early as possible in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All of the following statements about anti-Mullerian hormones are true, except:
options: It is best tested in the fasting state on day 2 of menstrual cycle
Lipopeptide secreted from granulosa cell of early antral follicle
Correlates with pregnancy rate of IVF cycle
It decreases sensitivity of the pre-antral follicles to FSH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lipopeptide secreted from granulosa cell of early antral follicle

All of the following statements about anti-Mullerian hormones (AMH) are true, except option B. AMH is a glycopeptide secreted by the granulosa cells of the pre-antral follicles and small antral follicles of the ovary.

In males, AMH inhibits the development of the Mullerian system and its absence can result in hermaphroditism. In the female, it helps in follicular development and oocyte maturation. In the absence of AMH, growing follicles are more responsive to FSH. This is because AMH reduces the sensitivity of pre-antral follicles to FSH (option D) thereby regulating the follicular growth.

Serum AMH predicts ovarian reserve in a woman with infertility or secondary amenorrhea. Also, AMH values decrease with age and can indicate menopause, owing to the reduced ovarian reserve. This makes AMH the best predictor for measuring ovarian reserve. However, recent studies have shown intercycle variations of AMH levels, hence it is recommended to measure AMH along with antral follicle count (on USG) on days 1-3 of the cycle (option A).

It is also a useful predictor of pregnancy rate in infertile women undergoing IVF (In-vitro fertilization) treatment (option C). It helps in assessing the ovarian response to exogenous gonadotropin stimulation, blastocyst formation, and miscarriage rates.

Values and interpretation:

• Normal value: 2–6.8 ng/mL
• Poor ovarian reserve: <1 ng/mL
• PCOD and hyperstimulation syndrome: >10 ng/mL
questions.learning: Lipopeptide secreted from granulosa cell of early antral follicle All of the following statements about anti-Mullerian hormones (AMH) are true, except option B.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is given to prevent neural tube defects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin B9

Folic acid (Vitamin B9) is given to prevent the incidence of neural tube defects.

Folic acid deficiency is implicated in neural tube defects like spina bifida, encephalocele, and anencephaly.

Supplementation of folic acid, in doses of 400 μg/day, prior to conception has been shown to cause a significant reduction in the incidence of spina bifida and other neural tube defects.

Reduced activity of the enzyme 5,10-methylene-THF reductase (MTHFR) caused by a common C677T polymorphism in the MTHFR gene is one of the causes of neural tube defects in folate deficiency.

Pearl PF1622: Folic Acid in Pregnancy

Condition
Daily dosage of folic acid

Prophylaxis - to prevent neural tube defects (NTDs)

400 mcg (WHO)

500 mcg (MoHFW- India)

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: 30 young volunteers with previous lifestyle modifications were contributing to drug trial for cholesterol levels based on statin therapy for 9 months. Which of the following tests is performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Paired t-test

This study involves a quantitative variable, i.e., blood cholesterol, and compares the before and after results of the same group. Hence, a paired T-test is used.

Tests of significance are used to check for significant association between two or more variables. Examples are the Student t-test, Paired t-test, Chi-square test, ANOVA, and Fischer-exact test.

McNemar's test is a non-parametric test for analysing paired nominal data. This test examines the marginal homogeneity of two dichotomous variables using a 2 x 2 contingency table. One independent variable with two dependent groups and one nominal variable with two categories (dichotomous) are needed for the test.
questions.learning: Paired t-test — This study involves a quantitative variable, i.e., blood cholesterol, and compares the before and after results of the same group. Tests of significance are used to check for significant association between two or more variables.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman was attacked by a rabid dog. The dog develops symptoms and passes away within a week. Which method is most effective for diagnosing rabies antemortem?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DFAT - Direct fluorescent antibody test

The most effective method for diagnosing rabies antemortem is DFAT (direct fluorescent antibody test).

Direct immunofluorescence test (direct-IF), also called a direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test, can be performed to detect rabies nucleoprotein antigens in specimens by using specific monoclonal antibodies tagged with fluorescent dye. Because of its high sensitivity and specificity, the DFA test is considered the “gold standard” method for rabies diagnosis. The best specimen is the hair follicle of the nape of the neck of the dog (most sensitive). Corneal impression smear can also be used. It is usually positive in the late stage with a sensitivity of 30%.

Negri bodies are pathognomonic of rabies virus infection. These are spherical-shaped cytoplasmic inclusion bodies. They contain an eosinophilic matrix, basophilic granules, and viral antigens. Negri body detection in histopathological staining of brain biopsies (hippocampus)—for postmortem diagnosis of rabies.

Rabies is a fatal infection of the central nervous system transmitted by the bite of a rabid animal. It is caused by rhabdoviruses. These viruses are enveloped, rod- or bullet-shaped, and contain single-stranded RNA.

Clinical features of rabies can be categorised into three phases: prodromal, encephalitic phase, and coma. The prodromal phase is characterised by malaise, anorexia, headache, and irritability. This is followed by the encephalitic stage, characterised by abnormal behaviour and seizures. They develop hydrophobia. Attempts to drink liquids cause painful spasms of the pharynx and larynx, producing a choking sensation. Therefore, the patients develop a phobia of even the sight or sound of water. Finally, seizures, coma, and death occur.

Laboratory diagnosis can be done on a postmortem or antemortem basis. Postmortem diagnosis is done by the demonstration of Negri bodies. These bodies are common in the pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum. Antemortem diagnosis is done from corneal scrapings, saliva, or skin biopsy. Demonstration of the virus is done using direct immunofluorescence.

Other methods used in the diagnosis are intracerebral inoculation in the mice, tissue culture, ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay), and PCR (polymerase chain reaction). Seller's technique (basic fuchsin and methylene blue in methanol) is used to stain brain impression smears, which has the advantage of allowing for simultaneous fixation and staining.

Reducing the stray dog population and vaccinating all dogs is the most cost-effective and logical way to reduce the incidence of rabies. The Animal Birth Control initiative by the Government of India is aimed at achieving this goal.

Rabies is a highly fatal viral disease caused by the Lyssavirus type 1, which affects the central nervous system. Dogs are considered the major source of rabies infection. Thus, immunization of dogs at the age of 3-4 months and booster doses at regular intervals are recommended to control rabies.

The spread of rabies can be:

* Centripetal:

* The virus enters the peripheral neurons, and it moves via retrograde fast axonal transport towards the spinal cord or brainstem at a speed of up to 250 mm/day

* Once within the CNS, it spreads quickly to other regions in the CNS through fast axonal transport. It infects neurons primarily but may rarely infect astrocytes.

* Centrifugal:

* After CNS infection is established, it spreads along the sensory and autonomic nerves to the salivary glands, adrenal glands, and skin.

* The rabies virus replicates in acinar cells of the salivary glands and is secreted in the saliva of rabid animals that serve as vectors.

External examination of the brain shows intense edema and vascular congestion. Neuronal dysfunction associated with an inflammatory reaction is seen, which is most severe in the brainstem involving the basal ganglia, spinal cord, and dorsal root ganglia.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is a primary skin lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Purpura

Purpura is a primary skin lesion. Crust, atrophy, and induration are secondary lesions.

It is a condition with red or purple discolored spots on the skin that do not blanch on applying pressure. The spots are caused by bleeding underneath the skin. It is seen:

• Vasculitis
• Thrombocytopenia
• Vitamin C deficiency

Option A: Crusts or scabs consist of dried-up discharge from the lesions.

Option B: Atrophy refers to loss of tissue. There may be fine wrinkling and increased translucency if the process is superficial.

Option D: Induration refers to dermal thickening that clinically presents as skin that feels thicker and firmer than normal on palpation.
questions.learning: Purpura Purpura is a primary skin lesion. Crust, atrophy, and induration are secondary lesions.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent profuse epistaxis and nasal obstruction. On examination, a reddish mass is seen in the nasopharynx. What is the investigation of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Contrast-enhanced CT

The investigation of choice for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) is Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT) because it best demonstrates bony anatomy and tumor extent.

• CECT findings:

• Intense contrast enhancement (high vascularity)
• Bony remodeling/destruction
• Holman–Miller sign (anterior bowing of posterior wall of maxillary sinus)

Why not other options:

• MRI: Better for soft tissue and intracranial extension, but not first-line
• DNE (Diagnostic nasal endoscopy): Helps visualize mass, but not definitive imaging
• Biopsy: Contraindicated due to risk of severe hemorrhage (highly vascular tumor)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient was brought to the ER after a road traffic accident. On examination, left-sided hydropneumothorax was noted. Thoracostomy was done and around 1800 ml of blood was drained in 1 hour. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: Continue resuscitation for the next 6 Hours
Administer a hemostatic agent through the chest tube
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Emergency thoracotomy

Given the significant blood loss (1800 ml) and the patient's critical condition, the most appropriate management in this scenario would be an emergency thoracotomy.

A thoracotomy is a surgical procedure in which an incision is made into the chest to access the thoracic cavity. It is performed in critical situations to control bleeding and repair injuries to the chest structures, including the lung and blood vessels.

In this case, the patient's condition is serious due to the combination of pneumothorax, hydrothorax, and a rapid blood loss of 1800 ml in just 1 hour. This level of bleeding suggests a severe injury to blood vessels or vital structures within the chest. Emergency thoracotomy would provide direct access to the bleeding source, allowing for immediate control of bleeding, repair of injuries, and restoration of stable conditions.

Indications for thoracotomy:

* Initial tube thoracostomy drainage of >1000 ml (penetrating injury) or >1500 ml (blunt injury) of frank blood

* Ongoing tube thoracostomy drainage of >200 ml/ hr for 3 consecutive hours in non-coagulopathic patients with hemothorax

* Caked hemothorax despite the placement of two chest tubes

* Massive air leak from chest tube with inadequate ventilation

* Open pneumothorax

* Great vessel injury

* Pericardial tamponade

* Cardiac herniation

* Tracheobronchial injury

* Esophageal perforation

Other Options:

Option A: Thoracentesis involves the removal of fluid or air from the pleural space using a needle or catheter. However, given the severity of the situation with rapid blood loss, this procedure alone would not adequately address the underlying issues or stop the significant bleeding.

Option B: Continued resuscitation for the next 6 hours is not appropriate in this scenario due to the patient's critical condition and substantial blood loss. Immediate intervention is required to stabilize the patient's condition and address the underlying causes of the blood loss.

Option C: While hemostatic agents can be useful in certain bleeding situations, the rapid blood loss and critical nature of the presented case call for a more immediate and direct approach, such as an emergency thoracotomy, to achieve rapid control of bleeding and prevent further complications.
questions.learning: Emergency thoracotomy Given the significant blood loss (1800 ml) and the patient's critical condition, the most appropriate management in this scenario would be an emergency thoracotomy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young male patient with a history of a motor vehicle accident is unable to pass urine. Blood is seen at the meatus. What is the most likely site of urethral injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Membranous urethra

In the given scenario of a young patient with urinary retention, blood at the meatus, and a history of a motor vehicle accident, the most likely site of injury is the membranous urethra. The given retrograde urethrogram shows contrast leakage at the membranous urethra.

Urethral injuries in men usually occur after catheterization or during cystoscopy. Injuries following external trauma are rare, but mainly affect the bulbar or the membranous urethra.

Membranous urethral rupture usually occurs following a road traffic accident, crush injury, or a fall. It is associated with pelvic fracture and extraperitoneal bladder rupture. Clinical features include urinary retention, blood at the meatus, and a high riding prostate on digital examination. Bruising is seen over the pubic area, scrotum, and penis.

Management is by inserting a suprapubic catheter. If there is an associated bladder rupture, the bladder will not be seen on the ultrasound, and management in such a case is by exploration, repair, and placement of a suprapubic catheter.

Other options:

Option A: Bulbar urethral injury occurs following a blow to the perineum with a fall astride injury during cycling or gymnasium accidents. A typical feature is a butterfly-shaped hematoma in the perineum. Other features such as urinary retention and meatal bleeding can also be present. Analgesia, antibiotics, and suprapubic catheterization are needed. The patient should be discouraged from passing urine. Definitive management is delayed urethroplasty after 8-12 weeks.

Options B and D: Spongy and penile urethral rupture can occur following a penile fracture during coitus. Hematuria and difficulty in voiding can be present in spongy urethral injury. A pop sound followed by severe penile pain and penile deformity is characteristic of penile urethral injury. Hematoma, blood at the meatus, and voiding difficulties are also seen.

Retrograde urethrogram shows loss of smooth contour of the urethra with extravasation of the dye in case of a spongy urethral rupture. Surgical repair is needed in both.
questions.learning: Membranous urethra — In the given scenario of a young patient with urinary retention, blood at the meatus, and a history of a motor vehicle accident, the most likely site of injury is the membranous urethra.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was admitted to the hospital for prolapsing rectal mass and painless rectal bleeding. Histopathological examination reveals enlarged and inflamed glands filled with mucin. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hamartoma

The given features are suggestive of a juvenile polyp, which are a type of hamartomatous polyp. They are benign growths that are composed of a disorganized mixture of different types of tissues.

Juvenile polyps are malformations of epithelium and lamina propria commonly located in the rectum. It is seen in children <5 years of age. The typical presentation is painless rectal bleeding. Sometimes, there may be a proliferating rectal mass.

The disease may be sporadic or syndromic.

• Sporadic juvenile polyp occurs as a single mass and is called a retention polyp.
• Juvenile polyposis syndrome is characterized by multiple hamartomatous polyps, which may be premalignant.

Morphologically, both of these types are indistinguishable.

• Gross appearance: They appear as pedunculated, smooth reddish lesions, and with cystic spaces.
• Microscopic appearance: The cysts appear as dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory debris.

Adenoma: Adenomas are benign tumors that arise from glandular tissue. While they may present with rectal bleeding, they are not commonly seen in young children and are not typically pedunculated like juvenile polyps.

Choristoma: Choristomas are non-neoplastic masses that arise from heterotopic tissue, i.e., tissues found in abnormal locations. They are not associated with juvenile polyps.
questions.learning: Hamartoma — The given features are suggestive of a juvenile polyp, which are a type of hamartomatous polyp. They are benign growths that are composed of a disorganized mixture of different types of tissues.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following procedure is shown in the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior ethmoidal nerve block

The procedure shown in the given image is an anterior ethmoidal nerve block.

The anterior ethmoidal nerve supplies the roof of the nasal cavity. It is a branch of the nasociliary nerve which in turn is a branch of the ophthalmic nerve (V1). It is sometimes used in endonasal surgery.

Other options:

Option A: In nasolacrimal duct syringing, the puncta of the nasolacrimal duct near the medial canthus of the eye is probed using a lacrimal cannula. The below image shows lacrimal syringing.

Option C: Infraorbital nerve block causes anesthesia in the distribution of infraorbital nerve which includes lower lid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip, and upper teeth. It is most commonly done for dental procedures.

Option D: Trephination of the frontal sinus is a surgical procedure done for the drainage of pus in acute frontal sinusitis. In this procedure, the incision is made on the floor of the frontal sinus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In patients undergoing elective colorectal surgery, when should parenteral antibiotic prophylaxis ideally be administered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Within 60 minutes before surgical incision

Parenteral antibiotic prophylaxis is most effective when adequate tissue concentrations are achieved at the time of skin incision. Therefore, prophylactic antibiotics should be administered within 60 minutes before surgical incision to minimize the risk of surgical site infection (SSI).

Why is B correct?

• Administration within 60 minutes before incision ensures optimal antibiotic levels in serum and tissues when bacterial contamination occurs during surgery.
• This is the recommended timing for most prophylactic antibiotics in elective colorectal surgery.

Why not the other options?

• A. Less than 10 minutes before incision: May not allow sufficient time to achieve effective tissue concentrations.
• C. 2 hours prior to surgery: Antibiotic levels may decline by the time of incision.
• D. 4 hours prior to surgery: Too early; inadequate tissue concentrations at the time of surgery.
questions.learning: Within 60 minutes before surgical incision Parenteral antibiotic prophylaxis is most effective when adequate tissue concentrations are achieved at the time of skin incision.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following logos will be seen in a contaminated biomedical waste management plant?
questions.explanation: Biohazard symbol A contaminated biomedical waste management plant handles infectious, hazardous materials and must be prominently marked with the Biohazard symbol (Option A). This logo is the international standard for labeling materials that pose a biological threat to humans or the environment. The Universal Recycling symbol (Option B) indicates that materials are suitable for recycling and is not a warning for infectious hazards. The Radiation hazard symbol (Option C) is used strictly for radioactive materials, such as those found in oncology or radiology departments. The High Voltage symbol (Option D) is a safety warning for electrical hazards and is not used to categorize clinical waste. Thus, the biohazard logo is the specific identifier for the presence of infectious biomedical waste.
questions.learning: Biohazard symbol — A contaminated biomedical waste management plant handles infectious, hazardous materials and must be prominently marked with the Biohazard symbol (Option A).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A tall obese person, who is a known hypertensive was recently diagnosed with metabolic syndrome on routine workup. Which of the following is most likely to be found in this patient?
options: Increase in uric acid and insulin
Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol

Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol is seen in patients with metabolic syndrome.

Metabolic syndrome is present if three or more of the following five criteria are met, which is given by NCEP-ATP III (National Cholesterol Education program and adult treatment panel III). It includes-

* Central obesity: waist circumference >102 cm (M), >88 cm (F)

* Hypertriglyceridemia: triglyceride level ≥ 150 mg/dL

* Low HDL cholesterol: <40 mg/dL and <50 mg/dL for men and women, respectively.

* Hypertension: blood pressure ≥130 mmHg systolic or ≥ 85 mmHg diastolic.

* Fasting plasma glucose level ≥100 mg/dL or specific medication or previously diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus.
questions.learning: Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol is seen in patients with metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome is present if three or more of the following five criteria are met, which is given by NCEP-ATP…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following methods is utilized for sterilizing a glass petri dish?
options: Autoclaving at 121 degrees Celsius for 30-60 minutes
Hot air oven at 160 degrees Celsius for 120 min- utes or less
Flash autoclaving at 134 degrees Celsius for 3 minutes
Hot air oven at 121 degrees Celsius for 30-60 minutes
questions.explanation: Hot air oven at 160 degrees Celsius for 120 minutes or less. Sterilization of glassware, such as petri dishes and pipettes, is most effectively achieved using dry heat in a Hot Air Oven. The standard sterilization cycle for glassware is 160 degrees Celsius for 120 minutes (2 hours). Higher temperatures like 170 or 180 degrees Celsius can be used for shorter durations. Autoclaving (Option A), which uses moist heat, is generally used for surgical instruments and media but is less ideal for dry glassware as it leaves them wet. Flash autoclaving (Option C) is an emergency method for unwrapped instruments. Option D is incorrect as 121 degrees Celsius in a hot air oven is insufficient for sterilization. Dry heat kills organisms by oxidative damage and protein coagulation. Therefore, the hot air oven at the specified temperature and time is the correct microbiological protocol for petri dishes.
questions.learning: Hot air oven at 160 degrees Celsius for 120 minutes or less. Sterilization of glassware, such as petri dishes and pipettes, is most effectively achieved using dry heat in a Hot Air Oven.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mutation in which of the following genes is most commonly associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is a neuroendocrine tumor arising from parafollicular C cells, and it is most commonly associated with mutations in the RET proto-oncogene. These mutations are found in both sporadic cases and familial syndromes such as Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2). RAS mutations (Option A) are more typically seen in follicular thyroid adenomas and carcinomas. BRAF mutations (Option B) are the most common genetic alterations found in papillary thyroid carcinoma. TP53 mutations (Option D) are strongly associated with highly aggressive anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Because RET activation is the primary driver of MTC, genetic testing for this mutation is essential for managing patients and screening their relatives
questions.learning: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is a neuroendocrine tumor arising from parafollicular C cells, and it is most commonly associated with mutations in the RET proto-oncogene.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Aromatic ring is seen in which of the following amino acids?
questions.explanation: In biochemistry, aromatic amino acids are those that contain a benzene-like ring in their side chains. The three primary aromatic amino acids are Phenylalanine, Tryptophan, and Tyrosine. Phenylalanine contains a simple phenyl ring. Tyrosine is derived from phenylalanine and contains a phenolic hydroxyl group. Tryptophan contains an indole ring. These amino acids are unique because they absorb ultraviolet light (typically at 280 nm), which is used by researchers to quantify protein concentration. Valine (Option A) and Lysine (Option D) are aliphatic amino acids. Cysteine and Methionine (Option C and D) are sulfur-containing amino acids. Beyond protein structure, these aromatic precursors are vital for synthesizing important neurotransmitters and hormones: phenylalanine and tyrosine lead to dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine; tryptophan leads to serotonin and melatonin. Knowledge of these structural categories is fundamental for understanding protein chemistry and the metabolic pathways of biologically active nitrogenous compounds in the human body
questions.learning: In biochemistry, aromatic amino acids are those that contain a benzene-like ring in their side chains. The three primary aromatic amino acids are Phenylalanine, Tryptophan, and Tyrosine.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presents with pain and swelling of the left wrist after a fall on an outstretched hand, and examination reveals a dinner-fork deformity. What type of displacement is most likely seen in this injury?
options: Proximal and ventral displacement of radius
Supination and dorsal displacement of radius
Proximal and dorsal displacement of ulna
Proximal and ventral displacement of ulna
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of an elderly woman with a "dinner fork deformity" after falling on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) is diagnostic of a Colles’ fracture. This is a fracture of the distal radius within 2.5 cm of the wrist joint. The "dinner fork" appearance is caused by the specific displacement of the distal radial fragment. The six classic displacements in a Colles’ fracture are: dorsal displacement (which creates the fork shape), dorsal tilt, lateral displacement, lateral tilt, proximal migration (impaction), and supination. Option B correctly identifies two of these key displacements (dorsal and supination). All other options are incorrect because they mention the "ulna" (which is usually not the primary displaced bone) or "ventral" displacement. Ventral (volar) displacement occurs in a Smith's fracture, also known as a "reverse Colles’," which results from a fall on a flexed wrist. Therefore, Colles' fracture is defined by its dorsal radial displacement
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of an elderly woman with a "dinner fork deformity" after falling on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) is diagnostic of a Colles’ fracture.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following protease inhibitors is most associated with QT interval prolongation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Saquinavir

Saquinavir, an HIV protease inhibitor, is most strongly associated with QT interval prolongation, which can predispose to serious ventricular arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes. Saquinavir can interfere with cardiac potassium channels (hERG channels), delaying ventricular repolarization and prolonging the QT interval on ECG.

Why not other options:

A. Atazanavir: Mainly causes indirect hyperbilirubinemia (UGT1A1 inhibition), not significant QT prolongation.

B. Darunavir: Generally well tolerated; main issues are rash and hepatotoxicity, not QT prolongation.

C. Indinavir: Associated with nephrolithiasis and hyperbilirubinemia, not QT prolongation.
questions.learning: Saquinavir Saquinavir, an HIV protease inhibitor, is most strongly associated with QT interval prolongation, which can predispose to serious ventricular arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 32-year-old man presents with history of recurrent jaundice over the previous decade. Family gives history of the patient having episodes of facial grimacing. Which one of the following is a clinical clue to the diagnosis?
options: Adenoma sebaceum in the mid face
Osler’s nodes at the finger tips
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kayser-Fleisher rings in the cornea

The combination of recurrent jaundice and facial grimacing (orofacial dystonia) in a young adult is highly suggestive of Wilson’s disease (hepatolenticular degeneration). A key clinical clue is the presence of Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings, which are brownish-green deposits of copper in Descemet’s membrane of the cornea, best detected by slit-lamp examination.

Why not the other options?

• A. Adenoma sebaceum in the mid face: Seen in Tuberous sclerosis.
• B. Erythema nodosum on the skin: Associated with sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, and streptococcal infections.
• D. Osler’s nodes at the fingertips: Painful nodules seen in infective endocarditis.
questions.learning: Kayser-Fleisher rings in the cornea — The combination of recurrent jaundice and facial grimacing (orofacial dystonia) in a young adult is highly suggestive of Wilson’s disease (hepatolenticular degeneration).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calcium

Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by calcium in the muscle.

Glycogen phosphorylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis and is decreased in the fed state.

In the muscle, the increased cytosolic calcium ion concentration initiates both contraction and glycogenolysis. Muscle phosphorylase kinase has four different subunits, α, β, γ, and δ. The α and β subunits are phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase. The δ subunit is identical to the calcium-binding protein calmodulin and binds four calcium ions. Calcium coordinates the activation of Glycogen Phosphorylase with the contraction of the muscle.

Glycogen phosphorylase catalyzes the cleavage of α1 → 4 linkages of glycogen to single units of glucose 1-phosphate. It uses pyridoxal phosphate as the coenzyme. Different isoenzymes of glycogen phosphorylase are seen in the liver, muscles, and brain.

Other options:

Option B: During glycogenolysis, glucose 6-phosphate allosterically inhibits glycogen phosphorylase.

Option C: Insulin entirely suppresses glycogenolysis in the skeletal muscle and liver.

Option D: In glycogenolysis protein phosphatase is inactivated by inhibitor proteins in response to cAMP, to maintain the glycogen phosphorylase in an active state.
questions.learning: Calcium Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by calcium in the muscle. Glycogen phosphorylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis and is decreased in the fed state.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the recommended free residual chlorine level in a well after chlorination to ensure effective disinfection?
questions.explanation: For well chlorination, the recommended standard is to achieve a free residual chlorine level of about 0.5 ppm after 1 hour of contact time. However, in practice and exam interpretation, 0.3 ppm after 1 hour is accepted as the minimum effective residual level to ensure adequate disinfection. This level indicates that sufficient chlorine remains after reacting with organic matter, ensuring continued antimicrobial activity and safe drinking water. Why other options are incorrect: (B) 0.5 ppm after 2 hours: Although effective, the standard reference is based on 1-hour contact time, not 2 hours. (C) 0.8 ppm after 1 hour: Higher than required; not a standard recommendation. (D) 1.5 ppm after 2 hours: Excessive and unnecessary; may affect taste and safety. Thus, the accepted exam answer is 0.3 ppm after 1 hour

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a prodrug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primidone

Among the given options primidone is not a prodrug.

Prodrugs are drugs that are in their pharmacologically inactive form. They are converted to their active forms by metabolism.

The prodrug may offer advantages over the active form in being more stable, having better bioavailability, or fewer side effects and toxicity. Some prodrugs are activated selectively at the site of action. The given options are examples of prodrugs:

• Sulindac is a sulfoxide prodrug used in inflammatory diseases including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, acute gouty arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis.
• Proguanil is a prodrug and its active metabolite is cycloguanil. It is used in the treatment and prevention of malaria.
• Fluro-uracil is a prodrug having the active metabolite as fluorouridine monophosphate
questions.learning: Primidone Among the given options primidone is not a prodrug. Prodrugs are drugs that are in their pharmacologically inactive form.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which agency collects data and publishes large scale surveys continuously regarding morbidity, family planning, vital events?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. National Sample Survey

The National Sample Survey collects data and publishes large-scale surveys continuously regarding morbidity, family planning, vital events.

The National Sample Survey(NSS), headed by a Director-General, is responsible for the conduct of large-scale sample surveys in diverse fields all over India.

Data are collected through national household surveys on various socio-economic subjects. Besides these surveys, NSS collects data on rural and urban prices and plays a significant role in the improvement of crop statistics through supervision of the area enumeration and crop estimation surveys of the State agencies.  It also maintains a frame of urban area units for use in sample surveys in urban areas.

The four types of survey methods are :

* Health interview (face-to-face) survey

* Health examination survey

* Health records survey

* Mailed questionnaire survey

The cause of death is noted by the Sample registration system (SRS), the Death certificate, and via lay reporting

Other Options:

Option A: Civil Registration System also known as Vital Registration System, is managed under the Ministry of Home Affairs by the Office of the Registrar General of India. Birth and death registration in India is undertaken by this system and is registered within 21 days.

Option C: Sample Registration System, a Biannual system conducted every 6 months, and assess indicators such as crude birth rate, death rate, Infant mortality rate, Maternal mortality rate, and so on.

Option D: Central Bureau of Health functions as the national health data repository, responsible for the collection, analysis, and dissemination of health statistics to support evidence-based policy and planning.
questions.learning: National Sample Survey — The National Sample Survey collects data and publishes large-scale surveys continuously regarding morbidity, family planning, vital events.

• Reflects early CNS response to dehydration
• Appears before severe signs
• More reliable clinically than isolated physical signs

| Eyes | Normal | Sunken

not thirsty | Thirsty, drinks eagerly

(1 second)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A lactating mother reports breast cramping during breastfeeding. Which hormone is primarily responsible for this sensation?
questions.explanation: The "breast cramps" or tingling sensation reported by a breastfeeding mother during the "let-down" reflex is directly caused by Oxytocin (Option D) . When an infant suckles at the nipple, sensory signals are sent to the posterior pituitary, triggering the release of oxytocin. This hormone travels to the breast, where it causes the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli, squeezing milk into the ducts. These rhythmic contractions are often perceived as cramping. Prolactin (Option C) is responsible for the actual production of milk (galactopoiesis), while estrogen (Option B) and progesterone (Option A) are involved in breast development during pregnancy but actually inhibit milk production until their levels drop after delivery. Therefore, oxytocin is the hormone definitively responsible for the mechanical ejection of milk and the associated maternal cramping. This same hormone also causes uterine contractions postpartum, helping the uterus return to its pre-pregnancy size

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Please identify the anatomical structure indicated in the provided image.
questions.explanation: The extensor pollicis longus (EPL) is a deep muscle of the posterior compartment of the forearm. It originates from the posterior surface of the ulna and interosseous membrane and its tendon passes around Lister’s tubercle of the radius. It then inserts into the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb. Its primary function is to extend the thumb at both the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, and it also assists in extension at the wrist. In anatomical diagrams, EPL is identified by its long tendon crossing obliquely toward the distal thumb, forming the medial boundary of the anatomical snuffbox. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Abductor pollicis brevis → Thenar muscle (palm), not forearm (B) Extensor pollicis brevis → Inserts into proximal phalanx (shorter tendon) (C) Abductor pollicis longus → Inserts into base of 1st metacarpal

questions.text: Which of the following vaccines has not been introduced to the immunization programme in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Influenza

Influenza vaccine (Flu shot) has not been introduced to the National Immunization Programme in India.

The Influenza vaccine provides protection against viral flu caused by the influenza virus.

Note: Bacterial Hemophilus influenzae type-b (Hib) vaccine is different from the viral influenza (Flu) vaccine. HiB is a part of the pentavalent vaccine.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following features is not considered a favorable prognostic indicator in a middle- aged woman diagnosed with breast carcinoma presenting with a lump in her right breast?
questions.explanation: Breast cancer prognosis is determined by tumor biology and molecular markers. Her2 overexpression (Option C) is considered an unfavorable prognostic marker, as it is associated with aggressive tumor growth, a higher risk of recurrence, and a poorer overall survival rate compared to Her2-negative tumors. In contrast, the Luminal subtype (Option A) is a favorable marker because these tumors are typically estrogen-receptor positive and respond well to endocrine therapy. A low Ki67 index (Option B) is favorable as it indicates a low percentage of actively dividing cells. Mucinous carcinoma (Option D) is a specific histological type that generally carries a better prognosis than common invasive ductal carcinoma. Therefore, Her2 positivity is the only choice listed that traditionally signifies a more dangerous clinical course, although modern targeted therapies like trastuzumab have significantly improved the outlook for these patients

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus presents with a black, foul-smelling nasal discharge. Examination reveals a necrotic mass in the nasal cavity with erosion of the nasal septum and hard palate. What is the most likely diagnosis responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a black, necrotic nasal mass with erosion of the palate in an elderly diabetic patient is pathognomonic for Rhino-orbital-cerebral Mucormycosis. This is an aggressive, life-threatening fungal infection caused by Mucorales, which thrives in diabetic patients, especially those in ketoacidosis. The fungus is angioinvasive, causing vascular thrombosis and subsequent tissue necrosis (hence the black color). Aspergillosis (Option A) can cause invasive sinusitis but is generally less hyper-acute than mucormycosis. A foreign body (Option C) would cause foul-smelling discharge but rarely systemic necrosis or extensive bony erosion. Rhinosporidiosis (Option D) typically presents with friable, strawberry-like polyps rather than black necrosis. Immediate management includes aggressive surgical debridement and high-dose intravenous Amphotericin B. Therefore, given the rapid destruction and diabetic history, Mucormycosis is the most likely and most dangerous diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a black, necrotic nasal mass with erosion of the palate in an elderly diabetic patient is pathognomonic for Rhino-orbital-cerebral Mucormycosis.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 4

Small cell (oat cell) carcinoma of the lung is a highly aggressive neuroendocrine tumor strongly associated with cigarette smoking.

• Usually arises centrally near the hilum, not peripherally.
• Shows early hematogenous metastasis.
• Frequently causes paraneoplastic syndromes, especially SIADH (ectopic ADH) and ectopic ACTH.
• Surgery is rarely used because the tumor is usually metastatic at diagnosis; treatment is mainly chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman is suspected to have endometriosis. Which of the following is the investigation of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Laparoscopy

For endometriosis, the investigation of choice which can help with both the diagnosis and treatment is laparoscopy. It is used to locate the sites, take a biopsy and surgically remove the deposits.

Endometriosis is the presence of endometrium at a site outside the uterine cavity. It can be found in ectopic sites such as the ovary, pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligaments, appendix, pelvic lymph nodes, lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) scar endometriosis, umbilicus, and lung.

Dysmenorrhea is the most common presenting symptom, associated with abdominal and pelvic pain, menorrhagia, dyspareunia and infertility. Laparoscopy is the gold standard modality for the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis. Typical characteristics include 'powder-burn' - puckered black spots, red vascular, bluish, blackish cysts, chocolate cysts, and dense adhesions in the pelvis.

For minimal disease, medical management with NSAIDs and oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are given if associated menstrual complaints are present. OCPs inhibit gonadotropin release and decrease the menstrual flow. For moderate to severe diseases oral progestogens, GnRH agonists or danazol that antagonize estrogenic effects on the endometrium, causing endometrial atrophy are used.

Surgery is preferred in patients with infertility. Endometrial deposits are destroyed by electrocautery/laser, and resection of endometrioma can be done. Total hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy is a definitive and most effective therapy for women with endometriosis who do not wish to retain fertility.
questions.learning: Laparoscopy For endometriosis, the investigation of choice which can help with both the diagnosis and treatment is laparoscopy. It is used to locate the sites, take a biopsy and surgically remove the deposits.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following are characteristic features of cerebral palsy? I. Disorder of movement II. Permanent nature III. Progressive course IV. Disorder of posture Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture causing activity limitation, resulting from a non-progressive insult to the developing fetal or infant brain. Although the brain lesion is non-progressive, the clinical manifestations may change with growth due to musculoskeletal complications.

• I. Disorder of movement ✔

• Cerebral palsy primarily affects voluntary movement, leading to spasticity, dyskinesia, ataxia, or hypotonia.

• II. Permanent nature ✔

• CP is a permanent neurological disorder. Although symptoms can improve with therapy, the underlying brain injury is irreversible.

• III. Progressive course ✘

• The brain lesion is non-progressive.
• Functional problems may evolve over time, but the primary neurological injury does not worsen.

• IV. Disorder of posture ✔

• Abnormal posture due to impaired muscle tone and motor control is a defining feature of CP.
questions.learning: I, II and IV Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture causing activity limitation, resulting from a non-progressive insult to the developing fetal or infant brain.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most commonly involved artery in pseudoaneurysm formation:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Femoral artery

The most commonly involved artery in pseudoaneurysm is the femoral artery.

A true aneurysm involves all three vessel wall layers, while a pseudoaneurysm involves only the intimal and medial layers. Pseudoaneurysms are most commonly iatrogenic due to repeated arterial puncture for blood sampling or catheterization procedures which injure the arterial wall. The most commonly used artery in endovascular surgeries is the femoral artery, and hence, also the most commonly involved in the formation of pseudo aneurysms.

Aneurysms are usually pulsatile on palpation and a systolic bruit can be heard on auscultation.

Doppler ultrasound reveals a bidirectional, 'to-and-fro' flow of blood which is known as the yin-yang sign.

Treatment options include endovascular stent insertion, ultrasound-guided thrombin injection, and surgical repair.

Other options:

Option A: Aortic aneurysm can be types - thoracic or abdominal. They are usually seen in heritable conditions like Marfan syndrome or vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos.

Option C: The most common peripheral aneurysm is the popliteal aneurysm (80% of the cases) followed by the femoral aneurysm.
questions.learning: Femoral artery — The most commonly involved artery in pseudoaneurysm is the femoral artery. A true aneurysm involves all three vessel wall layers, while a pseudoaneurysm involves only the intimal and medial layers.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which graft option is used least often during coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery?
questions.explanation: In coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), surgeons use various blood vessels to bypass blocked coronary arteries. The internal mammary artery (Option B), specifically the Left Internal Mammary Artery (LIMA), is the "gold standard" graft due to its excellent long-term patency. The long saphenous vein (Option A) from the leg is the most common "venous" graft used when multiple bypasses are required. The radial artery (Option D) is also frequently used as an arterial graft with good patency rates. The intercostal artery (Option C) is virtually never used as a conduit for CABG. Its anatomical position, relatively small size, and importance in providing collateral circulation to the spinal cord make it a poor and risky choice for a coronary graft. Therefore, among the choices provided, the intercostal artery is the "least frequently utilized"—essentially not used at all—in standard cardiac bypass practice

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient presents with complaints of chronic diarrhea, fatigue, and tiredness. On examination, his nail findings are shown below. Lab investigations show Hb as 8 gm%. Which of the following is the best treatment approach for this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iron supplements

Since the patient has chronic diarrhea there is malabsorption of nutrients in this patient. He has anemia from his lab investigations and his nail findings suggest koilonychia(spooning of nails) which is a characteristic finding in iron deficiency anemia. Thus the preferred treatment for this patient is iron supplements.

Malabsorption syndrome refers to a spectrum of conditions of various etiologies that arises due to diminished absorption of one or more dietary nutrients.

Anemia may be present when there is defective absorption of iron, folate, or vitamin B12.

The majority of the patients with iron deficiency anemia present with easy fatigability, tachycardia, palpitations, and dyspnea on exertion. Severe deficiency causes skin and mucosal changes like

* smooth tongue

* brittle nails

* koilonychia- spooning of nails

* cheilosis- fissures at the corner of the mouth

* pica- craving for specific foods that are not rich in iron.

Laboratory investigation of iron deficiency anemia

The peripheral smear will show small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic) cells with an increased area of central pallor. Pencil-shaped cells can be seen which is called poikilocytosis.

Serum iron levels- It represents the amount of circulating iron bound to transferrin. The normal range for the serum iron is 50–150 μg/dL. It is decreased in iron deficiency anemia.

Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)- It is an indirect measure of the circulating transferrin. The normal levels are 300–360 μg/dL. The levels are increased in IDA.

Transferrin saturation- The normal levels are 25–50%. The levels are decreased in IDA.

Serum ferritin- Free iron is toxic to the body. Therefore it is bound to a protein called apoferritin to form ferritin. Adult males have serum ferritin values averaging 100 μg/L, while adult females have levels averaging 30 μg/L. The serum ferritin level is the most convenient laboratory test to estimate iron stores. It is decreased in IDA.

Evaluation of bone marrow iron stores- can be done by performing bone marrow biopsy and using the Prussian stain to stain the iron stores. It is rarely done these days due to the availability of the serum ferritin estimation tests.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old man is found in the desert after being lost for two days without access to food or water for more than 24 hours and presents with stable vital signs. During this dehydrated state, which segment of the kidney is responsible for the greatest amount of water reabsorption?
questions.explanation: In the human kidney, the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) is responsible for the bulk reabsorption of water and solutes. Approximately 65-70% of the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed iso-osmotically in the PCT, regardless of the person's hydration status. While the collecting duct (Option D) is the site where "facultative" water reabsorption occurs under the influence of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) during dehydration, it only accounts for the final 5-10% of reabsorption. The Loop of Henle (Option B) reabsorbs about 15% of the filtered water, and the distal convoluted tubule (Option C) reabsorbs roughly 5%. Although the collecting duct is the regulatory site that concentrates urine during water deprivation, the PCT remains the anatomical part where the absolute maximum volume of water is reabsorbed from the filtrate. Understanding this distinction between "obligatory" reabsorption in the PCT and "facultative" reabsorption in the distal segments is fundamental in renal physiology

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A professional singer develops difficulty in producing high-pitched notes after undergoing thyroid surgery. Her voice is not hoarse, but she is unable to raise the pitch effectively. Which nerve is most likely to have been injured?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN)
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (IBSLN)
questions.explanation: The EBSLN innervates the cricothyroid muscle, which is responsible for tensing the vocal cords to produce high-pitched sounds. Injury to this nerve, often occurring during thyroid surgery within Joll's Triangle, results in an inability to raise voice pitch without causing hoarseness, as the vocal cord's ability to adduct remains intact. Professional voice users are highly sensitive to this change. The internal branch (Option B) is purely sensory and its injury leads to loss of sensation above the cords, not pitch changes. The recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option C) supplies the majority of intrinsic laryngeal muscles; damage here causes vocal cord palsy and prominent hoarseness. The glossopharyngeal nerve (Option D) is involved in oropharyngeal sensation and taste, having no role in vocal cord tension

questions.text: A 4-year-old male child with a body weight of 15kg and height of 100cm is admitted with renal failure. His blood urea was 100 mg/dL and serum creatinine was 1 mg/dL. What is the closest calculated eGFR in the patient?

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following instruments is shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lim’s forceps

The instrument shown in the image above is Lim's forceps.

Lim's forceps are a type of surgical instrument used in ophthalmic procedures. They are designed for delicate manipulations within the eye during surgery. These forceps typically have fine tips and a delicate grip, allowing surgeons to handle delicate tissues with precision.

Other options:

Option B: McPherson suture tying forceps are commonly used in ophthalmic surgery for grasping and tying sutures. They have a fine, curved tip which allows surgeons to manipulate sutures within the eye or in areas where precision is required, such as in delicate eye surgeries like cataract surgery.

Option C: Corneoscleral forceps are specialized instruments used in eye surgery for handling the cornea and sclera, the outer layers of the eye. These forceps have a unique design that allows surgeons to securely grasp and manipulate these tissues during various procedures, such as corneal transplantation or scleral flap surgery.

Option D: Lens holding forceps are surgical instruments used in ophthalmic procedures involving the removal or manipulation of the lens of the eye. They are designed to securely grasp the lens during procedures such as cataract surgery or intraocular lens implantation, allowing surgeons to manipulate the lens safely and precisely.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with a unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, and excessive lacrimation. He also complains of hemifacial pain on clenching of teeth. On examination, pupillary reaction, light reflex, and accommodation reflex are normal. Which of the following marked nerves is involved in the above scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The above patient presents with features suggesting an involvement of the trigeminal nerve. The structure marked 3 is the trigeminal nerve.

Other marked structures:

• 1- Optic nerve. The normal visual field and light reflex rules out the involvement of the optic nerve.
• 2- Oculomotor nerve. Normal accommodation and pupillary reflex rule out the involvement of the oculomotor nerve.
• 4- Facial nerve. Absence of motor involvement of the face rule out the involvement of the facial nerve.

The trigeminal nerve leaves the anterior aspect of the pons as a small motor root and a large sensory root. The large sensory root expands to form the crescent-shaped trigeminal ganglion, which lies within a pouch of dura mater called the trigeminal or Meckel's cave. The ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular nerves arise from the anterior border of the ganglion.

Branches of the trigeminal nerve:

• The ophthalmic nerve (V1)

• Leaves the skull through the superior orbital fissure to enter the orbital cavity.
• Contains only sensory fibers

• Cornea (photophobia)
• The skin of the forehead, scalp, eyelids, and nose
• The mucous membrane of paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity

• The maxillary nerve (V2)

• Leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum.
• Contains only sensory fibers from

• Teeth of the upper jaw
• The skin of the face over the maxilla
• The mucous membrane of the nose, the maxillary sinus, and the palate

• The mandibular nerve (V3)

• Leaves the skull through the foramen ovale.
• Contains both sensory and motor fibers.
• Sensory from:

• The skin of the cheek, over mandible, and side of the head
• Teeth of the lower jaw and temporomandibular joint (hemifacial pain on clenching of teeth)
• The mucous membrane of the mouth and anterior part of the tongue

• Motor to:

• Muscles of mastication (pterygoids, masseter, and temporalis)
• Tensor tympani
• Anterior belly of digastric
• Mylohyoid
questions.learning: 3 The above patient presents with features suggesting an involvement of the trigeminal nerve. The structure marked 3 is the trigeminal nerve.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Calcitonin is a marker of which malignancy?
questions.explanation: Calcitonin is a highly specific tumor marker for Medullary thyroid cancer (MTC). MTC arises from the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid gland, which are physiologically responsible for the secretion of calcitonin. Serum calcitonin levels are used for the initial diagnosis, monitoring of treatment efficacy, and surveillance for recurrence in patients with MTC. Papillary (Option A) and Follicular (Option B) thyroid cancers arise from the follicular cells and use Thyroglobulin as their primary tumor marker. Anaplastic thyroid cancer (Option D) is a highly aggressive, undifferentiated malignancy that typically does not produce reliable biochemical markers. Medullary thyroid cancer can occur sporadically or as part of the Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) type 2 syndromes. Because MTC is often associated with germline mutations in the RET proto-oncogene, identifying an elevated calcitonin level often prompts genetic testing and screening of family members to detect the disease at a preventable stage
questions.learning: Calcitonin is a highly specific tumor marker for Medullary thyroid cancer (MTC). MTC arises from the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid gland, which are physiologically responsible for the secretion of calcitonin.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A baby playing unsupervised was brought with complaints of difficulty in swallowing for the last few hours. The X-ray image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
options: Soft tissue calcification in the neck
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Foreign body in the esophagus

The clinical picture of the child presenting with difficulty in swallowing and the chest X-rays (AP and lateral) showing a circular homogenous opacity in the neck region is suggestive of a foreign body (coin) lodged in the esophagus.

Foreign bodies commonly ingested by children are coins, disk batteries, and small toy items. In adults, it is usually a food bolus (mostly meat) that gets lodged.

The flat surface of a coin is seen on the anteroposterior view (AP view) and the edge is seen on the lateral view. This indicates that it is oriented in the coronal plane, which is seen when it is lodged in the esophagus (and not in the trachea).

Initial symptoms are choking, gagging, and coughing followed by excessive salivation, dysphagia, food refusal, vomiting, or pain in the neck and throat. Respiratory symptoms such as stridor, wheezing, cyanosis, or dyspnea are seen if the esophageal foreign body impinges on the larynx or tracheal wall.

Imaging with chest and abdominal X-rays should be performed in AP and lateral positions. Chest CT should always be performed if oesophageal perforation is suspected.

Endoscopic removal of the esophageal foreign body is the procedure of choice. It should be performed

1. Immediately in esophageal obstruction, disk batteries, and sharp pointed objects.
2. Within 12-24h in non-pointed objects, pointed objects in the stomach, and coins in the esophagus.
3. Non-urgent removal in objects in stomach >2.5cm in diameter, and disk battery in the stomach (up to 48h)

Other options:

Option A: For coins lodged in the trachea, the edge is seen anteroposteriorly view and the flat side is seen in the lateral view of the X-rays (oriented in the sagittal plane).

Option C: Artifacts refer to an appearance or unintended structure that is not normally seen on the radiograph and is produced by some artificial means. It can occur due to technical or processing errors while taking a radiograph.

Option D: Soft tissue calcification in the neck is due to physiologic or pathological conditions. Commonly encountered soft tissue calcifications in the head and neck region include tonsilloliths, carotid artery calcifications, and calcified stylohyoid ligaments.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not included as a component of the Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) program?
questions.explanation: The Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) program in India is a comprehensive health initiative focused on improving specific health outcomes. Its primary components include Safe motherhood (antenatal, intrapartum, and postpartum care), Children and newborn care (immunization and management of childhood illnesses), and the Screening and treatment of STIs and RTIs to ensure reproductive health. While Women education and empowerment (Option B) is a vital socio-economic goal and a critical determinant of health, it is not a direct clinical or structural component of the RCH program's service delivery framework. The program's interventions are specifically designed to reduce maternal, infant, and child mortality and morbidity through medical and nutritional support. Options A, C, and D are the foundational pillars of the RCH strategy, ensuring that essential health services reach mothers and children. Recognizing the specific boundaries of public health programs is necessary for correctly identifying the targeted medical interventions provided at primary and secondary healthcare levels

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following proteins functions as a pro-apoptotic factor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. BAX

Cell stress / DNA damage

↓

BAX / BAK activation

↓

Mitochondrial membrane permeabilization

↓

Cytochrome c release

↓

Caspase activation

↓

Apoptosis

BAX is a pro-apoptotic member of the BCL-2 family that promotes mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization. It facilitates release of cytochrome c from mitochondria, activating the intrinsic apoptotic pathway.

This leads to caspase activation and programmed cell death.

BCL-2, BCL-XL, and MCL-1 are anti-apoptotic proteins that inhibit mitochondrial apoptosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is a finding of large bowel obstruction?
options: Dilated loops of intestine with plica circularis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dilated loops with haustrations

Dilated bowel loops with haustrations is a feature of large bowel obstruction.

In large bowel obstruction, the colon is distended proximally with the distal portion collapsed. The colon is considered dilated if it is more than 6 cm in diameter while the cut off for caecum is 9cm.

Other options:

Dilated loops of the intestine with plica circularis (valvulae conniventes) and predominantly central loops are features of the small bowel obstruction. The small bowel is considered dilated if it is more than 3 cm in diameter.

The string of pearls sign is also a feature of small bowel obstruction seen in plain radiographs or CT. It represents a row of gas bubbles trapped between the valvulae conniventes.

Differences in small and large bowel obstruction on radiography are listed below:

Small bowel
Large bowel

Valvulae conniventes
Present in jejunum
Absent

No of Loops
Many
Few

Distribution of loops
Central
Peripheral

Haustra
Absent
Present

Diameter
3-5 cm
>5 cm

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the investigation shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The image displays a classic Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP), which is a contrast-enhanced X-ray study of the urinary tract. In this modality, radiopaque contrast is injected intravenously and excreted by the kidneys, opacifying the renal calyces, pelvis, ureters, and the bladder on serial X-rays. It is traditionally used to detect stones, obstructions, or structural anomalies. A Retrograde Pyelogram (Option B) involves injecting contrast directly through a ureteric catheter from below, rather than through the bloodstream. CT Urography (Option C) provides cross-sectional, 3D reconstructed images with much higher detail than plain X-ray based IVP. Magnetic Resonance Urography (Option D) uses T2-weighted sequences without ionizing radiation and does not show real-time excretion in the same manner. Despite the rise of CT, IVP remains a useful tool for evaluating basic urinary tract anatomy and function

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with a 3cm sub-areolar mass in her left breast. She reports bloody nipple discharge but denies pain, redness or systemic symptoms. On examination, the mass is firm and non-tender. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intraductal papilloma

The given clinical scenario of unilateral bloody nipple discharge with a palpable mass beneath the areola and histopathology showing a central fibrovascular core with papillae arborizing within the lumen are suggestive of a solitary intraductal papilloma.

Intraductal papilloma is a benign, proliferative breast disorder without atypia. It is defined as Localized hyperplasia of the ductal epithelium within the duct. According to the ANDI (Aberrations of normal development and involution of breast tissue) classification, it is an aberration of normal epithelial turnover. It comprises a central fibrovascular core and papillary projections of the epithelium and myoepithelial cells. The papillary lesions in a duct are of three types:

* Solitary papilloma

* Papillomatosis: five or more papillomas

* Juvenile papillomatosis, also called Swiss cheese disease

Intraductal papilloma is commonly seen in premenopausal women. It is the most common cause of spontaneous nipple discharge from a single duct. These papillomas are located close to the nipple and are associated with bloody nipple discharge. Sometimes, a palpable mass under the areola may be present.

A triple assessment, consisting of clinical examination, imaging, and pathology, should be performed to exclude carcinoma. Ultrasonography may reveal a dilated subareolar duct and a papillary growth within. A ductoscopy shows a firm, palpable nodule inside the duct. Most duct papillomas are located up to a distance of 5 cm from the nipple.

The treatment for single-duct discharge is microdochectomy, which involves making a tennis racquet-shaped incision and removing the papilloma and a single duct involved. Hadfield’s procedure(cone excision of ducts) is used when multiple ducts are involved.

Other options:

Option A. Ductal carcinoma in situ: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a neoplastic proliferation of epithelial cells limited by the basement membrane. It involves the ducts and lobules. It is not associated with a loss of E-cadherin expression. It typically presents as a suspicious area on a mammogram rather than a palpable mass with bloody discharge.

Option C. Lobular carcinoma in situ: Histologically, LCIS consists of a monomorphic population of cells with oval or round nuclei and small nucleoli involving ducts and lobules. Mucin-positive signet ring cells are commonly present. The histological image is given below:

Option D. Fibroadenoma: This is a benign breast tumor that is usually firm, rubbery, and mobile. They occur in women in their 20s and 30s, and they are frequently multiple and bilateral. Histology shows delicate and often myxoid stroma that resembles normal intralobular stroma. The epithelium may be surrounded by stroma (pericanalicular pattern) or compressed and distorted by it (intracanalicular pattern) as shown below:
