questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fracture of the jugular canal can present as
options: Loss of taste sensation in anterioir 2/3rd of tongue
Loss of taste sensation in posterior 1/3rd of tongue
Loss of general sensation in anterior 2/3rd of tongue
Loss of motor sensation in anterior 2/3rd of tongue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Loss of taste sensation in posterior 1/3rd of tongue

Fracture of the jugular canal affects glossopharyngeal nerve and presents as loss of taste sensation in the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue.

The lingual nerve which is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve gives general sensation, chorda tympani branch of facial nerve gives taste sensation for the anterior 2/3rd of tongue. Both taste and general sensation of the posterior 1/3rd is by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The muscles of the tongue, with the exception of palatoglossus, are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve. Palatoglossus is supplied via the pharyngeal plexus.

The other nerves passing through the jugular foramen are glossopharyngeal(cranial nerve IX), vagus(cranial nerve X), and accessory nerve(cranial nerve XI).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the correct dose of administration of antenatal steroids for lung maturity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dexamethasone 6 mg 12 hours apart 4 doses

The correct dose of administration of antenatal steroids for lung maturity is dexamethasone 6 mg 12 hours apart 4 doses.

Maternal administration of corticosteroids is advocated where the pregnancy is less than 34 weeks. This helps in fetal lung maturation. This is beneficial when the delivery is delayed beyond 48 hours of the first dose. The benefit persists as long as 18 days. Either betamethasone 12 mg IM 24 hours apart for two doses or dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses is given. Betamethasone is the steroid of choice (RCOG–2004).

Antenatal steroids also reduce the incidence of respiratory distress syndrome, necrotizing enterocolitis, intraventricular hemorrhage and patent ductus arteriosus.

Risks of antenatal corticosteroid use:

• Premature rupture of the membranes especially with evidence of infection, as the infection may flare-up
• Insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus where patients need insulin dose readjustment
• Transient reduction of fetal breathing and body movements.
questions.learning: Dexamethasone 6 mg 12 hours apart 4 doses — The correct dose of administration of antenatal steroids for lung maturity is dexamethasone 6 mg 12 hours apart 4 doses.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the maximum duration for TRALI to occur after blood transfusion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 6 hours

The maximum duration for TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) to occur after blood transfusion is upto 6 hours. TRALI is sudden-onset respiratory failure that occurs during or soon after blood transfusion.

The pathogenesis involves a two-hit hypothesis:

• Priming event - increased sequestration and sensitization of neutrophils in the microvasculature of the lung
• Second hit - the factor (most commonly MHC class I antigens) present in the transfused blood product activates the primed neutrophils
questions.learning: 6 hours The maximum duration for TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) to occur after blood transfusion is upto 6 hours. TRALI is sudden-onset respiratory failure that occurs during or soon after blood transfusion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Jones criteria for the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever has several major and minor criteria. Which of the following are included in the major or minor criteria of Jones criteria? 1. Carditis 2. Erythema nodosum 3. Polyarthralgia 4. Short PR interval 5. Sydenham chorea
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, and 5

The diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever is based on the Jones criteria, which include major and minor manifestations along with evidence of a preceding Group A streptococcal infection.

Jones Criteria (Acute Rheumatic Fever)

Major Criteria

• Carditis
• Polyarthritis
• Chorea
• Erythema marginatum
• Subcutaneous nodules

Minor Criteria

Clinical:

• Arthralgia
• Fever

Laboratory:

• Elevated ESR / CRP
• First-degree atrioventricular (AV) block
questions.learning: 1, 3, and 5 The diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever is based on the Jones criteria, which include major and minor manifestations along with evidence of a preceding Group A streptococcal infection.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the image?
questions.explanation: The image displays a classic uterine inversion, an obstetric emergency where the uterine fundus collapses into the cavity and protrudes through the cervix into the vagina. It is often caused by excessive cord traction or fundal pressure before the placenta has separated. The patient typically presents with sudden postpartum hemorrhage and shock that is often disproportionate to the visible blood loss. Uterine rupture (Option B) involves a tear in the uterine wall and usually presents with fetal distress and internal bleeding, not a protruding vaginal mass. A cervical polyp (Option C) is a small, benign growth that does not appear as a massive tissue protrusion. Vaginal vault prolapse (Option D) occurs gradually after a hysterectomy and is not an acute postpartum event. Immediate manual repositioning is required to save the patient's life
questions.learning: The image displays a classic uterine inversion, an obstetric emergency where the uterine fundus collapses into the cavity and protrudes through the cervix into the vagina.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Therapeutic index is used for assessing which of the following factors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Safety

Therapeutic index is used to assess the safety of the drug administered.

Therapeutic index = TD50/ED50

• TD50 (Median toxic dose) = Dose required to produce a toxic effect in 50% of animals tested.
• ED50 (Median effect dose) = Dose required to produce a therapeutic effect in 50% of the individuals.

Option B: Efficacy is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug. It expresses the effect produced by the receptors when bound by a certain drug.

Option C: Potency refers to the concentration (EC50) or dose (ED50) required to produce 50% of maximum effect where EC50 is the concentration of agonist resulting in a half-maximal response.

Option D: Median toxic dose is the dose required to produce a toxic effect in 50% of animals tested. Lethal dose is the dose required to kill 50% of animals tested.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Malaria detection on the field is done by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HRP2 antigen

In field settings, rapid diagnostic tests, such as those detecting Histidine-Rich Protein 2 (HRP2) antigen, are commonly used for malaria detection.

Rapid diagnostic tests are simple, quick, and require minimal resources, making them ideal for field use where laboratory facilities may be unavailable. HRP-2 antigen detection used in rapid diagnostic tests for malaria is specific for P. falciparum.

Rapid diagnostic tests are based on the detection of antigens using immunochromatographic methods. They are less sensitive than microscopy and cannot differentiate between species except P. falciparum. The 2 antigens detected are:

• pLDH (parasite lactate dehydrogenase)- pan malarial antigen
• HRP-2 (histidine-rich protein 2)- specific for P.falciparum.

Other options

Option A: Thick smears are more sensitive for detecting malaria parasites, they require laboratory facilities and skilled personnel, making them less practical for field settings.

Option B: Thin smears are used primarily for species identification and quantification of parasites, but like thick smears, they are unsuitable for field settings due to resource requirements.

Option D: Quantitative buffy coat (QBC): This method is highly sensitive but requires special equipment (a fluorescent microscope and centrifuge), making it unsuitable for field use.
questions.learning: HRP2 antigen — In field settings, rapid diagnostic tests, such as those detecting Histidine-Rich Protein 2 (HRP2) antigen, are commonly used for malaria detection.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The following image indicates:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Occulomotor palsy

The given image is suggestive of oculomotor nerve palsy.

The central image shows the primary position of gaze where the patient's left eye is deviated down and out with ptosis of the left eyelid. From the eye movements in other positions, it can be seen that adduction and elevation are absent and depression is reduced in the left eye. All of these findings are indicative of oculomotor nerve palsy.

3rd Cranial nerve(oculomotor nerve) palsy presents with:

• Ptosis due to weakness of levator palpebrae superioris muscle (LPS)
• Abduction and depression in the primary position (down and out) due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus(6th nerve supply) and superior oblique muscles(4th nerve supply)
• Dilated pupil and defective accommodation due to parasympathetic palsy (involvement of Edinger Westphal parasympathetic supply)
• Limited adduction, elevation and depression due to ipsilateral paralysis of medial rectus, inferior oblique and inferior rectus .

Option A: Trochlear(4th cranial) nerve palsy presents with superior oblique muscle paralysis.

Clinical findings of trochlear nerve palsy include:

•  Hypertropia (elevation) in the primary position
• Extorsion that is greatest in abduction
• Compensatory head posture with contralateral face turn and head tilt with chin slightly depressed. This position is assumed to avoid Diplopia.
• Limitation of depression
• Normal abduction and elevation.

The below given image depicts 4th cranial nerve palsy.

Option B: Lateral rectus palsy is seen in cases of isolated Abducens nerve palsy. These patients present with esotropia/convergent squint in primary position with limitation of abduction on the side of the lesion. This is due to unopposed action of the medial rectus muscle in the affected eye.

There is also a compensatory head turn towards the side of the lesion to reduce the symptom of Diplopia. The adduction is normal in lateral rectus palsy.

Option C: Internuclear opthalmoplegia occurs following an injury to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). A unilateral lesion to the MLF leads to the failure of adduction in the ipsilateral eye with a normal abduction of the contralateral eye.

The below given image depicts the pathogenesis of Inter nuclear opthalmoplegia in detail.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Shield ulcer is seen in which of the following?
questions.explanation: A shield ulcer is a specialized, serious complication seen in severe cases of Spring catarrh (also known as Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis or VKC). VKC is a chronic, bilateral, allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva, most common in young boys living in warm, dry climates. The ulcer is typically oval or transverse, located in the upper half of the cornea. It is thought to result from the mechanical rubbing of giant papillae ("cobblestones") on the upper tarsal conjunctiva against the corneal surface, combined with toxic inflammatory mediators. Phlyctenular conjunctivitis (Option B) involves small yellowish nodules at the limbus. Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (Option C) also causes corneal issues but the "shield ulcer" is specifically pathognomonic for VKC. Autoimmune conditions (Option D) can cause various peripheral corneal ulcers (like Mooren's) but not this specific type. Management of a shield ulcer is difficult, requiring intensive topical steroids, lubricants, and occasionally surgical debridement to promote healing and prevent permanent scarring

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is a true statement about obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD)?
options: Atypical antipsychotics is the first line treatment
Prevalence is 7 -10 percent in general population
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Depression is a common comorbidity

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is commonly associated with depression. The lifetime prevalence of the major depressive disorder in patients with OCD is 67 percent. Other common psychiatric comorbidities in patients with OCD are social phobia, alcohol use disorders, panic, and personality disorders.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) comprises symptoms that include intrusive thoughts, preoccupations, and compulsions. These recurrent obsessions or compulsions cause severe distress to the patient. The patient might have an obsession, a compulsion, or both.

An obsession is a thought, feeling, or sensation that is repetitive and intrusive. A compulsion is a conscious, recurrent behavior, eg: counting, checking, and are done to reduce the anxiety associated with the obsession. However, this act may not reduce the anxiety and might increase the anxiety even more.

Symptom patterns:

• Contamination - This is the most common symptom pattern of OCD.  The patient feels that the objects are contaminated. They repeatedly wash their hands or avoid touching objects which are thought to be contaminated. In extreme cases, patients may rub the skin off their hands due to excessive hand washing or may refuse to leave the house in fear of germs.
• Pathological doubt - This is the second most common symptom pattern. The patient presents with an obsession with doubt and a compulsion to check. This obsession arises due to possible danger or violence (e.g., forgetting to turn off the stove or not locking a door) which is followed by multiple trips to check, for example, if the stove is turned off, if the door is locked, etc.
• Intrusive thoughts -This is the third most common symptom pattern. These patients have intrusive obsessional thoughts without compulsion. These thoughts could be sexual or an aggressive act that the patient doesn't agree. The patients might report themselves to the police or confess to a spiritual leader.
• Symmetry - This is the fourth most common pattern which can lead to a compulsion of slowness. Patients can take hours to eat a meal or shave their faces.

Diagnosis:

1. Presence of obsessions, compulsions or both
2. Symptoms are time-consuming
3. Symptoms not related to substance abuse
4. Not better explained by other mental disorders

Treatment of OCD includes:

• Pharmacotherapy: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI) or clomipramine
• Behavioral therapy: Approaches include:

• exposure and response prevention
• desensitization
• thought stopping
• flooding
• implosion therapy
• aversive conditioning

A combination of behavioral and pharmacotherapy is most effective.

Other options

Option A - Atypical antipsychotics are not the first-line in the treatment of OCD. They can be given only when SSRIs and clomipramine (tricyclic antidepressant) are not effective.

Option B - The prevalence of OCD among the general population is 2-3 percent and not 7-10 percent.

Option D - Contamination is the most common obsession.
questions.learning: Depression is a common comorbidity Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is commonly associated with depression. The lifetime prevalence of the major depressive disorder in patients with OCD is 67 percent.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What type of cataract is typically seen on slit- lamp examination in a patient with a history of long-term corticosteroid use?
questions.explanation: Prolonged use of corticosteroids, whether topical, systemic, or inhaled, is a well-known cause of "Posterior Subcapsular Cataract" (PSC). On slit lamp examination, these appear as a granular, "bread-crumb" like opacity located in the central posterior cortex of the lens. PSCs are particularly disabling because they are located near the nodal point of the eye, causing significant glare and vision loss in bright light. Option A (Morgagnian) is a stage of age-related cataract where the cortex liquefies. Option C (Sunflower cataract) is characteristic of Wilson's disease (copper deposition). Option D (Snowflake cataract) is classic for uncontrolled diabetes mellitus. PSCs can also be seen in patients with chronic intraocular inflammation (uveitis) or high myopia. Because steroid-induced cataracts can occur rapidly, any patient on long-term steroid therapy must undergo regular ophthalmic examinations to monitor for both cataract formation and secondary ocular hypertension (glaucoma)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents to you with multiple anogenital warts. The biopsy of these lesions showed squamous atypia. Which of the following human papillomavirus types are considered high-risk?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HPV 18

Human papillomavirus (HPV) types 16 and 18 are considered high-risk types that are commonly implicated in cervical, vaginal and vulval cancer. Other high-risk types include HPV types 31, 33, and 35.

The E6 protein of high-risk types binds to the p53 gene while the E7 protein inactivates the pRb gene. p53 and pRb are tumor suppressor genes that when inactivated results in uncontrolled cell proliferation. The most common type of cancer seen is squamous cell carcinoma. The image below depicts vulval carcinoma which is also associated with HPV infection.

The image given above shows anogenital warts pointing to condyloma acuminata (venereal warts). It is commonly caused by HPV types 6 and 11. However, rarely HPV 16 and 18 can cause it too. It is sexually transmitted. Patients are advised not to involve in intercourse when active genital warts are present. It can appear discrete or may coalesce to resemble cauliflower-like growths. 20% of cases may develop into cervical, vaginal, or vulval cancers. Risk factors include oral contraceptives and pregnancy. The condition is diagnosed by colposcopy.

The presence of koilocytes on histopathological examination is pathognomonic of the virus. These are cells with irregular and hyperchromatic nuclei, perinuclear halo, and peripheral cytoplasmic condensation. These cells disappear when there are dysplastic changes.

The image below depicts koilocytes.

Other options:

Option A - HPV type 2 is responsible for common warts in non-genital regions.

Options C and D - HPV types 6 and 11 are responsible for anogenital warts and laryngeal papillomatosis.
questions.learning: HPV 18 Human papillomavirus (HPV) types 16 and 18 are considered high-risk types that are commonly implicated in cervical, vaginal and vulval cancer. Other high-risk types include HPV types 31, 33, and 35.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the outpatient department with pain, redness, and swelling around his great toe. His serum uric acid is elevated. His mother also reports that he frequently bites his lips and has spasticity and dystonia. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: The combination of juvenile gout (painful, swollen great toe with hyperuricemia) and the behavioral hallmark of self-mutilation (lip biting), along with spasticity, is diagnostic of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. This disorder results from a deficiency of Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). HGPRT normally recycles purines; without it, purines are shunted into the degradation pathway, producing excessive uric acid. Serum uric acid levels are typically very high (e.g., ). Homocysteine oxidase (Option A) and Dihydrothymidine oxidase (Option B) are not involved in purine metabolism or the Lesch-Nyhan phenotype. Xanthine oxidase (Option D) is actually the enzyme that produces uric acid; its deficiency would cause hypouricemia, not hyperuricemia. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is a rare X-linked condition, explaining why the patient is a male. Management focuses on lowering uric acid with allopurinol and managing neurological and behavioral symptoms with supportive therapy and physical restraints
questions.learning: The combination of juvenile gout (painful, swollen great toe with hyperuricemia) and the behavioral hallmark of self-mutilation (lip biting), along with spasticity, is diagnostic of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which instrument is used to measure both the humidity of air and its dew point temperature?
questions.explanation: A sling psychrometer is a specialized instrument used to measure the relative humidity and dew point of the air. It consists of two thermometers: a "dry-bulb" that measures the actual air temperature and a "wet-bulb" covered in a water-saturated wick. By whirling the instrument in the air, evaporation cools the wet-bulb; the difference between the two temperatures (the psychrometric depression) is then used with standardized tables to determine humidity. A Kata thermometer (Option B) is primarily used to measure the cooling power of air and low air velocities. A Barometer (Option C) measures atmospheric pressure. A Dial thermometer (Option D) provides a simple reading of the current temperature but cannot measure humidity on its own. Accurate measurement of air humidity is critical in occupational health to assess heat stress and in hospitals to maintain appropriate environmental conditions for patient care and equipment longevity. Psychrometers are fundamental tools in environmental sanitation and meteorology
questions.learning: A sling psychrometer is a specialized instrument used to measure the relative humidity and dew point of the air. It consists of two thermometers: a "dry-bulb" that measures the actual air temperature and a "wet-bulb" covered in a water-saturated wick.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Innate immunity forms the 1st line of defence. Why is it faster than adaptive immunity?
options: It is acquired genetically and is present since birth
It recognises pre-determined patterns against common pathogens
It cannot differentiate between the self and the foreign antigens
It forms a memory response following a previous infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It recognises pre-determined patterns against common pathogens

Innate immunity behaves like a pre-installed security system -always ON, no updates needed.

It works faster because it recognizes PAMPs (Pathogen-Associated Molecular Patterns) using PRRs (Pattern Recognition Receptors).

• These PAMPs are common, conserved structures across microbes:

• LPS (Gram-negative bacteria)
• Peptidoglycan (Gram-positive bacteria)
• dsRNA (viruses)

• PRRs are already present on immune cells like:

• Macrophages
• Dendritic cells
• Neutrophils

| Feature | Innate Immunity | Adaptive Immunity

| ------- | --------------- | -----------------

| Onset | Immediate (minutes–hours) | Delayed (days)

| Specificity | Non-specific | Highly specific

| Receptors | PRRs (germline encoded) | TCR/BCR (somatic recombination)

| Memory | No | Yes

| Response to repeat infection | Same | Enhanced

| Examples | Macrophages, NK cells | B cells, T cells

A. It is acquired genetically and is present since birth

Partially true but NOT the reason for speed

• Yes, innate immunity is genetically encoded
• But being present ≠ being fast
• Speed is due to instant recognition (PRRs), not just presence

C. It cannot differentiate between the self and the foreign antigens

• Innate immunity can distinguish self vs non-self
• Uses:

• Absence of “self markers”
• Detection of danger signals (DAMPs)

• If it couldn’t → constant autoimmunity (which is not the case)

D. It forms a memory response following a previous infection

• That is a feature of adaptive immunity
• Memory = B cells + T cells
• Innate immunity = no classical memory (except minor “trained immunity” concept)
questions.learning: It recognises pre-determined patterns against common pathogens Innate immunity behaves like a pre-installed security system -always ON, no updates needed.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: While doing a subclavian venous catheterization, the patient suddenly desaturated and on examination of the chest, there was hyper resonance in the apical area of the right lung. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumothorax

A common complication of subclavian vein catheterization is pneumothorax and it is the diagnosis in this case as there is hyper resonance and sudden desaturation.

However, the most common complication of a central line insertion is an arterial puncture.

Complications of central vein catheterization are

* Arterial puncture- this is the most common complication.

* Cardiac tamponade is the most important life-threatening complication. It occurs as a result of puncture of intrapericardial superior vena cava, right atrium, or right ventricle.

* Pneumothorax- injury to the underlying pleura may lead to pneumothorax. This is more common in subclavian vein catheterization.

* Chylothorax can occur particularly in left subclavian vein catheterization. But it is not the most common.

* Injury to the associated nerves like brachial plexus, stellate ganglion, phrenic nerve, or vocal cords.

* Thromboembolism leading to venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism is more common with femoral veins.

* Infections

Central venous catheterization is the insertion of the catheter into a large central vein. The veins preferred largely depend on the underlying disease in the patient, the clinical setting, and the expertise of the doctor.

The internal jugular vein is preferred when the patient has:

* Bleeding diathesis- Bleeding from this vein can be easily detected and can be controlled with pressure.

* Pneumothorax- The lesser risk of injury to the lung

* Needs cardiac pacing- right internal jugular vein is used.

Femoral or subclavian veins can be used in patients when the neck is immobilized using a cervical collar.

The below image shows subclavian vein catheterization.

The below image shows catheterisation into jugular vein

Below image shows radiograph of subclavian vein catherisation

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman is diagnosed with simple endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. What would be the most appropriate treatment option for her condition?
questions.explanation: For a 55-year-old (postmenopausal) woman with endometrial hyperplasia, the presence of atypia is the most critical factor in determining treatment. Atypical hyperplasia is considered a premalignant condition, with a roughly 30% risk of progressing to or harboring co-existing endometrial carcinoma. In a postmenopausal patient who has completed childbearing, the definitive and most suitable treatment is a simple hysterectomy (Option A). This removes the source of potential malignancy entirely. Medical management with progestogens like Medroxyprogesterone (Option B) or a Levonorgestrel-IUS (Option C) is generally reserved for younger patients wishing to preserve fertility or those unfit for surgery. Radiotherapy (Option D) is used for diagnosed invasive cancer, not for premalignant hyperplasia. Therefore, given the high risk of occult carcinoma associated with atypia in this age group, surgical removal of the uterus is the standard of care to ensure complete oncological safety

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the underlying condition as shown in the below radiograp
questions.explanation: The radiograph of the newborn suggests imperforate anus, a congenital anomaly in which the anal opening is absent or obstructed, preventing the normal passage of stool. Imperforate anus is part of a spectrum of anorectal malformations, which vary in severity and complexity. It occurs in approximately 1 in 5,000 live births and can affect both males and females. On the radiograph, there is an absence of gas in the rectum and sigmoid colon, indicating distal bowel obstruction. The presence of abdominal distension further supports this diagnosis, as accumulation of intestinal contents leads to swelling of the abdomen. Reasons for excluding other options : Meningocele is a neural tube defect involving herniation of meninges and is not identified on an abdominal radiograph. Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung’s disease) causes bowel obstruction but typically shows gas patterns extending to the colon and does not involve absence of the anal opening. Pyloric stenosis leads to vomiting due to gastric outlet obstruction and does not affect the distal bowel or rectal gas pattern
questions.learning: The radiograph of the newborn suggests imperforate anus, a congenital anomaly in which the anal opening is absent or obstructed, preventing the normal passage of stool.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Nuclear signalling pathways are all except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rat proteins

Rat proteins are not nuclear signalling pathways. Recombinant rat IFN- is a bioactive protein intended for use in cell culture applications.

Importin:

• Transporting protein molecules into nucleus by binding to specific recognition sequences, called Nuclear Localization Sequences (NLS).
• 2 subunits, importin α and importin β.

Caveolins:

• Family of integral membrane proteins that are principal components of caveolae membranes
• Involved in receptor-independent endocytosis.
• Acts as scaffolding proteins within caveolar membranes by compartmentalizing and concentrating signaling molecules.

NF-kB

• Part of a prototypical proinflammatory signaling pathway
• based on the role of NF-κB in the expression of proinflammatory genes including cytokines, chemokines, and adhesion molecules

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old female presents with generalized swelling, facial puffiness, hypertension, and frothy urine. She also reports a history of recurrent oral ulcers, photosensitivity, and intermittent joint pain. Investigations reveal positive ANA and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, decreased serum C3 and C4 levels, and proteinuria of 4.2 g/day. What is the most likely underlying mechanism responsible for her renal injury?
options: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis causing glomerular damage
Formation and deposition of immune complexes in the glomeruli with subsequent complement activation
Autoantibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Formation and deposition of immune complexes in the glomeruli with subsequent complement activation

The patient has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with lupus nephritis, characterized by proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), edema, hypertension, positive ANA, anti-dsDNA antibodies, and low C3/C4 levels, photosensitivity, oral ulcers and arthritis. The renal injury in lupus nephritis is caused by Type III hypersensitivity, in which circulating antigen-antibody immune complexes deposit in the glomeruli, activate the classical complement pathway, and trigger inflammation, leading to glomerular damage.

Why not the other options?

• A. ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis causing glomerular damage: Seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; typically ANCA-positive and complement levels are normal.
• B. T-lymphocyte-mediated cytotoxic injury (Type IV hypersensitivity): Characteristic of diseases such as contact dermatitis and type 1 diabetes mellitus, not lupus nephritis.
• D. Autoantibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane: Seen in Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease), which presents with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which structures pass between superior and middle constrictor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IX nerve (Glossopharyngeal Nerve)

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) passes between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictor muscles along with the stylopharyngeus muscle.

Key anatomical concept (gaps of constrictors):

1.      Above superior constrictor:

o    Levator veli palatini

o    Auditory (Eustachian) tube

o    Tensor velu palatini

o    Ascending pharyngeal artery

2.      Between superior & middle constrictor:

o    Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

o    Stylopharyngeus muscle

3.      Between middle & inferior constrictor:

o    Internal laryngeal nerve

o    Superior laryngeal vessels

4.      Below inferior constrictor:

o    Recurrent laryngeal nerve

o    Inferior laryngeal vessels
questions.learning: IX nerve (Glossopharyngeal Nerve) — The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) passes between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictor muscles along with the stylopharyngeus muscle.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely condition affecting the umbilical region of a 39-year-old obese man who has recently begun exercising at the gym?
questions.explanation: The image shows a rounded swelling directly at the umbilicus in an adult obese man who recently started exercising. This is typical of an umbilical hernia, where abdominal contents protrude through a weakness in the umbilical ring. Increased intra-abdominal pressure (such as during exercise or obesity) is a common precipitating factor. Umbilical hernias in adults usually present as a central bulge at the navel, which may become more prominent on straining or standing and may reduce on lying down. Hy other options are incorrect: (A) Omphalocele : A congenital condition in newborns, where abdominal organs herniate into a sac at the umbilicus. Not seen in adults. (B) Gastroschisis : Another congenital defect, where bowel loops protrude outside the abdomen without a covering sac, usually to the right of the umbilicus. Again, only in newborns. (D) Paraumbilical hernia : Occurs adjacent to (not exactly at) the umbilicus. The swelling in the image is clearly central, not lateral
questions.learning: The image shows a rounded swelling directly at the umbilicus in an adult obese man who recently started exercising. This is typical of an umbilical hernia, where abdominal contents protrude through a weakness in the umbilical ring.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Inferior thyroid artery is the branch of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyrocervical trunk

Inferior thyroid artery is a branch of thyrocervical trunk, which in turn, is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. The inferior thyroid artery loops upwards anterior to the medial border of the scalenus anterior, turns medially just below the sixth cervical transverse process, and then descends on longus colli to the lower border of the thyroid gland.

Relations between the terminal branches and recurrent laryngeal nerve are very variable and of considerable surgical importance.
questions.learning: Thyrocervical trunk Inferior thyroid artery is a branch of thyrocervical trunk, which in turn, is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Most likely diagnosis of the image given below?
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates a severe open neural tube defect characterized by the complete absence of the cranial vault and the exposure of the brain tissue (area cerebrovasculosa), which is the definition of anencephaly. If the spinal column is also open, it is termed craniorachischisis. Microcephaly (Option A) involves a small but intact skull and brain. Myelomeningocele (Option C) is a localized protrusion of the spinal cord and meninges through a bony defect, usually in the lumbosacral region. Cervical spina bifida (Option D) is a localized spinal defect in the neck. Anencephaly results from the failure of the cranial neuropore to close during the 4th week of gestation, as discussed in Q.229. This is a lethal condition, and most affected fetuses are either stillborn or die shortly after birth. Universal periconceptional folic acid supplementation has dramatically reduced the incidence of this devastating malformation
questions.learning: The image demonstrates a severe open neural tube defect characterized by the complete absence of the cranial vault and the exposure of the brain tissue (area cerebrovasculosa), which is the definition of anencephaly.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with continuous diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, bloating, and weight loss over the past two weeks. She reports recent camping in a rural area and consumption of untreated stream water. On examination, her temperature is normal, and mild tenderness is noted in the right upper quadrant. Stool analysis reveals trophozoites and cysts, with microscopic observation showing the characteristic “falling leaf” motility. Which organism is most likely responsible for her symptoms?
questions.explanation: The history of drinking untreated stream water during a camping trip, followed by bloating, flatulence, and "greasy" or continuous diarrhea, is the classic presentation for Giardiasis. The pathognomonic laboratory finding for Giardia lamblia is the observation of pear-shaped trophozoites with a "falling leaf" motility on a wet mount of fresh stool. Giardia trophozoites use their ventral sucking discs to attach to the intestinal mucosa, leading to malabsorption and weight loss. Salmonella typhi (Option A) causes enteric fever, characterized by high fever and "pea soup" diarrhea, which is inconsistent with the patient's normal temperature. Entamoeba histolytica (Option B) causes amoebic dysentery, typically presenting with bloody stools and trophozoites that may contain ingested RBCs, rather than "falling leaf" motility. Cryptosporidium parvum (Option D) also causes waterborne diarrhea, especially in immunocompromised individuals, but is identified by acid-fast staining of oocysts, not by the distinctive flagellated motility of Giardia. Thus, Giardia lamblia is the only diagnosis fitting all clinical and microscopic clues
questions.learning: The history of drinking untreated stream water during a camping trip, followed by bloating, flatulence, and "greasy" or continuous diarrhea, is the classic presentation for Giardiasis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a girl who has normal language development but predominantly focuses on watching her own hands and shows minimal social interaction with others?
questions.explanation: Rett's Syndrome is the correct diagnosis. A girl with normal early development who subsequently shows hand-wringing/hand-watching stereotypies and social withdrawal is the classic presentation of Rett's syndrome — an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder occurring exclusively in females. Key Diagnostic Features: 1. Occurs exclusively in females 2. Normal early development followed by regression 3. Characteristic hand stereotypies — wringing, watching, mouthing 4. Social withdrawal and loss of purposeful hand use 5. Language may be preserved initially then regresses Why other options are wrong: (A) ADHD is incorrect because ADHD presents with inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity — not hand stereotypies or social withdrawal. No characteristic hand-focusing behavior occurs in ADHD. (B) Autism is incorrect because while autism shows social withdrawal, it occurs in both sexes, lacks the characteristic hand-watching stereotypies and normal early developmental period followed by regression specific to Rett's. (C) Asperger's Syndrome is incorrect because Asperger's presents with normal intelligence, social difficulties, and restricted interests — no hand stereotypies, regression, or gender specificity as seen in Rett's syndrome. **************
questions.learning: Rett's Syndrome is the correct diagnosis. A girl with normal early development who subsequently shows hand-wringing/hand-watching stereotypies and social withdrawal is the classic presentation of Rett's syndrome — an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The audiogram of a patient who presented with a gradually progressive hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo is given below. Which among the following would be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ménière's disease

The given audiogram is seen in Ménière's disease in its early stages. It shows an upsloping/ascending curve suggesting that the lower frequencies are affected first.

Presbycusis, ototoxicity, and sound-induced hearing loss have downsloping audiograms since the higher frequencies are affected first in these conditions.

Points to remember in PTA audiogram:

* AC abnormal, BC normal, Air-bone gap present – conductive deafness

* Downsloping/descending audiogram- higher frequencies affected first like in presbycusis, ototoxicity, noise induced hearing loss.

* Upsloping/ascending audiogram - lower frequencies are affected first like in early stages of Meniere's disease.

* U shaped/trough shaped/cookie bite shaped audiogram suggests midfrequency hearing loss and is seen in congenital hearing loss and cochlear otosclerosis.

* Acoustic dip - characteristic dip in both AC and BC at 4000 Hz

* Carhartz notch - dip at 2000 Hz in BC curve
questions.learning: Ménière's disease — The given audiogram is seen in Ménière's disease in its early stages. It shows an upsloping/ascending curve suggesting that the lower frequencies are affected first.

options: Having a disease of chronic origin

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Match the following:

A. Urine bag
B. Nasogastric tube
C. Underwater seal bag
D. Suction cannula
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4

A-3, B-1, C-2, and D-4 is the correct option.

A: Uro bags are used for the collection of urine. They are usually attached to Foley's catheter, which is placed to drain the bladder (commonly in postoperative patients).

B: Nasogastric tube/Ryle’s tube is used for nasogastric feeding/stomach wash/aspiration.

C: An underwater seal bag is used for the collection of drainage fluid from the thoracic cavity. It acts as a one-way valve allowing air to leave the pleural cavity, but it cannot be drawn back in by the negative pressure that is created in the intrathoracic cavity.

D: A metallic suction cannula is used to clear the operative field by suctioning secretions/blood and aspirating the fluid from various cysts and in a procedure like a hydrocele.
questions.learning: A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4 A-3, B-1, C-2, and D-4 is the correct option. A: Uro bags are used for the collection of urine.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Identify the correct sequence regarding the family cycle?
options: Formation, extension, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction, dissolution, extinction
Formation, extension, complete extension, complete contraction, contraction, dissolution, extinction
Extension, Formation, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction, dissolution, extinction
Formation, extension, complete extension, con-traction, complete contraction, extinction, dissolution
questions.explanation: The family life cycle describes the standard developmental stages a family unit passes over time. The correct physiological and sociological sequence begins with Formation (marriage). This is followed by Extension, as the first child is born, and Complete Extension when the final child arrives. The Contraction phase begins as the first child leaves the home, progressing to Complete Contraction when all children have moved out (the "empty nest"). Dissolution occurs with the death of one spouse, and the cycle ends in Extinction when the remaining spouse passes away. Options B, C, and D present incorrect chronological orders of these events. Understanding these stages is essential for public health planning, as the health needs and socio-economic risks vary significantly between a family in the extension phase versus the complete contraction phase. For example, geriatric care becomes the priority during dissolution, while maternal and child health dominates the extension phases. This framework helps clinicians provide age-appropriate screening and support to families
questions.learning: The family life cycle describes the standard developmental stages a family unit passes over time. The correct physiological and sociological sequence begins with Formation (marriage).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 77-year-old woman is found dead in her home. On autopsy, hemopericardium secondary to ventricular wall rupture is seen. How long before her death did she probably have a myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3–7 days

Free wall rupture typically occurs during the period when the infarcted myocardium is at its structurally weakest — usually day 3 to day 7 post-MI (occasionally up to \~10 days, rarely beyond 2 weeks).

Why this timing:

• By day 1–3, coagulative necrosis has occurred, but the tissue is still reasonably cohesive.
• Around days 3–7, macrophages actively phagocytose and digest the necrotic myofibers (myomalacia cordis), and neutrophilic/granulation tissue infiltration causes maximal structural weakening — collagen deposition hasn't yet caught up to provide tensile strength.
• This makes the ventricular wall most vulnerable to rupture under intraventricular pressure during this window.
• By >2 weeks, granulation tissue matures into fibrous scar, which is mechanically stronger and resistant to rupture.
questions.learning: 3–7 days Free wall rupture typically occurs during the period when the infarcted myocardium is at its structurally weakest — usually day 3 to day 7 post-MI (occasionally up to \~10 days, rarely beyond 2 weeks).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with elevated blood pressure and an 8-hour history of left-sided facial paralysis and weakness. CT scan is normal. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with signs of an ischemic stroke (facial paralysis and weakness). A normal CT scan in this setting is expected, as ischemic changes often take 12–24 hours to appear on non-contrast CT. The crucial factor for the next step is the timing: the symptoms have persisted for 8 hours. Intravenous thrombolysis (Option C) is strictly limited to a window of 4.5 hours from symptom onset; therefore, she is ineligible. Intravenous labetalol (Option B) is only indicated if the BP is (for thrombolysis) or (for general management). Her BP of should be allowed to remain high to maintain cerebral perfusion (permissive hypertension). Oral Nifedipine (Option D) is contraindicated due to the risk of precipitous BP drops. Therefore, because she is outside the thrombolysis window and her BP does not meet emergency thresholds, the definitive next step is supportive observation and neurological monitoring
questions.learning: The patient presents with signs of an ischemic stroke (facial paralysis and weakness). A normal CT scan in this setting is expected, as ischemic changes often take 12–24 hours to appear on non-contrast CT.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with a history of treated tuberculosis now presents with hemoptysis. Based on the given chest X-ray, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The history of a prior TB infection combined with a Chest X-ray showing a solid mass within a pre-existing upper-lobe cavity is highly suggestive of an Aspergilloma (fungal ball). The characteristic radiological sign is the Monod sign, where a thin crescent of air surrounds the solid fungal mass. Hemoptysis is the most common and serious symptom, often occurring when the fungus erodes into adjacent blood vessels. Bronchogenic carcinoma (Option A) can also present with hemoptysis but is usually an irregular mass rather than a mass inside a cavity. Hydatid cysts (Option C) are fluid-filled and have a different appearance (like the "water-lily sign"). A lung abscess (Option D) typically shows a cavity with an air-fluid level and acute symptoms. While asymptomatic aspergillomas can be observed, those causing significant hemoptysis often require surgical resection or bronchial artery embolization, as the fungal ball is largely inaccessible to systemic antifungals
questions.learning: The history of a prior TB infection combined with a Chest X-ray showing a solid mass within a pre-existing upper-lobe cavity is highly suggestive of an Aspergilloma (fungal ball).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following features differentiate delirium from dementia in Alzheimer's disease?
options: Acuity of onset and loss of consciousness
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acuity of onset and loss of consciousness

Delirium is characterized by acute onset of symptoms and is often accompanied by diminished or loss of consciousness and cognition. This feature is useful to clinically differentiate between delirium and dementia.

Dementia is a group of diseases marked by chronic, progressive cognitive impairment with clear consciousness.
questions.learning: Acuity of onset and loss of consciousness Delirium is characterized by acute onset of symptoms and is often accompanied by diminished or loss of consciousness and cognition.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with loss of sensation on the lateral aspect of the sole. Which of the following nerve roots is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. S1

The lateral aspect of the sole corresponds to the S1 dermatome, supplied via branches of the tibial nerve.

S1 root involvement is classically associated with sensory loss over the lateral foot and sole, often seen in L5–S1 disc pathology.

L4 and L5 supply medial leg and dorsum of foot, while S2 mainly supplies the posterior thigh and perineal region.
questions.learning: S1 The lateral aspect of the sole corresponds to the S1 dermatome, supplied via branches of the tibial nerve. S1 root involvement is classically associated with sensory loss over the lateral foot and sole, often seen in L5–S1 disc pathology.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the procedure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myelography

The procedure depicted in the image represents myelography.

Myelography is a procedure used to evaluate spinal conditions. X-ray myelography can be used to evaluate the spinal canal in patients with spondylolisthesis. While MRI has largely replaced X-ray myelography it is done when there is a contraindication to MRI (Eg; non-compatible pacemaker, severe claustrophobia).
questions.learning: Myelography — The procedure depicted in the image represents myelography. Myelography is a procedure used to evaluate spinal conditions.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Egg proteins are considered to be the best among food proteins because: I. Of their biological value II. Of their digestibility III. They contain all the essential amino acids IV. Their calorie content is higher than proteins of vegetable sources Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and III

Egg protein is considered the reference (gold standard) protein because it has a high biological value, is highly digestible, and contains all the essential amino acids in optimal proportions required for human growth and tissue repair.

Why is B correct?

• I. High biological value ✅

• Egg protein has the highest biological value (\~100) among natural food proteins.

• II. High digestibility ✅

• Nearly 97–98% of egg protein is digested and absorbed.

• III. Contains all essential amino acids ✅

• Egg is a complete protein, providing all essential amino acids in adequate amounts.

• IV. Their calorie content is higher than proteins of vegetable sources ❌

• Calories depend on the amount of protein and fat, not on the protein source. Both animal and vegetable proteins provide 4 kcal/g.
questions.learning: I, II and III Egg protein is considered the reference (gold standard) protein because it has a high biological value, is highly digestible, and contains all the essential amino acids in optimal proportions required for human growth and tissue repair.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is represented by each of the following growth curves?
options: 1- Brain, 2- Waldeyer's ring, 3- somatic growth, 4- Testicular growth
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1- Brain, 2- Waldeyer's ring, 3- somatic growth, 4- Testicular growth

The correct answer is 1- Brain, 2-  Waldeyer's ring, 3- somatic growth, 4- Testicular growth.

Curve 1: The neural growth(brain) attains 90% of the growth by the age of 2 years.

Curve 2: The tonsils are collections of lymphatic tissue located within the pharynx. They collectively form a ringed arrangement, known as Waldeyer’s ring. Tonsils/lymphatic growth in children occur between 4-8 years of age and then shrink down in adult age.

Curve 3: Somatic growth shows a sigmoid curve, rapid growth in the initial years, and then during puberty.

Curve 4: Testicular growth/Gonadal growth starts during puberty, before that the curve is flat.
questions.learning: 1- Brain, 2- Waldeyer's ring, 3- somatic growth, 4- Testicular growth The correct answer is 1- Brain, 2- Waldeyer's ring, 3- somatic growth, 4- Testicular growth.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy has been observed by his parents to be increasingly clumsy for the past 6 months. On physical examination, there is a cauliflower-like growth in the left eye along with leukocoria and an absent red reflex. The microscopic appearance of the specimen shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Which is the causative gene in the given condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rb gene

The clinical history of a boy presenting with progressive clumsiness and eye findings such as leucocoria, absent red reflex, and cauliflower like growth along with the microscopic finding of Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes is highly suggestive of retinoblastoma, which occurs due to a mutation in the Rb gene located on chromosome 13q14.

Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision.

Clinical features of retinoblastoma:

* Present within the first two years of life

* Leukocoria

* Strabismus

* Painful red eye with secondary glaucoma

* Orbital inflammation mimicking orbital or pre-septal cellulitis.

* Orbital invasion or visible extraocular growth may occur in neglected cases.

* Metastatic disease involving regional lymph nodes and the brain before the detection of ocular involvement is rare.

Signs:

* An intraretinal tumor is a homogeneous, dome-shaped white lesion that becomes irregular, often with white flecks of calcification.

* An endophytic tumor projects into the vitreous as a white mass that may "seed" into the gel.

* An exophytic tumor forms multilobular subretinal white masses and causes an overlying retinal detachment.

Investigations:

* Red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope is a simple screening test for leukocoria.

* Dilated fundus examination using indirect ophthalmoscope

* MRI of the orbit + brain is the investigation of choice.

The HPE image below shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, the clustering of small blue cuboidal or short columnar cells around a central lumen.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy. The commonly used three-drug regimen is the CVE regimen consisting of vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy. Enucleation is done when:

* Tumor involves more than half of the retina

* Optic nerve is involved

* Glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved

In the stage of extraocular extension, the globe bursts through the sclera, usually near the limbus or the optic disc. This is followed by rapid fungation and involvement of extraocular tissues resulting in marked proptosis. Distant metastasis occurs through the lymphatic spread and the direct extension by continuity to the optic nerve and brain.

Other options:

Option B: COL5A1 mutation affects type 5 collagen. This mutation is seen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Option C: Retinitis pigmentosa occurs due to inherited or acquired mutations in the rhodopsin gene.

Option D: NOTCH1 is the most commonly affected gene in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL).

questions.text: What is the pattern of inheritance in neural tube defects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Multifactorial inheritance

The pattern of inheritance in neural tube defects(NTDs) is multifactorial inheritance.

Multifactorial inheritance refers to traits that are caused by a combination of inherited, environmental, and stochastic factors. NTDs and a number of other congenital malformations, such as cleft lip and palate, can recur in families, but inheritance for the majority of affected individuals does not occur in a straightforward, mendelian inheritance pattern. In this situation, multiple genes and environmental factors together likely contribute to the pathogenesis.

These include the following:

Children (congenital malformation)

Adults

Pyloric stenosis

Neural tube defects

Congenital heart defects

Congenital dislocation of hip

Cleft lip and cleft palate

Diabetes Mellitus

Hypertension

Coronary heart disease

Gout

Schizophrenia

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient was brought to the ER after RTA, his RR is 25/min, BP is 80/45mmHg. On examination, hyper-resonance is heard over the left side of the chest. The chest X-ray performed is given below. What would be the appropriate management in this case?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS
Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS

The given clinical scenario and the given chest radiograph are suggestive of pneumothorax. It is managed by inserting wide-bore needle in 5th ICS followed by placing an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS.

Tension pneumothorax and simple pneumothorax have similar signs, symptoms, and examination findings, but hypotension qualifies the pneumothorax as a tension pneumothorax.

Immediate management includes inserting a wide-bore needle in the 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line.

Definitive management includes insertion of the intercostal tube in the triangle of safety. If a sucking wound is present, then it is covered with gauze pieces and taped on 3 sides.

Remember: (Acc to ATLS 10th edition)

* In adults, needle thoracotomy location changed to 5th ICS mid axillary line from 2nd ICS midclavicular line.

* In the pediatric age group, the thoracotomy location remains at the 2nd ICS midclavicular line.
questions.learning: Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS The given clinical scenario and the given chest radiograph are suggestive of pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with pain and swelling of the right knee. Radiography reveals an eccentric, lytic “soap-bubble” lesion involving the epiphysis of the distal femur. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray shows a displaced patellar fracture in a 25-year-old presenting with pain and swelling of the right knee. The white arrow points to fragmentation and displacement of patellar fragments, confirming patellar fracture. Key Radiological Features visible: 1. Disrupted patellar continuity with visible fragment separation 2. Displaced bony fragments near the patella 3. Soft tissue swelling around the knee joint 4. Arrow specifically indicating the fracture site Why other options are wrong: (B) Tibial fracture is incorrect because the tibial cortex appears completely intact without any visible fracture line, periosteal reaction, or bony displacement in the tibial region. (C) Foreign body is incorrect because the radio-opaque opacity seen represents displaced bony patellar fragments — not an extrinsic foreign body. The density corresponds anatomically to the patella rather than an external object. (D) Femur fracture is incorrect because the distal femur appears structurally intact with no visible cortical break, fracture line, or displacement of femoral fragments anywhere in the image

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: 2 medical students are conducting a study to see the effects of acclimatization at high altitudes. Which of the following will not be seen in the same?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoventilation

Hypoventilation is not a part of high-altitude acclimatization.

A person constantly exposed to high altitude slowly acclimatizes to the low PaO2 so that the deleterious effects of the same can be reduced. This occurs mainly via the following mechanisms:

* Increased pulmonary ventilation

* Increase RBC and Hb

* Increased diffusing capacity of the lungs

* Increased vascularity of the peripheral tissues

* Increased ability of the tissue cells to use O2, despite low Po2.

Increased pulmonary ventilation: Low PO2 immediately stimulates the arterial chemoreceptors and causes increased alveolar ventilation. The immediate increase may blow off large quantities of CO2, lowering PCO2 and increasing pH which in turn may inhibit the brain stem respiratory centre via peripheral chemoreceptors. But this effect fades away in a few days and the respiratory centre activity returns to normal. Continued exposure to high altitude further increase the ventilation

Increase in red blood cells and hemoglobin concentration: Hypoxia triggers increased RBC production. Hematocrit slowly increases even up to 60%, and blood volume rises and together leading to hemoglobin and myoglobin rise

Increased diffusing capacity after acclimatization: Pulmonary capillary volume expands leading to an increased surface area of diffusion while an increase of pulmonary volume occurs which also increases the surface area of diffusion. Pulmonary arterial pressure rises leading to the opening of normally poorly perfused areas of the lung whereby diffusion further increases

Peripheral circulatory system changes during acclimatization: There is an initial rise in cardiac output to compensate for the low RBC and Hb which later falls to normal once these values rise due to erythropoiesis. Capillary angiogenesis occurs to improve blood flow, especially in the non-pulmonary tissues

Cellular acclimatization. Changes also occur at the cellular level with an increase in numbers of mitochondria and cellular respiration in organisms living at high altitudes than the ones living at sea level.
questions.learning: Hypoventilation Hypoventilation is not a part of high-altitude acclimatization. A person constantly exposed to high altitude slowly acclimatizes to the low PaO2 so that the deleterious effects of the same can be reduced.

questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents with recurrent renal calculi, proximal muscle weakness, and low mood. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated serum PTH with normal serum calcium. Primary hyperparathyroidism is suspected. Which of the following is the investigation of choice for preoperative localization of the abnormal gland?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tc-99m sestamibi scan

• Recurrent renal stones + proximal weakness + depression → classic hyperparathyroid symptom cluster
• ↑ PTH with normal Ca → early / normocalcemic primary hyperparathyroidism

Why Tc-99m Sestamibi is IOC

• Mechanism: Radiotracer (Tc-99m sestamibi) is taken up by mitochondria-rich parathyroid adenoma cells
• Shows persistent uptake in abnormal parathyroid tissue (vs thyroid washout)
• High sensitivity for detecting single adenoma (most common cause)

Step 4: Why not other options?

• A) Neck ultrasound

• Operator dependent
• Misses ectopic glands

• B) MRI neck

• Used only if sestamibi inconclusive

• D) CT neck

• 4D-CT used in difficult/recurrent cases, not first-line

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the muscle that is defective in the given image.
questions.explanation: The image illustrates the Trendelenburg sign, where the pelvis drops toward the unsupported side during the swing phase of gait. This indicates a weakness or paralysis of the hip abductors on the stance leg side, specifically the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus. These muscles are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. Normally, they contract on the weight-bearing side to keep the pelvis level. The gluteus maximus (Option B) is the primary extensor of the hip. The piriformis (Option C) and obturator internus (Option D) are lateral rotators of the hip. A positive Trendelenburg sign can be caused by superior gluteal nerve injury, hip dislocation, or fractures of the greater trochanter. Patients often compensate for this weakness by leaning their trunk toward the affected stance leg, a movement known as a Trendelenburg gait or compensated gluteal lurch. This is a fundamental clinical sign in orthopedics and neurology for assessing hip stability

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of leg swelling accompanied by diarrhea. Several family members report experiencing similar symptoms, and mustard oil is commonly used in their household diet. Based on this history, what is the most likely cause of her condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of multiple family members developing acute edema (leg swelling) and gastrointestinal symptoms (loose stools) after consuming mustard oil is pathognomonic for Epidemic Dropsy. This condition is caused by the contamination of mustard oil with argemone oil, which contains the toxic alkaloid Sanguinarine. Sanguinarine causes widespread capillary leakage and heart failure, leading to the characteristic edema. Clavine alkaloids (Option A) are associated with ergotism. BOAA (-oxalyl-amino-alanine) (Option C) is the toxin in Lathyrus sativus (Kesari dal) that causes neurolathyrism (spastic paraplegia). Pyrrolizidine alkaloids (Option D) are found in Crotalaria seeds and cause hepatic veno-occlusive disease. Because the family’s symptoms of swelling and diarrhea are directly linked to mustard oil ingestion, Sanguinarine toxicity from argemone contamination is the definitive cause
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of multiple family members developing acute edema (leg swelling) and gastrointestinal symptoms (loose stools) after consuming mustard oil is pathognomonic for Epidemic Dropsy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old known case of Parkinson's disease presents with severe oropharyngeal dysphagia and recurrent episodes of aspiration pneumonitis. CXR reveals bilateral bronchiectasis. What is the most appropriate long-term management plan for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PEG tube

This patient has:

• Parkinson's disease → impaired swallowing
• Oropharyngeal dysphagia → aspiration risk
• Recurrent aspiration pneumonitis
• Result: Bronchiectasis

The root cause is aspiration, not just secretion retention.

Severe oropharyngeal dysphagia in Parkinson’s disease causes recurrent aspiration, leading to aspiration pneumonitis and secondary bronchiectasis.

The most effective long-term strategy is prevention of further aspiration, achieved by PEG tube feeding.

| Benefit | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Prevents aspiration | Bypasses oropharynx

| Ensures nutrition | Long-term feeding

| Reduces lung injury | Stops recurrent pneumonitis

Airway clearance methods or antibiotics do not address the primary problem of unsafe swallowing.

| Approach | Example | Role

| -------- | ------- | ----

| Cause control |  PEG in aspiration | MOST IMPORTANT

| Airway clearance | Physiotherapy | Supportive

| Mucolytics | NAC | Symptomatic

| Antibiotics | Macrolides | Exacerbations
questions.learning: PEG tube — This patient has: • Parkinson's disease → impaired swallowing • Oropharyngeal dysphagia → aspiration risk • Recurrent aspiration pneumonitis • Result: Bronchiectasis The root cause is aspiration, not just secretion retention.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The first heart sound coincides with which phase of the cardiac cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isovolumetric contraction

The first heart sound coincides with the isovolumetric contraction phase of the cardiac cycle.

The time between the closure of the mitral valve and the opening of the aortic valve is the isovolumic contraction period. It begins with the closure of mitral and tricuspid valve which is responsible for the first heart sound. During this period, the ventricles contract as a closed chamber till the aortic and pulmonary valves open.

Events of the Cardiac Cycle

Systole

* Isovolumetric Contraction
The ventricular muscle continues to contract, even though the ventricular volume does not change, with all valves closed.
It correlates with the ‘c’ wave of JVP.

* Ventricular Ejection
When the ventricular pressures rise above aortic and pulmonary pressures the valves open, and ventricular ejection begins. Peak pressures in the left and right ventricles are about 120 and 25 mmHg, respectively.

Diastole

* Protodiastole
Before the semilunar valve closes, even though ventricular muscle is relaxed, blood flow into great vessels is due to momentum of blood.

* Iso-volumetric Relaxation
The ventricular muscle continues to relax, even though the ventricular volume does not change, with all valves closed.

* Ventricular Filling
Isovolumetric relaxation ends when the ventricular pressure falls below the atrial pressure and the AV valves open, permitting the ventricles to fill.

* Atrial Systole
During the last third of diastole, the atria contract and give additional thrust to the inflow of blood into the ventricles. It correlates with 'a' wave in JVP.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A Post-operative immobile patient develops sudden onset severe calf pain. The best investigation to be done is?
questions.explanation: A immobile post-operative patient presenting with sudden calf pain and swelling is a classic scenario for Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). The best (and first-line) investigation for confirming a suspected DVT is Duplex Ultrasonography. It is non-invasive, highly sensitive, and specific for identifying clots in the leg veins by visualizing the thrombus and demonstrating a lack of compressibility. CTPA (Option A) is the gold standard for pulmonary embolism, not for initial calf DVT diagnosis. X-ray (Option C) cannot visualize soft-tissue clots. While a D-dimer assay (Option D) is a useful screening tool, it is often elevated post-operatively regardless of a clot, making it non-specific and less useful in this specific surgical context. Early diagnosis and initiation of anticoagulation (e.g., LMWH) are essential to prevent the clot from propagating and causing a life-threatening pulmonary embolism. Immobile patients require active thromboprophylaxis with mechanical devices and pharmacological agents
questions.learning: A immobile post-operative patient presenting with sudden calf pain and swelling is a classic scenario for Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). The best (and first-line) investigation for confirming a suspected DVT is Duplex Ultrasonography.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Anti-PLA2R antibodies, which are directed against the ‘M-type phospholipase A2 receptor’, are a key biomarker for which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary membranous nephropathy

Anti-PLA2R antibodies are directed against the M-type phospholipase A₂ receptor (PLA2R) on podocytes and are a highly specific biomarker for primary membranous nephropathy. They are present in a large proportion of patients with primary membranous nephropathy and can also be useful for monitoring disease activity and response to treatment.

Why not the other options?

• B. IgA nephropathy: Characterized by mesangial deposition of IgA, often presenting with recurrent hematuria.
• C. Crescentic glomerulonephritis: Associated with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, with causes including anti-GBM antibodies and ANCA-associated vasculitis.
• D. Mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis: A histological pattern seen in several diseases; anti-PLA2R is not its characteristic biomarker.
questions.learning: Primary membranous nephropathy Anti-PLA2R antibodies are directed against the M-type phospholipase A₂ receptor (PLA2R) on podocytes and are a highly specific biomarker for primary membranous nephropathy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A middle-aged male patient presents with protrusion of the chin, excessive sweating, impaired glucose tolerance, and enlargement of hands and feet. Which of the following is a growth hormone receptor antagonist used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pegvisomant

The clinical features of protrusion of the chin, excessive sweating, impaired glucose tolerance, and enlargement of hands and feet are suggestive of acromegaly. Pegvisomant is a growth hormone receptor antagonist used to treat this condition.

Acromegaly is commonly caused due to growth hormone-secreting somatotroph adenoma. It occurs secondary to mutations of the pituitary-specific gene PIT-1.

Patients present with frontal bossing, increased hand and foot size, mandibular enlargement with prognathism, widened space between the lower incisor teeth, soft tissue swelling resulting in increased heel pad thickness, coarse facial features, and large fleshy nose.

Serum IGF-1 levels (elevated) and GH suppression test with oral glucose are useful in the diagnosis. The levels of GH do not reduce in response to the oral glucose load.

Transsphenoidal surgical resection of the tumor, octreotide, and pegvisomant will be helpful in the management of this condition.

Other options:

Option A: Octreotide is a synthetic analog of somatostatin. It is used for the treatment of acromegaly and secretory diarrhea.

Option C: Cabergoline is a dopamine D2 receptor agonist. It is used as a first-line drug for the treatment of hyperprolactinemia.

Option D: Oglcegepant is a calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) antagonist. It is used for the treatment of migraine.
questions.learning: Pegvisomant — The clinical features of protrusion of the chin, excessive sweating, impaired glucose tolerance, and enlargement of hands and feet are suggestive of acromegaly.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which protein, having structural homology with plasminogen, is responsible for myocardial infarction and stroke?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. LP(a)

LP(a) or Lipoprotein(a) consists of one mole of LDL attached to one mole of apo(a). The apo(a) component shows structural homologies to plasminogen, which is clinically significant. This similarity to plasminogen, a key protein in the fibrinolytic system, allows LP(a) to inhibit fibrinolysis (the normal breakdown of blood clots). Consequently, LP(a) promotes both atherosclerosis and thrombosis, significantly increasing the risk of premature coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction, and stroke.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A chronic smoker presents with bilateral pitting pedal edema and abdominal distension. Examination reveals ascites and the presence of an S3 gallop on cardiac auscultation. What underlying abnormalities or defects are most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a chronic smoker with bilateral pitting pedal edema, abdominal distension, and ascites indicates significant "right-sided heart failure." In chronic smokers, this is often "cor pulmonale"—right heart failure secondary to chronic lung disease (like COPD). The presence of an S3 gallop reflects a volume-overloaded state in the ventricle. In the context of right heart failure and chronic lung disease, the most common valvular defect observed is Tricuspid Regurgitation (TR). As the right ventricle dilates from high pulmonary pressures, the tricuspid valve annulus also stretches, preventing the leaflets from closing properly. This backflow of blood into the right atrium and then the systemic venous system causes the elevated JVP, hepatomegaly (ascites), and peripheral edema seen here. Aortic (Option A, C) and Mitral (Option D) defects involve the "left" side of the heart and would more likely present with pulmonary edema (crackles) before systemic venous congestion. Thus, tricuspid regurgitation is the classic valvular association for this clinical picture

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the most prevalent cause of macrocytic anemia among the options provided?
questions.explanation: Macrocytic anemia is characterized by an elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV > 100 fL). Among the provided options, Vitamin B12 deficiency is the most prevalent cause, specifically when considering megaloblastic anemia. B12 is essential for DNA synthesis; its absence leads to impaired nuclear maturation while cytoplasmic growth continues, resulting in large, immature cells. Alcohol consumption (Option C) is a very common cause of "non-megaloblastic" macrocytosis, but it is often less frequent or severe than B12 or folate deficiencies in general clinical populations. Bone marrow disorders (Option B), such as myelodysplastic syndrome, and drug-induced causes (Option D), like hydroxyurea or zidovudine, are significant but less common than nutritional deficiencies. Therefore, because Vitamin B12 deficiency is a leading global cause of macrocytic megaloblastic anemia, it remains the most prevalent and classically identified etiology in this context
questions.learning: Macrocytic anemia is characterized by an elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV > 100 fL). Among the provided options, Vitamin B12 deficiency is the most prevalent cause, specifically when considering megaloblastic anemia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Two compartments each contain 1 L of water and are separated by a semipermeable membrane permeable to water and glucose but impermeable to fructose. Which statement is true at equilibrium?
options: Fructose concentration becomes equal in both compartments
Water level becomes equal in both compartments
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Water is more in compartment 1

• Glucose is permeable and diffuses until its concentration becomes equal on both sides.

• Fructose cannot cross the membrane.
• Therefore, fructose acts as the effective osmole.

• Initially, compartment 1 contains more fructose.

• Water moves toward compartment 1 by osmosis.
• Hence, compartment 1 gains water and its volume increases.

• Water levels do not become equal.

• Glucose concentration becomes equal because it diffuses freely.
• Fructose concentration remains unequal because it cannot diffuse.

• The direction of water movement is determined by the impermeant solute.
