questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented to OPD with complaints of severe pain during erection and abnormal curvature of the penis for the last 6 months. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Peyronie’s disease

The clinical scenario is indicative of Peyronie's disease.

Peyronie's disease is characterized by penile deformity, palpable penile plaques, erectile dysfunction, and pain on erection. It causes the penis to bend, usually towards the side of the plaque. It can be associated with Dupuytren's contracture as a part of the Galezia triad (Dupuytren's contracture, retroperitoneal fibrosis, Peyronie's disease).

Some cases may resolve spontaneously. If not, conservative measures such as oral tamoxifen, vitamin E, terfenadine, intralesional verapamil, etc. can be attempted. Intralesional collagenase has also been used. Penile extenders/ traction devices have also been used.

However, if none of these methods are effective, surgical management can be tried using Nesbit's procedure.

Nesbit's procedure is indicated when all other interventions have failed and the patient is experiencing difficulties in their sexual and personal life due to this condition. The procedure is started by creating an artificial erection by injecting normal saline.

Following this, an elliptical excision is done on the convex side of the penis (opposite to the thickened plaque). The width of the excised tissue depends on the degree of penile deformity. The side with the plaque is left as it is.

Other options:

Marion's disease is a condition where hypertrophy of the internal sphincter leads to bladder outlet obstruction.

Priapism means persistent erection lasting longer than 4 hours and it is a surgical emergency (in case of ischemic priapism).
questions.learning: Peyronie’s disease — The clinical scenario is indicative of Peyronie's disease. Peyronie's disease is characterized by penile deformity, palpable penile plaques, erectile dysfunction, and pain on erection.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which skin condition shows coral-red fluorescence when examined under a Wood’s lamp?
questions.explanation: Erythrasma is a common superficial bacterial infection of the intertriginous areas (axilla, groin) caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum. The pathognomonic diagnostic finding is the presence of coral-red fluorescence when the skin is viewed under a Wood’s lamp. This distinct color is produced by the bacterium's secretion of porphyrins. Acanthosis nigricans (Option B) is a sign of insulin resistance and shows hyperpigmented, velvety plaques. Allergic contact dermatitis (Option C) and Cutaneous candidiasis (Option D) do not exhibit this specific fluorescence pattern. Candidiasis characteristically shows "satellite lesions" and a white curd-like surface. Clinically, erythrasma appears as well-demarcated, reddish-brown, scaly patches that can be mistaken for fungal infections. Treatment typically involves topical or oral macrolide antibiotics like erythromycin or clindamycin. Accurate identification via Wood's lamp allows for rapid bedside diagnosis and prevents unnecessary antifungal therapy for a bacterial condition
questions.learning: Erythrasma is a common superficial bacterial infection of the intertriginous areas (axilla, groin) caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum. The pathognomonic diagnostic finding is the presence of coral-red fluorescence when the skin is viewed under a Wood’s…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient is incidentally found to have an asymptomatic Grade I meningioma on MRI, confirmed by histopathology. What is the most appropriate initial management approach for this patient?
questions.explanation: A 45-year-old patient with a confirmed Grade I meningioma via histopathology is best managed with surgical excision. The histopathological confirmation itself implies tissue acquisition, and at this age with a confirmed tumor, definitive treatment is warranted. Gross Total Resection (GTR) offers potential cure with minimal recurrence rates, making surgery the gold standard. Why Other Options Are Wrong: A. Reassurance : While watch-and-wait suits truly incidental, unbiopsied, small meningiomas in elderly patients, a histopathologically confirmed tumor in a young 45-year-old demands definitive treatment due to long life expectancy and cumulative growth risk. C. Chemotherapy : Meningiomas are notoriously chemoresistant. No chemotherapeutic agent has proven efficacy in Grade I meningioma. Completely inappropriate here. D. Radiotherapy : Reserved for Grade II/III, post-operative residual disease, or surgically inaccessible tumors. It is not a primary treatment for resectable Grade I meningioma
questions.learning: A 45-year-old patient with a confirmed Grade I meningioma via histopathology is best managed with surgical excision. The histopathological confirmation itself implies tissue acquisition, and at this age with a confirmed tumor, definitive treatment is…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The most rapid lab diagnosis of pulmonary TB can be done by _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sputum microscopy

The most rapid diagnosis of pulmonary TB can be done by Sputum microscopy with results in 30 minutes.

* It has the least sensitivity and specificity.

* Smears are stained by Ziel Neelson acid fast stain.

The other methods and the time they take are:

CBNAAT: Gives results within 90 minutes. Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test is a Mycobacterium tuberculosis-specific automated, cartridge based nucleic acid amplification assay, having fully integrated and automated amplification and detection using real-time PCR.

Sputum culture takes approximately 2 to 8 weeks.

Radiometric BACTEC method takes approximately 2-3 weeks.

Pearl PF1307: Diagnostic algorithm for Pulmonary TB – National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP) 2020 Guidelines

A presumptive pulmonary TB patient should undergo both Sputum examination and Chest X-ray.

If sputum and CXR is negative, CB NAAT should be done when the clinical suspicion is high:

As is inferred from the above table, irrespective of chest X ray findings, CB-NAAT is done in all cases where sputum examination is negative for diagnosis.

CB-NAAT is also performed in all microbiologically confirmed and notified cases of TB for drug susceptibility testing.

The following protocol is used for CB-NAAT testing:
questions.learning: Sputum microscopy — The most rapid diagnosis of pulmonary TB can be done by Sputum microscopy with results in 30 minutes. * It has the least sensitivity and specificity. * Smears are stained by Ziel Neelson acid fast stain.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Revised A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholelithiasis. Picture of the resected gall bladder is shown as below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gall bladder carcinoma

The diagnosis is gallbladder carcinoma.

The gross specimen shows a resected gallbladder with multiple gallstones impacted in the lumen. The irregularly thickened wall, mucosal changes, and firm, indurated areas indicate tumor growth and inflammation.

Gallbladder carcinoma

* Gallbladder carcinoma is a rare malignancy that affects the elderly population; it is associated with a poor prognosis, except when diagnosed at the early stages.

* The histologic subtypes are papillary, nodular, and tubular carcinomas.

Clinical features:

* It is usually indistinguishable from cholecystitis or cholelithiasis.

* Features include right upper quadrant pain, abdominal discomfort, nausea, and vomiting.

Diagnosis:

* It is usually diagnosed when patients undergo cholecystectomy for gallstones.

* Laboratory diagnosis in 80% of the cases is made by detection of elevated levels of carbohydrate antigen (CA) 19-9 in assays.

* Ultrasonography (USG) is often indicative of a thickened irregular gallbladder wall or a lesion replacing the gallbladder.

* Computed tomography (CT) can detect the presence of a tumour and its invasion and can be used for identifying its stage of development

* Percutaneous transhepatic or endoscopic retrograde cholangiography and subsequent bile cytology can help establish the diagnosis of gallbladder cancer.

* Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography is a non-invasive imaging method that allows for a complete clinical assessment of the vascular, nodal, and hepatic architecture and other adjacent organs.

Treatment options for carcinoma gall bladder found incidentally after cholecystectomy:

* Up to stage Ia and stage Ib with negative margins: Standard cholecystectomy

* Stage Ib with perineural, lymphatic, vascular invasion and stage II: Extended cholecystectomy

* Chemotherapy is not required in an early gall bladder cancer. Radiation has no role.

Treatment of gallbladder carcinoma (in general):

T1a: Simple cholecystectomy

T1b, T2, T3: Radical cholecystectomy

T4: Unresectable, chemotherapy and palliative nonsurgical therapy are provided.

N1: Regional lymphadenectomy

N2: Radical cholecystectomy plus hepatopancreatic duodenectomy
questions.learning: Gall bladder carcinoma — The diagnosis is gallbladder carcinoma. The gross specimen shows a resected gallbladder with multiple gallstones impacted in the lumen.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following types of pain stimulus is associated with the Carrageenan-induced experimental pain model?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inflammatory stimulus

The Carrageenan-induced pain model also called the Carrageenan-Induced Paw Edema model is a well-known model of acute inflammation.

It is employed to evaluate the anti-inflammatory properties of a variety of synthetic and natural substances. A non-antigenic phlogistic polysaccharide derived from red seaweed, carrageenan is frequently added to processed foods as a thickening, stabilising, gelling, and emulsifying agent. The activation of the complement system and inflammatory mediators is caused by the sulphated sugars found in carrageenan.

Carrageenan is injected subcutaneously into the plantar surface of the rat paw to cause inflammation. This process results in temporary inflammation and acute swelling, which peaks 3 to 5 hours after injection and subsides in 24 hours.

Postcapillary venules dilate due to the action of carrageenan, causing inflammatory cells and fluid to exude. During this process, a number of proinflammatory mediators are released. The cyclooxygenase pathway's activation is commonly associated with the carrageenan model. A biphasic curve represents the edema caused by carrageenan.

Part of the initial phase of inflammation caused by carrageenan is attributed to injection trauma and the release of acute phase mediators, particularly bradykinin, histamine, and serotonin. The second phase of carrageenan-induced inflammation, which happens about three hours after carrageenan is added, is mostly caused by prostaglandins.
questions.learning: Inflammatory stimulus — The Carrageenan-induced pain model also called the Carrageenan-Induced Paw Edema model is a well-known model of acute inflammation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following cannot help in differentiating psoriatic arthritis from other forms of arthritis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Presence of diarrhea

The presence of diarrhea is not a characteristic symptom of psoriatic arthritis, therefore, it cannot help in differentiating the condition from other forms of arthritis.

Psoriatic arthritis can sometimes be associated with inflammatory bowel disease causing diarrhea. However, diarrhea is not specific to psoriatic arthritis and can occur in other types of arthritis such as reactive arthritis and certain types of infectious arthritis.

Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory type of arthritis mainly affecting the distal interphalangeal joints. In most cases, psoriasis precedes arthritis. Other features include nail changes (pitting, horizontal ridging, onycholysis, yellowish discoloration, hyperkeratosis), dactylitis, enthesitis, and tenosynovitis. The Classification of Psoriatic Arthritis (CASPAR) criteria are a useful tool for early diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis.

Other options:

Option A: Dactylitis is a characteristic feature of psoriatic arthritis, referring to the inflammation of an entire finger or toe. It is not commonly seen in other types of arthritis.

Option C: Enthesitis (inflammation of the entheses) is a hallmark of psoriatic arthritis and is less common in other forms of arthritis like rheumatoid arthritis.

Option D: Nail pitting (small depressions on the surface of the nails) is a feature strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis and is rarely seen in other forms of arthritis.
questions.learning: Presence of diarrhea — The presence of diarrhea is not a characteristic symptom of psoriatic arthritis, therefore, it cannot help in differentiating the condition from other forms of arthritis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 67-year-old man presents with progressive yellowing of the eyes for 3 weeks, associated with dark urine, pale stools, and unintentional weight loss. He denies abdominal pain, fever, or gastrointestinal bleeding. Examination reveals scleral icterus without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory evaluation shows: • Total bilirubin: 7.2 mg/dL • Alkaline phosphatase: markedly elevated Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrates a mass in the head of the pancreas causing compression of both the common bile duct and pancreatic duct. Which of the following molecular alterations is most commonly associated with the pathogenesis of this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. KRAS activation

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, especially involving the head of the pancreas, commonly presents with painless obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stools, elevated ALP). The most frequent early genetic event in its pathogenesis is activating mutation of the KRAS oncogene, leading to constitutive activation of downstream proliferative signaling pathways (MAPK pathway).

Pancreatic cancer follows a stepwise progression (PanIN lesions) involving:

• Early: KRAS activation
• Intermediate: CDKN2A (p16) loss
• Late: TP53 and SMAD4 mutations

Why not other options?

A. APC mutation → Seen in colorectal carcinoma (adenoma-carcinoma sequence)

B. BCL2 overexpression → Associated with follicular lymphoma (anti-apoptotic protein)

C. BRAF mutation → Seen in melanoma, hairy cell leukemia, some colorectal cancers

c-MYC amplification → Seen in Burkitt lymphoma and various aggressive malignancies
questions.learning: KRAS activation Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, especially involving the head of the pancreas, commonly presents with painless obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stools, elevated ALP).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions does not contraindicate the use of beta-blockers?
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism does NOT contraindicate the use of beta-blockers. In fact, beta-blockers can be used safely and are sometimes even beneficial in hypothyroid patients. Hypothyroidism is associated with decreased heart rate and reduced cardiac output, and while beta-blockers further slow the heart, they are not absolutely contraindicated. Moreover, beta-blockers are classically used in hyperthyroidism to control sympathetic overactivity symptoms, but hypothyroidism itself poses no direct contraindication to their use. Why other options are wrong: (A) Asthma is incorrect because asthma is a absolute contraindication to beta-blockers, especially non-selective ones like propranolol. Beta-blockade causes bronchoconstriction by blocking β₂ receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, potentially triggering life-threatening bronchospasm in asthmatic patients. (B) Glaucoma is incorrect as a contraindication because beta-blockers like timolol eye drops are actually used TO TREAT glaucoma by reducing aqueous humor production. Therefore glaucoma is not a contraindication but rather an indication for beta-blockers. (C) Bradycardia is incorrect because bradycardia is a absolute contraindication to beta-blockers. Since beta-blockers slow AV conduction and reduce heart rate, administering them to an already bradycardic patient can cause severe bradycardia, heart block, or even cardiac arrest
questions.learning: Hypothyroidism does NOT contraindicate the use of beta-blockers. In fact, beta-blockers can be used safely and are sometimes even beneficial in hypothyroid patients.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A homogenous sample of 4 groups was taken as shown below. The height and weight of each group had a correlation coefficient of 0.6. What will be the total coefficient of correlation of the whole group?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Equal to 0.6

In a homogenous sample or population, the total coefficient of correlation (r) will be the average of the individual correlation coefficients. Therefore in the given condition, it will be the same as 0.6

The given scattergram shows the correlation coefficient of height and weight of 4 homogenous samples. Averaging methods are appropriate when several different samples are independently drawn from the same or a homogenous population and the interest is in aggregating those values.

Therefore the total correlation coefficient of the whole group will be:

r = (sum of correlation coeffiecient of each sample) ÷ (total no. of samples)

= (0.6 + 0.6  + 0.6 + 0.6) ÷ 4 = 2.4 ÷ 4

= 0.6

Note: A correlation between 2 variables does not demonstrate any causal relationship between those variables, no matter how strong it is. Correlation is merely a measure of a statistical association between the variables. Therefore inferring a causal relationship between two variables on the basis of a correlation is a common and fundamental error.
questions.learning: Equal to 0.6 In a homogenous sample or population, the total coefficient of correlation (r) will be the average of the individual correlation coefficients.

questions.text: Pandemic that occurred in 2009 was due to which influenza virus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. H1N1

Recent influenza pandemic occurred in 2009 due to the emergence of a novel H1N1 influenza A virus.

Past influenza pandemics:

• 1968 pandemic due to H3N2 virus
• 1957-58 pandemic due to H2N2 virus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents to the clinic with complaints of burning sensation during urination and a purulent discharge from the penis for the past 5 days. He has had unprotected sexual intercourse with a new partner two weeks ago. On examination, the urethral meatus is erythematous, and there is a noticeable purulent discharge. A Gram stain of the discharge reveals intracellular gram-negative diplococci. The patient is otherwise healthy and has no known drug allergies. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
options: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million Units intramuscularly
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cefixime 400 mg orally

Urethritis + purulent discharge

↓

Gram stain → GN diplococci

↓

Gonorrhea

↓

Use cephalosporin

↓

Cefixime

Intracellular gram-negative diplococci indicate Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Third-generation cephalosporins are first-line therapy for uncomplicated gonorrhea. Oral cefixime is an accepted alternative when parenteral therapy is not used. Penicillin resistance is common, and doxycycline/metronidazole do not treat gonorrhea.

| Infection | Drug

| --------- | ----

| Gonorrhea | Ceftriaxone / Cefixime

| Chlamydia | Doxycycline / Azithromycin

| Syphilis | Penicillin

| Trichomonas | Metronidazole
questions.learning: Cefixime 400 mg orally Urethritis + purulent discharge ↓ Gram stain → GN diplococci ↓ Gonorrhea ↓ Use cephalosporin ↓ Cefixime Intracellular gram-negative diplococci indicate Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 30-week primigravida c/o reduced vision at night. She has been avoiding papaya, mango, and other fruits throughout her pregnancy as she thinks they could be abortifacients. It is the primary duty of which of the following workers to provide counseling and information to the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ASHA

Amongst the given options, it is the duty of the ASHA to provide counseling and information to this pregnant patient

An ASHA is a trained female community health activist and a resident woman of the village with a formal education of at least up to 10th grade. She should preferably be in the age group of 25 to 45 years (married/divorced/widow) and have qualities such as good communication skills and leadership skills. The general norm of selection recommends having one ASHA for 1000 population, but in tribal, hilly, and desert areas, the norm could be relaxed to one ASHA per habitation.

Roles of ASHA:

• To create awareness and provide information to the community on determinants of health such as nutrition, basic sanitation, and hygienic practices
• To counsel women on birth preparedness, the importance of safe delivery, breast-feeding and complementary feeding, immunization, and contraception
• To counsel women on the prevention of common infections including reproductive tract infection/sexually transmitted infection
• To mobilize the community and help them in accessing health and health-related services.
• To arrange and escort pregnant women and children requiring treatment/admission to the nearest pre-identified health facility
• To inform sub-center/primary health center about the births and deaths in her village and any unusual health problems/disease outbreaks in the community
• To promote the construction of household toilets under the total sanitation campaign

Other Options:

Option A (ANM): An Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) is a trained health worker who provides basic healthcare services, including antenatal care, delivery, and postnatal care. Although an ANM can provide counseling and information to pregnant women, the primary responsibility for this role lies with the ASHA worker.

Option B (AWW): An Anganwadi Worker (AWW) is responsible for providing basic health care, nutrition, and preschool education to children under the age of six, pregnant women, and lactating mothers. While AWWs play a vital role in maternal and child health, counseling pregnant women on health-related issues is not their primary responsibility.

Option C (Trained birth attendant): A trained birth attendant is responsible for assisting with childbirth and providing postpartum care. Although they may provide some counseling and information, this role is primarily focused on the delivery process rather than ongoing counseling throughout pregnancy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about Plasmodium species:
options: Drug resistant falciparum is seen in India
Presence of duffy blood group antigen is protective against vivax
Severe malaria with shock is called algid malaria
Relapse is seen in P. ovale
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Presence of duffy blood group antigen is protective against vivax

The absence, not the presence, of the Duffy blood group antigen, is protective against P. vivax because the Duffy antigen normally serves as the receptor for Plasmodium vivax.

Drug Efflux pumps are the primary mode of resistance for Chloroquine. It is mediated by an ABC transporter encoded by P. falciparum multidrug resistance gene 1 (Pfmdr1). The resistance of P. falciparum to chloroquine increased over time and is present across all regions of the country.

Algid malaria is a rare complication of severe malaria characterized by hemodynamic collapse manifesting as shock with pronounced metabolic changes and hypothermia.

Relapse is seen in cases of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale.

Malaria relapse :

True relapse is caused due to Hypnozoites.

These are resting forms.

In the case of Plasmodium vivax and ovale two kinds of sporozoites are seen, some of which :

• multiply inside hepatic cells to form -  Schizonts
• others persist and remain dormant as -  hypnozoites

From time to time some are activated to become schizonts and release merozoites, which go on infecting RBCs producing clinical relapse.

In the case of Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium malariae, the initial tissue phase disappears completely and no hypnozoites are found, hence technically relapse is not seen.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The most common organ injuries in air blast shock waves will be?
questions.explanation: In an explosion, air blast shock waves primarily damage gas-containing organs due to the rapid pressure changes at air-tissue interfaces. The Lungs are the most commonly injured internal organ in primary blast injuries. This "blast lung" involves pulmonary hemorrhage, edema, and alveolar rupture, often leading to severe respiratory distress or air embolism. The auditory system (tympanic membrane rupture) is the most frequent overall blast injury, but the lung is the most critical organ affected. The Intestine (Option A) is the second most common gas-containing organ injured, often suffering mural hematomas or delayed perforation. The Kidney (Option C) and Heart (Option D) are solid or fluid-filled organs that are relatively more resistant to primary blast waves compared to the air-filled lungs. Clinicians managing blast victims must have a high index of suspicion for lung injury, even in the absence of external trauma, as symptoms may be delayed for several hours
questions.learning: In an explosion, air blast shock waves primarily damage gas-containing organs due to the rapid pressure changes at air-tissue interfaces. The Lungs are the most commonly injured internal organ in primary blast injuries.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presents with chronic swelling and pain over the upper tibia.There is no history of trauma. His radiographic image is shown below. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Brodie's abscess

The given clinical scenario of a child with prolonged swelling and pain over the upper tibia, along with a radiograph showing a lytic lesion with a dense sclerotic rim and minimal periosteal reaction, suggests the diagnosis of Brodie's abscess.

Brodie's abscess is a localized form of subacute osteomyelitis that occurs when organisms of low virulence infect an immunocompetent host. The abscess is walled off by the thickening of the surrounding bone trabeculae. It most commonly involves the metaphysis of the proximal tibia and distal femur.

The patient is typically a child or adolescent experiencing prolonged pain near a large joint for several weeks or months. Symptoms may include a limp, slight swelling, muscle wasting, and localized tenderness.

The typical radiographic finding is a circumscribed, round or oval radiolucent cavity measuring 1-2 cm in diameter, surrounded by a halo of sclerosis, with minimal or no periosteal reaction. The radioisotope scan shows markedly increased activity. MRI may be helpful in diagnosis. Open biopsy with curettage is indicated if there is any doubt in the diagnosis.

Differential diagnoses include:

* Cystic tuberculosis

* Eosinophilic granuloma

* Osteoid osteoma

* Ewing's sarcoma

Treatment:

* Immobilization and antibiotics (flucloxacillin and fusidic acid) intravenous for 4-5 days, followed by oral administration for another 6 weeks; healing may take up to 12 months

* Curettage is needed if the x-rays show no healing after conservative management.

The following X-ray and MRI images show Brodie's abscess of the radius in a patient.

Other options:

Option A: A Simple bone cyst is a solitary, usually unilocular cystic bone cavity lined by a fibrous membrane and filled with serous or serosanguinous fluid. Majority of cases are asymptomatic, and found incidentally.

Option B: Osteoid osteoma is a benign tumor formed of osteoid and woven bone. It is common in men and most commonly occurs in the diaphysis of the femur. It is characterized by night pains relieved by medication. Nidus of osteoid osteoma is seen in the cortex and hence CT is the investigation of choice.

Option D: Aneurysmal bone cysts are benign, locally destructive, multiloculated cysts filled with blood. They are eccentric, expansile, and lytic lesions. Most occur in patients younger than 20 years old. There is a slight female preponderance. The most common sites involved are the proximal humerus, distal femur, and proximal tibia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient develops a broad QRS complex tachycardia following a myocardial infarction. His blood pressure is 120/85 mm Hg, and the ECG findings are provided. What is the most appropriate management in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with a broad QRS complex (>120 ms), regular, monomorphic tachycardia following an MI, which is diagnostic of sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT). With a blood pressure of 120/85 mm Hg, the patient is hemodynamically stable. According to ACLS guidelines, the first-line pharmacological treatment for stable VT is IV amiodarone. Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic that suppresses ventricular ectopy and is safe in structural heart disease. Labetalol (Option B) is an antihypertensive and has no role in acute VT termination. Metoprolol (Option C), while used post-MI for prevention, is not the primary choice for terminating an active VT episode and carries a risk of hypotension. Nitroglycerin (Option D) is used for ischemic chest pain but does not treat the underlying arrhythmia. Therefore, IV amiodarone is the most appropriate intervention for this stable, post-MI tachycardia
questions.learning: The patient presents with a broad QRS complex (>120 ms), regular, monomorphic tachycardia following an MI, which is diagnostic of sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which method is considered the most effective for evaluating the extent of muscle relaxation?
questions.explanation: In clinical anesthesia, monitoring the depth of neuromuscular blockade is essential for safe intubation and reversal. The Train of Four (TOF) stimulation is globally recognized as the most effective and standard method for evaluating the extent of muscle relaxation. TOF involves delivering four supramaximal electrical stimuli at 0.5-second intervals. The ratio of the fourth twitch to the first twitch (TOF ratio) provides a reliable quantitative measure of the degree of blockade. Tetanic stimulation (Option A) is used to detect residual curarization but is painful and less routinely precise than TOF. Double-burst stimulation (Option B) is useful for manual detection of subtle fade but is secondary to TOF. Electromyography (Option D) is an investigative tool for primary muscle disorders rather than a routine perioperative monitor. Therefore, TOF remains the gold standard for clinicians to ensure complete recovery of muscle strength before extubation

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient comes to the casualty with life-threatening injuries. There was no time for taking consent. The doctor started doing life-saving procedures with all precautions, and despite best efforts, the death of the patient occurred. The doctor is not responsible under which doctrine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Doctrine of anticipation

Under IPC 92, the doctor can perform life-saving procedures in a patient with life-threatening injuries without obtaining consent. The guiding principle is whether the delay in treatment in order to obtain consent would result in harm to the patient. This is the doctrine of anticipation.

Under some circumstances like emergencies, informed consent may be neither possible nor necessary.

IPC 92 states that nothing is an offense by reason of any harm which it may cause to a person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, even without that person’s consent, if the circumstances are such that it is impossible for that person to signify consent, or if that person is incapable of giving consent, and has no guardian or other person in lawful charge of him from whom it is possible to obtain consent in time for the thing to be done with benefit.

Other options:

'Res Ipsa Loquitor' means 'the thing or fact speaks for itself'. It is obvious evidence for the negligent act committed. For example, swabs left in the abdominal cavity post laparotomy.

The doctrine of extended consent: It is used in unanticipated conditions during surgery. This comes into play when a surgeon encounters an unanticipated abnormality within the field of surgery. It is called the “extension doctrine,” and it assumes that the surgeon is using reasonable judgment. For example, a surgeon incurred no liability for draining some ovarian cysts during the course of an appendectomy. The condition must be one that was unforeseen, and the patient must not have expressly refused such an intervention.

Doctrine of conjugated consent - Dummy option (No such consent has been defined).
questions.learning: Doctrine of anticipation Under IPC 92, the doctor can perform life-saving procedures in a patient with life-threatening injuries without obtaining consent.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 25 year old male patient was given cisatracurium for neuromuscular blockade. Which of the following is not true regarding the class to which the drug belongs?
options: Their action is potentiated by Mg2+ and antagonized by Ca2+
Characteristic train of four fade present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Metabolized by pseudo cholinesterase

Cisatracurium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker (NDNMB) belonging to the benzylisoquinolinium group.

• Act as competitive antagonists at nicotinic (Nm) acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
• Prevent depolarization → flaccid paralysis
• Potentiation and antagonism:

• Mg²⁺ → potentiates blockade (↓ ACh release)
• Ca²⁺ → antagonizes blockade (↑ ACh release)

• Neuromuscular monitoring:

• Shows train-of-four (TOF) fade, a hallmark of non-depolarizing block

Unique Feature of Cisatracurium:

• Undergoes Hofmann elimination (organ-independent degradation)
• Also minor ester hydrolysis
• NOT metabolized by pseudocholinesterase

Hence, option C is incorrect

Why not other options:

A. Competitive inhibition at ACh receptors: True

B. Mg²⁺ potentiation, Ca²⁺ antagonism: True

D. TOF fade present: True (characteristic of non-depolarizing block)

questions.text: Which of the following would be considered as an absolute contraindication for insertion of copper T to a patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Unmotivated patient

An unmotivated patient or someone who does not consent to the procedure should never be taken up for a procedure.

Contraindications for use of copper intrauterine devices (IUDs)

• Uterine abnormality with a distorted uterine cavity
• Active uterine and pelvic infection
• Known or suspected uterine or cervical malignancy
• Genital bleeding of unknown etiology
• Mucopurulent cervicitis
• Wilson disease
• A previously placed IUD that has not been removed
• An inability to place or retain the device

Note:

An unmotivated patient is an absolute contraindication. Out of the given options, this would be the best answer.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following techniques is used to detect autoantibodies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Indirect immunofluorescence

Circulating autoantibodies in serum are best detected by indirect immunofluorescence.

The two-step indirect immunofluorescence assay is used to find out if a serum specimen contains antibodies specific to a particular organism. A known antigen is first attached to a slide. After incubating the slide with a serum sample, the sample is removed, the slide is washed, and a second fluorescein-labelled anti-immunoglobulin is added. If the patient’s serum contains the organism-specific antibodies, the organism will appear green under the fluorescence microscope.

This assay is the accepted method for identifying autoantibodies in autoimmune disorders (such as antinuclear antibodies) and detecting antibodies to certain microorganisms (eg, T. pallidum)

Other options:

Option A:  Enzyme-linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) is a type of heterogenous enzyme immunoassay that involves the use of an immunosorbent, an absorbing material specific for one of the components of the reaction: the antigen or antibody. It mainly detects antigens of infectious agents present in clinical specimens like rotavirus detection in fecal specimens and HIV detection.

Option C: Flow cytometry is a laser-based method that analyzes the cells and cell components based on the presence of certain cell surface molecules which are named as per cluster of differentiation (CD) nomenclature. It is very effective for the study of the immune system and its response to infectious diseases and cancer.

Option D: Fluorescent In Situ Hybridisation (FISH) is a simple technique for the detection of specific DNA sequences in cells/tissues. It uses fluorescent labelled probes to bind to complementary DNA. FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections.
questions.learning: Indirect immunofluorescence Circulating autoantibodies in serum are best detected by indirect immunofluorescence. The two-step indirect immunofluorescence assay is used to find out if a serum specimen contains antibodies specific to a particular organism.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman (P1L1) with one living child is planning to conceive again and has been newly diagnosed with Graves’ disease. Which antithyroid drug is preferred for use during early pregnancy?
questions.explanation: For women with hyperthyroidism planning a pregnancy, Propylthiouracil (PTU) is the drug of choice during the early gestation (first trimester) (Option A). PTU is preferred because it is more highly protein-bound and crosses the placenta less readily than other options, and most importantly, it is not associated with the specific "methimazole embryopathy". Methimazole (Option B) and its prodrug Carbimazole (Option C) are associated with rare but severe congenital defects such as aplasia cutis, choanal atresia, and esophageal atresia when used in early pregnancy. Many protocols involve switching the patient to PTU for the first trimester and then back to Methimazole for the remainder of the pregnancy to minimize PTU-related maternal hepatotoxicity. Therefore, to protect the fetus during organogenesis, PTU is the definitive standard recommendation for early pregnancy management of Graves' disease
questions.learning: For women with hyperthyroidism planning a pregnancy, Propylthiouracil (PTU) is the drug of choice during the early gestation (first trimester) (Option A).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following hormones is exclusively secreted by adrenal gland but not by the ovaries of females?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. DHEA-S

DHEAS is exclusively secreted from the adrenals but not by ovaries because ovaries lack the enzyme dehydroepiandrosterone-sulphotransferase needed to form DHEAS.

90% of DHEA is synthesised by the adrenals and 10% comes from the ovaries.
questions.learning: DHEA-S DHEAS is exclusively secreted from the adrenals but not by ovaries because ovaries lack the enzyme dehydroepiandrosterone-sulphotransferase needed to form DHEAS.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the incorrect match.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 4- Lamina propria

Among the given options, Option B represents an incorrect match, as the structure labeled as 4 is showing the basement membrane and not lamina propria.

The given image is of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, as it shows irregular cells, which are attached to the basement membrane(marked as 4 in the image). It appears to be multi-layered. However, there is actually only one layer of cells. The multi-layered appearance is due to the fact that the nuclei of epithelial cell(marked as 3 in the image) lie at different levels.

The epithelium shows hair-like projections called cilia (marked as 1 in the image) and goblet cells (marked as 2 in the image). Goblet cells secrete mucous which helps to trap dust entering the passages. The cilia are capable of movement and help in the clearance of mucous.

Example include epithelium lining the trachea and in large bronchi.
questions.learning: 4- Lamina propria Among the given options, Option B represents an incorrect match, as the structure labeled as 4 is showing the basement membrane and not lamina propria.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young man presents with gradually worsening drooping of the eyelids that becomes more pronounced by evening and improves after rest or in the morning. He also experiences easy fatigability that increases as the day progresses. The ptosis shows marked, temporary improvement following application of an ice pack over the eyes. Based on these features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of fatigable ptosis (eyelid drooping that worsens with activity or as the day progresses) is the hallmark of Myasthenia Gravis (MG). MG is an autoimmune disorder where antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. The positive ice pack test (Option A) is highly suggestive; cold temperatures decrease acetylcholinesterase activity, allowing more acetylcholine to remain in the synaptic cleft, which briefly improves muscle strength. Huntington chorea (Option B) involves movement disorders and dementia. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Option C) causes progressive muscle wasting and permanent weakness rather than diurnal fatigability. External ophthalmoplegia (Option D) refers to paralyzed eye muscles but is a descriptive sign that can be caused by MG, not a standalone diagnosis here. Therefore, the characteristic combination of worsening evening symptoms and improvement with cold/rest confirms Myasthenia Gravis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of fatigable ptosis (eyelid drooping that worsens with activity or as the day progresses) is the hallmark of Myasthenia Gravis (MG).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old male child presents with a history of spontaneous excessive bruising and haemarthrosis. On investigation, he has a normal platelet count, prolonged PTT, and a normal PT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemophilia A

The most likely diagnosis is Haemophilia A. Bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis) following minor trauma is particularly characteristic of hemophilia.

* Hemophilia A, the most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding, is caused by mutations in factor VIII, an essential cofactor for factor IX in the coagulation cascade.

* Hemophilia A is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait and thus affects mainly males and homozygous females.

* About 30% of patients have no family history; their disease is caused by new mutations.

* Hemophilia A -  clinical severity correlates well with the level of factor VIII activity.

* Those with less than 1% of normal levels have a severe disease; those with 2% to 5% of normal levels have moderately severe disease, and those with 6% to 50% of normal levels have mild disease.

* A tendency toward easy bruising and massive hemorrhage after trauma or operative procedures.

* Spontaneous hemorrhages frequently occur in regions of the body that are susceptible to trauma, particularly the joints, where they are known as hemarthroses.

* Recurrent bleeding into the joints leads to progressive deformities that can be crippling.

* Petechiae are characteristically absent.

* Patients with hemophilia A have a prolonged PTT and a normal PT results that point to an abnormality of the intrinsic coagulation pathway.

* Factor VIII-specific assays are required for diagnosis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man is found dead in a swimming pool. On autopsy, both the lungs and stomach are filled with water, and there is mucoid froth around the nose and mouth. What is the most likely mode of death in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wet drowning

Wet drowning is characterized by aspiration of water into the lungs and stomach, along with fine, persistent froth at the mouth and nostrils.

• Water enters airways → lungs fill with fluid → impaired gas exchange → hypoxia
• Swallowing of water → water present in stomach
• Froth formation:

• Due to mixing of air + water + mucus
• Appears as fine, white, persistent (mucoid) froth

Autopsy findings:

• Heavy, waterlogged lungs
• Frothy fluid in airways
• Water in stomach
• May have diatoms in organs (if antemortem drowning)

Why not other options:

• Dry drowning: No water in lungs (laryngospasm)
• Near drowning: Survival after drowning attempt
• Cardiac arrest: No typical drowning features

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which type of thyroid carcinoma is most commonly associated with prior radiation exposure and is characterized by frequent RET/ PTC rearrangements and BRAF mutations?
questions.explanation: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common form of thyroid cancer and is strongly associated with a history of ionizing radiation exposure, particularly during childhood. Molecularly, it is characterized by RET/PTC rearrangements and BRAF mutations, which drive the tumorigenesis. Follicular carcinoma (Option A) is more often linked to iodine deficiency and typically shows RAS mutations or PAX8-PPAR$\gamma$ translocations. Anaplastic carcinoma (Option C) is a highly aggressive, undifferentiated tumor that often arises in long-standing goiters and has a very poor prognosis. Medullary carcinoma (Option D) arises from the C-cells and is uniquely associated with germline RET mutations in MEN 2 syndromes, but it is not classically linked to radiation exposure like the papillary type. Papillary carcinoma is distinguished histologically by "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei and Psammoma bodies. Due to its well-defined link to radiation and specific genetic markers, papillary carcinoma is the definitive answer. Early diagnosis usually leads to an excellent survival rate
questions.learning: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common form of thyroid cancer and is strongly associated with a history of ionizing radiation exposure, particularly during childhood.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): 1. Exudative phase lasts from day 7 to day 21 after exposure to a precipitating risk factor. 2. Proliferative phase is characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes. 3. Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg body weight) has significantly lower mortality compared to high tidal volume ventilation (12 mL/kg body weight). 4. PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤100 mm Hg is classified as severe ARDS. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4

• Statement 1. Exudative phase lasts from day 7 to day 21 after exposure to a precipitating risk factor: Incorrect. The exudative phase actually lasts from day 1 to day 7 after the precipitating insult (characterized by diffuse alveolar damage, hyaline membrane formation, and neutrophil-rich edema). The timeframe of day 7–21 actually corresponds to the proliferative phase, not the exudative phase.
• Statement 2. Proliferative phase is characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes: Correct. The proliferative phase (roughly days 7–21) is marked by proliferation of type II pneumocytes (which attempt to repair the damaged alveolar epithelium), fibroblast proliferation, and organization of the exudate.
• Statement 3. Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg body weight) has significantly lower mortality compared to high tidal volume ventilation (12 mL/kg body weight): Correct. This is based on the landmark ARDSNet (ARMA) trial, which showed that a lung-protective ventilation strategy using low tidal volumes (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) significantly reduced mortality compared to traditional higher tidal volumes (12 mL/kg), along with plateau pressure limitation (<30 cm H₂O).
• Statement 4. PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤100 mm Hg is classified as severe ARDS: Correct. As per the Berlin Definition of ARDS (2012), severity is graded by the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio (with PEEP ≥5 cm H₂O):

• Mild: 200–300 mm Hg
• Moderate: 100–200 mm Hg
• Severe: ≤100 mm Hg

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the statistical term for the value that occurs most frequently in a dataset?
questions.explanation: The mode is the measure of central tendency defined as the value that occurs with the highest frequency in a given data set. In a clinical setting, if "headache" is the most common symptom recorded among 100 patients, it represents the modal symptom. The median (Option A) is the middle value when the data is arranged in order. Standard deviation (Option C) is a measure of the dispersion or spread of data around the mean. The mean (Option D) is the arithmetic average of all values. The mode is particularly useful for categorical data or when identifying the "most typical" case in a distribution. Unlike the mean, the mode is not affected by extreme outliers, making it a robust measure for certain types of health statistics. Therefore, for the specific purpose of identifying the most frequent observation in patient records, the mode is the correct statistical term
questions.learning: The mode is the measure of central tendency defined as the value that occurs with the highest frequency in a given data set. In a clinical setting, if "headache" is the most common symptom recorded among 100 patients, it represents the modal symptom.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What strategies can be implemented to reduce the risk of endometrial cancer in a postmenopausal woman receiving hormone replacement therapy (HRT)?
questions.explanation: In postmenopausal women who have an intact uterus, undergoing unopposed estrogen therapy significantly increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and subsequently endometrial cancer. This occurs because estrogen causes continuous proliferation of the uterine lining. To decrease this risk, the standard and most effective measure is adding a progestogen to the estrogen therapy (Option D). Progesterone acts to "oppose" the stimulatory effect of estrogen, inducing a secretory change and ensuring the regular shedding or thinning of the endometrium. Combined oral contraceptive pills (Option A) are not typically used for postmenopausal HRT. Clonidine (Option B) and Vitamin E (Option C) may be used as non-hormonal treatments for hot flashes but have no protective effect on the uterine lining. Therefore, combined estrogen-progestogen therapy is the definitive standard of care for women with a uterus to prevent malignancy
questions.learning: In postmenopausal women who have an intact uterus, undergoing unopposed estrogen therapy significantly increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and subsequently endometrial cancer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient with carcinoma located at the anal verge, which of the following lymph node groups is most likely to be involved first?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Superficial inguinal nodes

Lymphatic drainage of the anal canal depends on its relation to the pectinate line.

Anal verge / below pectinate line Drains to:

• Superficial inguinal lymph nodes

Therefore, carcinoma at the anal verge first spreads to superficial inguinal nodes.

Important Anatomy

| Region | Lymphatic Drainage

| Above pectinate line | Internal iliac nodes

| Below pectinate line / anal verge | Superficial inguinal nodes

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
A COPD patient with a history of smoking presents with respiratory symptoms. High resolution CT showed panacinar emphysema. Which enzyme deficiency is associated with this condition?

Periodic Acid–Schiff = PAS

Alpha 1 anti trypsin = α1AT
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alpha-1 antitrypsin

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is associated with panacinar emphysema.

Panacinar or panlobular emphysema is associated with α1 antitrypsin (α1AT) deficiency. It is exacerbated by smoking. Panacinar occurs more commonly in lower zones and the anterior margins of the lung. In this type, the acini from respiratory bronchiole to terminal blind alveoli are uniformly enlarged.

α1AT deficiency is an autosomal-recessive disorder of protein misfolding. Deficiency of α1AT protein results in excessive degradation of alveoli by neutrophil elastase causing panacinar emphysema. It also causes liver disease as a consequence of the abnormal accumulation of the misfolded protein within hepatocytes.  α1AT deficiency is characterized by the presence of round-to-oval cytoplasmic globular inclusions in hepatocytes. These hepatocytes are strongly Periodic acid–Schiff positive and diastase resistant.

Trypsin, chymotrypsin, and elastase are endopeptidases. They cleave the internal peptide bonds. Trypsin is specific for cleavage at the sites of basic amino acids, while chymotrypsin and elastase are specific for cleavage at neutral amino acids.

Other options:

Option B: Elastase is inhibited by alpha-1 antitrypsin. In the case of alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency, there is the destruction of lung tissue (elastin) by the elastase released by macrophages.

Option C: Chymotrypsin degrades trypsin and protects the pancreas from trypsin-related injury.

Option D: Type 2 surfactant deficiency is associated with respiratory distress syndrome as type 2 pneumocytes produce the surfactant which decreases the surface tension.
questions.learning: Alpha-1 antitrypsin Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is associated with panacinar emphysema. Panacinar or panlobular emphysema is associated with α1 antitrypsin (α1AT) deficiency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 80-year-old man develops pain and swelling in the right calf following immobilization for a right intertrochanteric fracture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient possesses several classic risk factors for Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) (Option B): advanced age (80 years), a recent major lower limb fracture, and immobilization . The clinical signs of pain and swelling localized specifically to the calf muscle are the most common presentations of an acute clot in the lower extremity venous system. Chronic osteomyelitis (Option A) presents with long-term discharge and localized bone pain, not acute swelling. Compartment syndrome (Option C) is a surgical emergency characterized by "pain out of proportion" and loss of pulses, typically following acute crush injuries rather than prolonged immobilization. Arterial claudication (Option D) causes pain only during exercise that is relieved by rest. Therefore, because the patient fits the "Virchow's Triad" perfectly (stasis and vascular injury), DVT is the most probable and dangerous diagnosis. Clinicians must urgently confirm this with Doppler ultrasound to prevent a lethal pulmonary embolism
questions.learning: The patient possesses several classic risk factors for Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) (Option B): advanced age (80 years), a recent major lower limb fracture, and immobilization .

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the defect shown in the image:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Herbert pits

The image shows tiny lesions at the limbus, indicating Hebert's pits. This finding is seen in trachoma, which is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, more specifically the trachoma inclusion conjunctivitis (TRIC) serovars A, B, Ba, C.

Trachoma is a form of chronic infective conjunctivitis and is one of the leading causes of blindness. It has an ‘active’ inflammatory stage and a ‘cicatricial’ chronic stage.

The active inflammatory stage is more prevalent in children and presents with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and discharge (often mild symptoms). Examination findings at this stage show:

• Conjunctival follicles contain Leber cells (multinucleated lymphocytes)
• corneal Herbert's follicles (similar to conjunctival follicles)

Cicatricial chronic stage is seen in middle age. And when the chronic infection with sequelae sets in, the patient complains of pain, lacrimation, photophobia, and later blurring, and finally loss of vision. Conjunctiva shows concretions (whitish deposits of inspissated mucus in depressions called glands of Henle). Corneal signs include:

• Herbert pits (pitted scars in the limbal which are remnants of healed Herbert follicles)
• corneal opacity is seen in later stages.

There can be associated trichiasis ( when at least one eyelash rubs the eyeball) and entropion.

At present WHO grading with 'FISTO' is in use.

Trachoma is treated according to the WHO classification using the SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial hygiene, and Environmental improvement). Azithromycin is the antibiotic of choice, and surgery involves the correction of trichiasis and entropion. In case of significant corneal scarring, penetrating keratoplasty is done.

Other options:

Option B: Horner–Trantas dots (image below) are distinct white, chalky, gelatinous nodules made up of eosinophils and epithelial debris that appear at the limbus, and they are characteristic of limbal vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).

Option C: In giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC), gelatinous papillae initially appear as small, elevated nodules on the conjunctiva. These papillae eventually grow larger, forming macropapillae and giant papillae, and may be accompanied by Trantas dots at the limbus.

The image below shows giant papillae in the conjunctiva:

Option D: Progressive pannus in trachoma involves the infiltration of the cornea with new blood vessels developing in the upper part, lying between the epithelium and Bowman's membrane. As the condition advances, these superficial vessels contribute to the destruction of Bowman's membrane, with corneal infiltration occurring before significant vascularization.
questions.learning: Herbert pits — The image shows tiny lesions at the limbus, indicating Hebert's pits. This finding is seen in trachoma, which is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, more specifically the trachoma inclusion conjunctivitis (TRIC) serovars A, B, Ba, C.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A female patient presents with nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and loss of smell. On examination, foul-smelling discharge and yellowish-green crusts are present in the nasal cavity. She is found to have merciful anosmia. Which of the following finding can also be seen during the examination of her nose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Roomy nasal cavity

The clinical vignette of anosmia, foul-smelling discharge, and yellowish-green crusts in the nasal cavity points to a diagnosis of atrophic rhinitis. The other examination finding that is observed in atrophic rhinitis is a roomy nasal cavity.

Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic inflammation of the nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones. The exact etiology of this condition is not known.

The patients present with nasal obstruction, foul odor, merciful anosmia, greenish-grey crusting of the nasal passage, pale nasal mucosa, atrophied nasal turbinates, and epistaxis following the removal of the crusts. Roomy nasal cavity is seen due to the resorption of bones of the turbinates.

Treatment options for atrophic rhinitis include nasal irrigation using warm saline or an alkaline solution composed of sodium bicarbonate, sodium biborate, and sodium chloride (1:1:2) mixed with water.

Local antibiotics such as Kemicetine antiozaena solution, which contains chloromycetin, oestradiol, and vitamin D2, can be used. Topical applications of 25% glucose in glycerine, estradiol spray, and systemic administration of streptomycin, potassium iodide, or placental extract may also be employed.

Surgical management options include Young's operation, where flaps are raised within the nasal vestibule and both nostrils are completely closed, then opened after 6 months. During this time, the nasal mucosa may revert to a more normal state, and crusting is reduced. Another option is the modified Young's operation, where the nostrils are partially closed to avoid discomfort. The results of this modified approach are comparable to the original Young's operation.

Additionally, the nasal cavity can be narrowed through submucosal injection of teflon paste or by inserting fat, cartilage, or teflon strips beneath the mucoperiosteum.

The image below shows the endoscopic appearance of atrophic rhinitis:

Other options:

Option B: Nasal polyps are non-neoplastic masses of the edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. Nasal polyps can be antrochoanal polyps or ethmoidal polyps.

Option C: Inferior turbinate hypertrophy is associated with various mucosal diseases which include allergic rhinitis, infectious rhinitis, and vasomotor rhinitis. It can cause chronic nasal obstruction.

Option D: Foreign body nose is commonly seen in children and the child presents with unilateral, foul-smelling nasal discharge.
questions.learning: Roomy nasal cavity — The clinical vignette of anosmia, foul-smelling discharge, and yellowish-green crusts in the nasal cavity points to a diagnosis of atrophic rhinitis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While calculating the ‘total dependency ratio’, which one of the following is used in the denominator?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Population 15 to 64 years

The Total Dependency Ratio (TDR) measures the burden of the dependent population on the working-age population.

Formula:

• Total Dependency Ratio = [(Population 0–14 years + Population ≥65 years) ÷ Population 15–64 years] × 100

Why is C. correct?

• Population 15–64 years forms the denominator because it represents the economically productive (working-age) population.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the lesion of vocal cord in the image given below :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Laryngeal papilloma

The image showing grape-like projections, involving the anterior part of the vocal cords depicts a laryngeal papilloma.

Laryngeal papilloma is a benign tumor of the larynx caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV type 6 and 11). They can occur in children, most commonly around 3 -5 years of age (juvenile papillomatosis), as well as in adults. They involve the supraglottic and glottic regions of the larynx. Seeding of the lesions can occur during invasive laryngeal procedures, such as intubation. They have a high recurrence rate and very low potential for malignancy.

Adult-onset laryngeal papillomatosis is less common and usually seen in males aged 30-50 years. It is less aggressive and involves the anterior part of the vocal cords. The treatment is the same as juvenile papillomatosis.

Patients present with hoarseness, aphonia, dyspnea, or stridor. Laryngoscopy shows pinkish to white grape-like projections that can be sessile or pedunculate with a visible central vascular core. The diagnosis is confirmed by direct laryngoscopy and biopsy. Treatment consists of micro-laryngoscopy and CO2 laser excision.

The image below depicts laryngeal papillomatosis on laryngoscopy:

Reinke's edema (Option A) is a collection of fluid in the subepithelial space of Reinke. It generally occurs in patients with vocal abuse or smoking. The vocal cords will show diffuse, symmetrical swelling.

The laryngoscopic image below shows Reinke's edema:

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following diagnostic criteria for acute pelvic inflammatory disease (PID): 1. Lower abdominal tenderness 2. Oral temperature >38°C 3. Adnexal tenderness 4. Cervical motion tenderness Which of the above are included in the minimum criteria for diagnosis of PID?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

The minimum clinical criteria for presumptive diagnosis of acute PID are the presence of any one of the following on pelvic examination:

1. Lower abdominal tenderness
2. Adnexal tenderness
3. Cervical motion tenderness

Therefore, 1, 3 and 4 → C.

Oral temperature >38°C is a supportive/additional criterion, not one of the minimum criteria.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman travels from Delhi to Leh (3500 feet) on vacation. She develops a headache, lightheadedness, nausea, fatigue, and shortness of breath shortly after arriving at the airport. Which of the following best describes the initial physiological disturbance and the body's immediate compensatory reaction?
options: Decreased alveolar PO2 stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors, leading to hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis
Increased barometric pressure causes hyperoxia, triggering central chemoreceptors to decrease ventilation
Shift of the O2-Hb dissociation curve to the right
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased alveolar PO2 stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors, leading to hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis

During the process of acclimatisation to high altitudes, respiratory alkalosis and hyperventilation occur as a result of stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors by decreased alveolar PO₂.

The symptoms of chest tightness and breathlessness following rapid ascent indicate acute mountain/altitude sickness, which can be prevented by gradual ascent with sufficient time for acclimatisation.

Following are the physiological changes that occur during acclimatisation:

* Initially there is hyperventilation leading to respiratory alkalosis. There is shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the left. But following this, there is also an increase in red blood cell 2,3-DPG, which tends to decrease the O₂ affinity of haemoglobin. Finally, the net effect is a small increase in P50, and this decrease in O₂ affinity makes more O₂ available to the tissues. But this increase in P50 is also limited because when the arterial PO₂ is markedly reduced, the decreased O₂ affinity interferes with O₂ uptake by haemoglobin in the lungs.

* Increased erythropoietin secretion, leading to an increase in circulating red blood cells

* Increased number of mitochondria

* Increased myoglobin to facilitate the movement of O₂ into the tissues.

* Increased tissue cytochrome oxidase

* Increased sympathetic tone

* Renal suppression of carbonic anhydrase and excretion of dilute alkaline urine bring the pH of the blood to normal.

* Decreased maximal exercise capacity (by ~1% for every 100 m gained above 1500 m)

On the ascent to high altitudes, the low partial pressure of oxygen leads to hypoxia and systemic arteriolar dilatation. Consequently, the capillary pressure rises with increased transudation of fluid into the brain tissue, and the following symptoms are seen:

* Headache

* Irritation

* Insomnia

* Breathlessness

* Nausea and vomiting

Treatment involves administration of oxygen, descent to a lower altitude, and administration of acetazolamide. Acetazolamide counteracts hypoxia by stimulating respiration and reducing the formation of cerebrospinal fluid, thereby reducing intracranial tension.

Portable hyperbaric chambers are increasingly being used in the treatment of high-altitude illnesses when rapid descent is not possible. These chambers are available in armed forces hospitals in high-altitude areas,

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Revised The vertical plane that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts is known as __________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coronal plane

The coronal plane is a vertical that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts.

Four imaginary planes are used in anatomical descriptions:

* Median (mid-sagittal) plane: Vertical plane that divides the body into equal right and left halves

* Sagittal plane: Vertical plane that divides the body into unequal right and left parts; parallel to the median plane

* Coronal (frontal) plane: Vertical plane that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts; perpendicular to the median plane

* Transverse (horizontal) plane: Horizontal plane that divides the body into upper and lower parts; perpendicular to both the sagittal and coronal planes

Note: Axial (or trans-axial) plane is a term used in radiology for the horizontal plane.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A newborn presents with hypoplasia of the zygomatic bones, micrognathia, malformed external ears, and downward-slanting palpebral fissures. The condition results from abnormal development of which of the following pharyngeal arches?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. First and second pharyngeal arches

The clinical features described are characteristic of Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis), an autosomal dominant disorder caused most commonly by mutations in the TCOF1 gene, resulting in defective neural crest cell migration into the first and second pharyngeal arches. This leads to abnormal development of facial bones and external ears.

The patient has the classic features of Treacher Collins syndrome:

• Hypoplasia of the zygomatic bones
• Micrognathia (mandibular hypoplasia)
• Malformed external ears (microtia)
• Downward-slanting palpebral fissures

Why not the other options?

• A. First pharyngeal arch only: Although the mandible and zygoma are first arch derivatives, external ear abnormalities also involve the second arch.
• B. Second pharyngeal arch only: Does not explain the marked mandibular and zygomatic hypoplasia.
• D. Third and fourth pharyngeal arches: These primarily contribute to the hyoid bone, laryngeal cartilages, pharyngeal muscles, and cranial nerves IX and X, not the facial skeleton.
questions.learning: First and second pharyngeal arches — The clinical features described are characteristic of Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis), an autosomal dominant disorder caused most commonly by mutations in the TCOF1 gene, resulting in defective…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Sour taste is mediated by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. TRPV1 Channel

Sour taste = H⁺ ions → activate ion channels (mainly TRP family like TRPV1) → depolarization

Sour taste is mediated by proton-sensitive ion channels activated by H⁺ from acids. TRPV1-related channels respond to acidity and depolarize taste receptor cells. This mechanism is ion channel–based, not GPCR mediated. T1R receptors are involved in sweet and umami, not sour taste.

Acidic food (↑ H⁺)

↓

H⁺ interacts with taste receptor cell

↓

Activation of TRPV1 / inhibition of K⁺ channels

↓

Depolarization

↓

Neurotransmitter release

↓

Gustatory nerve activation

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presented with a history of profuse vaginal discharge. The discharge has a fishy odour. Which of the following best describes the microscopic finding given below?
options: Epithelial cell with bacteria attached on cell surface
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Epithelial cell with bacteria attached on cell surface

The given clinical scenario of women with fishy odor vaginal discharge is suggestive of bacterial vaginosis (BV). The microscopic finding is vaginal epithelial cells with bacteria attached to their surface called clue cells, creating a poorly defined cellular border. They are the most reliable indicators of BV.

Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is characterized by a decrease in lactobacilli and an overgrowth of anaerobic bacterial species, including gardnerella, prevotella,mobiluncus, and bacteroides. Multiple or new sexual partners, having female partners, and engaging in oral sex are associated with a higher risk of BV. They may experience a foul-smelling (fishy odor) thin vaginal discharge.

The clinical diagnosis of BV is based on the presence of three out of four Amsel criteria: elevated vaginal pH (>4.5), thin noninflammatory discharge, >20% clue cells, and a fishy odor (positive whiff test) after adding 10% potassium hydroxide to a vaginal sample. creating a poorly defined cellular border.

BV is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preterm birth, preterm premature rupture of membranes, and postpartum endometritis. It also increases susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections, including HIV.

The recommended treatment options in nonpregnant women include oral metronidazole, metronidazole gel, or clindamycin cream. Alternative options include oral secnidazole, tinidazole, or clindamycin. Partner treatment is not needed.
questions.learning: Epithelial cell with bacteria attached on cell surface The given clinical scenario of women with fishy odor vaginal discharge is suggestive of bacterial vaginosis (BV).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A researcher is investigating the restriction (R) point, the first major checkpoint of the cell cycle that determines whether a cell will commit to DNA synthesis or exit the cell cycle into a quiescent (G₀) state. This checkpoint is located immediately before which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. S phase

The G₁/S checkpoint (Restriction point or R point) is the first and most important checkpoint of the cell cycle. It occurs in late G₁ phase, immediately before the S phase, where the cell decides whether to:

• Proceed to DNA replication (S phase), or
• Exit the cell cycle and enter the quiescent G₀ phase

Once a cell crosses this checkpoint, it is committed to completing the cell cycle, even if external growth factors are withdrawn.

The checkpoint assesses:

• Cell size
• Nutrient and energy availability
• Growth factor stimulation
• DNA damage

It is regulated by:

• Cyclin D–CDK4/6
• Cyclin E–CDK2
• Retinoblastoma (Rb) protein
• p53 (via p21 in response to DNA damage)

Why not the other options?

• A. G₂ phase: Incorrect. The G₂/M checkpoint occurs after DNA replication, ensuring DNA has been completely and accurately replicated before mitosis.
• B. M phase: Incorrect. The spindle assembly checkpoint occurs during metaphase, ensuring proper chromosome attachment before anaphase.
• C. S phase: ✅ Correct. The restriction point is located immediately before the S phase.
• D. G₀ phase: Incorrect. G₀ is not a phase that follows the checkpoint; rather, cells exit from G₁ into G₀ if they do not receive the signals required to pass the checkpoint.

High-yield pearl

| Cell cycle checkpoint | Location | Function

| --------------------- | -------- | --------

| G₁/S (Restriction point) | End of G₁, before S phase | Determines commitment to DNA replication; checks DNA damage, nutrients, growth factors

| G₂/M checkpoint | End of G₂ | Ensures DNA replication is complete and DNA is undamaged before mitosis

| Spindle checkpoint | Metaphase | Ensures all chromosomes are attached to spindle fibers before anaphase

Exam tip:

The G₁/S checkpoint is the commitment checkpoint of the cell cycle:

• Pass → Enter S phase and replicate DNA
• Fail → Cell arrests for repair or exits into G₀.
