questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: DNA is present in which one of the organelle?
questions.explanation: In animal cells, while the vast majority of genetic material is located within the nucleus, mitochondria are unique organelles that possess their own independent DNA. This mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is typically circular and is inherited maternally. It encodes for essential proteins required for the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation, which are the primary processes used to generate ATP for cellular energy. Lysosomes (Option B) are involved in intracellular digestion and waste removal but do not contain DNA. The endoplasmic reticulum (Option C) is responsible for protein and lipid synthesis but lacks its own genome. The cytoplasm (Option D) is the fluid environment of the cell where translation and glycolysis occur; while viral DNA might temporarily be present there during infection, it is not a normal site for cellular DNA storage. Mitochondrial DNA is essential for the organelle's function, and mutations in it can lead to various mitochondrial diseases affecting energy-hungry tissues like muscle and brain
questions.learning: In animal cells, while the vast majority of genetic material is located within the nucleus, mitochondria are unique organelles that possess their own independent DNA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presenting with bleeding gums and easy bruisability was diagnosed with scurvy. This is due to ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Defective collagen formation

Bleeding gums and easy bruisability seen in scurvy are due to defective collagen formation.

Scurvy results from the deficiency of vitamin C, which is required for the hydroxylation of prolyl and lysyl residues of collagen reactions. Hence, deficiency of vitamin C results in a defective prolyl hydroxylase activity, leading to defective collagen formation and resulting in generalized bleeding tendencies.

Hemorrhagic manifestations of scurvy include petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses at pressure points, epistaxis, gum bleeding, and characteristic perifollicular hemorrhages. Other manifestations are poor wound and fracture healing, hyperkeratosis of hair follicles, arthralgia, and muscle weakness. It also results in defective osteoid formation. Costo-chondral separation leads to the formation of tender nodules that are sharply angulated and are also known as the scorbutic rosary.

The cutaneous manifestations of scurvy include

• Phrynoderma over posterolateral arms which can then generalize over the back and thighs and legs.
• Corkscrew hairs -  fractured and coiled hairs due to impaired keratin cross‐links by disulfide bonds
• Perifollicular hemorrhage and purpura
• Lower limb edema
• Splinter hemorrhages

It is treated with vitamin C supplementation.

Other options:

Option A: Low calcium levels do not cause scurvy; they may contribute to other clinical conditions like osteoporosis or muscle cramps.

Option C: Inhibition of clotting factors is not responsible for scurvy. Vitamin K deficiency, however, can lead to the inhibition of clotting factors and cause bleeding tendencies.

Option D: Increased keratinization of epithelium is not the cause of scurvy. Vitamin A deficiency, on the other hand, can result in hyperkeratoses and epithelial changes, such as xerosis and Bitot's spots.
questions.learning: Defective collagen formation Bleeding gums and easy bruisability seen in scurvy are due to defective collagen formation. Scurvy results from the deficiency of vitamin C, which is required for the hydroxylation of prolyl and lysyl residues of collagen…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A woman presented with ulcerative lesion over the breast associated with erythema of surrounding skin and history of retraction of nipple. Biopsy revealed invasive ductal carcinoma. According to 8th edition of AJCC classification, the patient can be classified under which stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stage IIIb

The patient presenting with ulcerative lesion with inflammatory signs can be classified as Stage IIIb. Inflammatory breast carcinoma (stage T4d) is characterized by the skin changes of brawny induration, erythema with a raised edge, and edema (peaud’orange) involving >1/3rd of the breast.

T4d in the TNM staging of carcinoma breast points toward a diagnosis of inflammatory breast carcinoma. It shows extensive invasion and proliferation of tumor cells. Inflammatory breast cancer is the most aggressive subtype of breast cancer. The hallmark of this condition is the overexpression of e-cadherin. This results in increased tumor cohesion and the formation of tumoral clumps which can result in emboli. It has a particularly poor prognosis.

In addition to anatomical staging, the eighth edition of the AJCC TNM staging system includes the histological grade, ER, PR, HER2/neu and Ki-67 assessment, multigene testingwith Oncotype DXand the response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy to refine the prognostic information.
questions.learning: Stage IIIb — The patient presenting with ulcerative lesion with inflammatory signs can be classified as Stage IIIb. Inflammatory breast carcinoma (stage T4d) is characterized by the skin changes of brawny induration, erythema with a raised edge, and edema…

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the given disorder?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a pigmented skin lesion that exhibits several "ABCDE" warning signs of melanoma: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variegation (multiple shades), and a large Diameter. Melanoma is a highly aggressive skin cancer arising from melanocytes. Simple hyperpigmentation (Option B) would be more regular and uniform. Basal cell carcinoma (Option C) typically appears as a pearly papule with telangiectasia, though a pigmented variant exists. Squamous cell carcinoma (Option D) usually presents as a scaly, erythematous plaque or ulcerated nodule. Early diagnosis of melanoma is critical, as the risk of metastasis increases significantly with the depth of the lesion (Breslow thickness). Any suspicious pigmented lesion should undergo an excisional biopsy with a narrow margin for histopathological confirmation. If confirmed, a wider re-excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy may be required depending on the stage. Melanoma is responsible for the majority of skin cancer-related deaths, highlighting the importance of routine skin checks and sun protection
questions.learning: The image depicts a pigmented skin lesion that exhibits several "ABCDE" warning signs of melanoma: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variegation (multiple shades), and a large Diameter.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which anti-epileptic drug is commonly associated with gum hypertrophy and dizziness as side effects?
questions.explanation: Phenytoin is a first-line anti-epileptic drug that stabilizes neuronal membranes by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels. It is famously associated with gingival hyperplasia (gum hypertrophy) due to the overgrowth of collagen fibers in the gums. It also frequently causes dizziness, ataxia, and nystagmus as signs of dose-related toxicity. Regarding other options, Carbamazepine (Option A) commonly causes dizziness and diplopia but is not associated with gum hypertrophy. Levetiracetam (Option C) is generally well-tolerated but may lead to irritability and mood changes. Topiramate (Option D) is associated with cognitive slowing, weight loss, and kidney stones, but not gingival overgrowth. Long-term phenytoin use can also lead to other side effects like hirsutism, coarsening of facial features, and megaloblastic anemia. Therefore, the specific combination of gum hypertrophy and dizziness is a classic indicator of phenytoin therapy
questions.learning: Phenytoin is a first-line anti-epileptic drug that stabilizes neuronal membranes by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels. It is famously associated with gingival hyperplasia (gum hypertrophy) due to the overgrowth of collagen fibers in the gums.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with reduced hearing for the past 2-3 months. The otoscopy finding is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serous otitis media

The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with hearing loss for the past 2-3 months and the otoscopic finding is suggestive of serous otitis media. The given otoscopic image shows a dull and opaque tympanic membrane with clear effusion.

Serous otitis media is also known as secretory otitis media or mucoid otitis media or glue ear. It is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Glue ear is thought to happen due to either malfunctioning (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis or tonsillitis or rhinitis, palatal defects, tumors of nasopharynx) or increased secretory activity of the eustachian tube (allergy, unresolved otitis media, viral infections).

It is often seen in children of 5-8 years of age. They present with hearing loss not exceeding 40 dB, which is insidious in onset. Speech may be delayed and defective due to hearing loss. Mild earaches with a history of upper respiratory tract infection are usually seen.

On otoscopy,

• Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex
• Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus
• If the tympanic membrane is transparent fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss and audiometry reveals hearing loss in the range of 20-40 dB. On impedance audiometry, there is reduced compliance and a flat curve shifted to the negative side due to the presence of fluid. X-ray mastoid reveals clouding of air cells.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

• Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, antibiotics, and middle ear aeration techniques.
• Surgical management includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid, grommet insertion, tympanotomy, or cortical mastoidectomy.

Chronic glue ear sequelae include atrophic tympanic membrane and middle ear atelectasis, ossicular necrosis, tympanosclerosis, cholesterol granuloma, and retraction pockets.

Other options:

Option A: Myringitis bullosa is characterized by painful hemorrhagic blebs on the tympanic membrane and deep meatus. It occurs due to infection by a virus or mycoplasma.

Option C: Acute otitis media is an acute infection of the middle ear by pyogenic organisms. It presents with marked earache and hearing loss is seen in later stages. Otoscopy shows a red and bulging tympanic membrane.
questions.learning: Serous otitis media — The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with hearing loss for the past 2-3 months and the otoscopic finding is suggestive of serous otitis media.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which anesthetic induction agent is most commonly associated with hallucinations and vivid dreams during the recovery phase?
questions.explanation: Ketamine (Option A) is a dissociative anesthetic that acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist. Its most characteristic and bothersome side effect is emergence delirium, which occurs in up to 30% of adults. This phenomenon includes hallucinations, vivid dreams, confusion, and agitation during the recovery phase as the patient "emerges" from anesthesia. To minimize these effects, ketamine is often administered alongside a benzodiazepine like midazolam. Propofol (Option B) provides a pleasant recovery and is actually associated with euphoria rather than hallucinations. Thiopentone (Option C) and Etomidate (Option D) do not classically cause psychiatric emergence phenomena . Ketamine is highly valued for its analgesic properties and for maintaining spontaneous respiration, but its psychotropic side effects limit its use in adult elective surgery. Therefore, the specific side effect profile of vivid dreams and hallucinations is uniquely attributed to ketamine among the choices provided
questions.learning: Ketamine (Option A) is a dissociative anesthetic that acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist. Its most characteristic and bothersome side effect is emergence delirium, which occurs in up to 30% of adults.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which is the drug of choice for refractive testing in a child with squint?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1% atropine

1% atropine is the drug of choice in refractive testing in a child with a squint.

The most common cause of squint in children is due to ciliary spasm. Hence proper evaluation is required for refractive testing with cycloplegia as well. Atropine is used because of its high cycloplegic capacity and useful in children who inherently have high ciliary tone

Option B: Tropicamide is short-acting and the maximum effect lasts just 30 mins. Hence not preferred

Option C: Homatropine is less potent

Option D: Cyclopentolate has a shorter duration of action and has less cycloplegic effect. Hence not preferred
questions.learning: 1% atropine 1% atropine is the drug of choice in refractive testing in a child with a squint. The most common cause of squint in children is due to ciliary spasm.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All of the following are protected by OCPs except?
questions.explanation: Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs) are well-known to have several non-contraceptive benefits, but they do not protect against breast cancer. In fact, OCP use is associated with a slight increase in risk (approximately 25%), especially in women who start using them before age 24. In contrast, OCPs provide strong protection against carcinoma endometrium (Option B), reducing the risk by at least 30%, and ovarian cancer (Option D), reducing the risk by 30–50%. They also provide a protective effect against colonic (colorectal) cancer (Option C), with studies showing a risk reduction of 15–20%. Cancer of the breast is actually listed as an absolute contraindication for OCP use. Therefore, while OCPs are highly beneficial for preventing many gynecological and colonic malignancies, breast cancer risk is the notable exception

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which cell type is responsible for the production and secretion of surfactant?
questions.explanation: The alveoli of the lungs are lined by two main types of epithelial cells. Type II pneumocytes (Option B) are cuboidal cells that act as the "caretakers" of the alveolus. Their primary function is the synthesis and secretion of pulmonary surfactant, a phospholipid-protein complex stored in lamellar bodies. Surfactant is essential because it reduces surface tension at the air-water interface, preventing alveolar collapse (atelectasis) during expiration. Type I pneumocytes (Option A) are thin, flat cells that cover 95% of the alveolar surface and are optimized for gas exchange, but they do not produce surfactant. Sertoli cells (Option C) and Leydig cells (Option D) are located in the testes and are involved in spermatogenesis and testosterone production, respectively. A deficiency in surfactant, often seen in premature infants, leads to Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome. Therefore, Type II pneumocytes are the specific source of this life-saving substance
questions.learning: The alveoli of the lungs are lined by two main types of epithelial cells. Type II pneumocytes (Option B) are cuboidal cells that act as the "caretakers" of the alveolus.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
A patient following a skid resulting in a motor traffic accident was brought to the emergency room 2 hours later. On examination, he was stable with GCS 15/15. The pupil was reactive to light. Tenderness and bruising over the left lower chest wall with petechiae was seen. Severe tenderness was elicited in the left hypochondriac region and BP- 90/50 mm of Hg. What is the best investigation used in the ER?

GCS- Glasgow coma scale

FAST- Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. FAST

FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) is the best investigation that can be performed in the emergency room (ER) for this patient with a blood pressure of 90/50 mm Hg who has sustained blunt abdominal trauma.

Focussed assessment with sonography for trauma is a non-invasive investigation that can be performed rapidly in the emergency room. It helps in identifying an abnormal collection of fluid or blood. FAST is indicated in:

• Haemodynamically unstable patients who had a blunt abdominal trauma
• Patients who sustained penetrating abdominal trauma with no other indications for immediate laparotomy (signs of haemodynamic instability, peritoneal irritation, peritoneal penetration and gunshot wound with transperitoneal trajectory).

FAST includes an examination of four regions:

• Pericardial sac
• Hepatorenal fossa
• Splenorenal fossa, and
• Pouch of Douglas

It is an operator-dependent procedure with limited visualization of the retroperitoneal structures.

Other options:

Option B - A chest X-Ray is used to exclude hemothorax or pneumothorax in a hemodynamically normal patient with penetrating trauma above the umbilicus or a suspected thoracoabdominal injury. Since the given patient is alert, awake, and with no mention of any pelvic pain or tenderness, a pelvic X-Ray is not indicated either.

Option C - Diagnostic peritoneal lavage is an invasive procedure and requires surgical expertise. For these reasons, it is done only in centres where FAST and/ CT are not available.

Option D - CT scan requires transporting the patient and is time-consuming. Hence, it cannot be performed in the ER in a haemodynamically unstable patient.
questions.learning: FAST FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) is the best investigation that can be performed in the emergency room (ER) for this patient with a blood pressure of 90/50 mm Hg who has sustained blunt abdominal trauma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An elderly woman reports difficulty in buttoning her shirt and increased clumsiness in performing daily activities. On examination, the clinician asked her to make an 'O' using her thumb and index finger, which she was unable to do. Which of the following muscles is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flexor pollicis longus

Inability to make an “O” sign indicates weakness of flexion at the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, which is the primary action of flexor pollicis longus.

This muscle is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve (median nerve branch), and its paralysis produces the classic positive pinch sign.

Opponens pollicis and abductor pollicis brevis mediate opposition and abduction, while palmar interossei act on digits, not the thumb IP joint.
questions.learning: Flexor pollicis longus Inability to make an “O” sign indicates weakness of flexion at the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, which is the primary action of flexor pollicis longus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a perforated peptic ulcer is hypotensive on arrival but becomes hemodynamically stable after fluid resuscitation. Which triage category should be assigned?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Yellow

In mass casualty triage, patients are categorized according to the urgency of treatment and likelihood of survival.

A patient with a perforated peptic ulcer who is initially hypotensive but responds to fluid resuscitation and becomes hemodynamically stable requires urgent surgical intervention, but treatment can be delayed briefly without immediate threat to life. Therefore, the patient is assigned to the Yellow (Delayed) category.

Why not the other options?

• A. Red (Immediate): Patients with life-threatening injuries requiring immediate intervention, e.g., persistent shock, airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax.
• C. Green (Minor): Walking wounded with minor injuries.
• D. Black (Expectant/Dead): Dead or injuries incompatible with survival despite available resources.

questions.text: Interventional technique used for the management of cerebral aneurysm:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coiling

Cerebral Aneurysm-

• Localized dilatation of an artery (usually at branch points in Circle of Willis)
• Most common: Berry (saccular) aneurysm
• Risk: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) → sudden “worst headache of life”

Treatment Goal- Exclude aneurysm from circulation WITHOUT blocking parent artery

Cerebral aneurysm → Endovascular coiling is the standard minimally invasive treatment to prevent rupture/rebleed

| Feature | Coiling | Surgical Clipping

| ------- | ------- | -----------------

| Approach | Endovascular | Open surgery

| Invasiveness | Minimal | High

| Recovery | Faster | Slower

| Recurrence | Slightly higher | Lower

Clinical Insight

• After SAH:

• Secure aneurysm ASAP → coiling/clipping

• Prevents:

• Rebleeding (highest risk in first 24 hrs)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman presents with a unilateral throbbing headache associated with nausea and vomiting. She has had similar episodes in the past where the headache usually lasts for 1-2 days. Bright light increases her discomfort and she prefers sitting in a dark room. Which of the following drugs can be used to decrease her headache episodes in the future?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Propranolol

Multiple unilateral throbbing headaches associated with nausea, vomiting, and photophobia suggest a diagnosis of migraine headaches and the drug used in the prophylaxis is propranolol.

Drugs used in the prophylaxis of migraine:
• Beta-blockers: propranolol
• Tricyclic antidepressants: amitriptyline
• Serotonergic: methysergide
• Anticonvulsants: valproate, topiramate
• Other classes: flunarizine
• Pizotifen

Sumatriptan is used in the treatment of an acute attack of a migraine.

Migraine:

The classic migraine is associated with an aura and can be:

a)Visual (most common)

* Zigzag lines

* Tunnel vision

* Scotoma

* Transient visual loss

b)Sensory

* Tingling sensation of hands, which spreads proximally

Note:

The most common negative visual aura is scotoma.
questions.learning: Propranolol Multiple unilateral throbbing headaches associated with nausea, vomiting, and photophobia suggest a diagnosis of migraine headaches and the drug used in the prophylaxis is propranolol.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with stridor, and endotracheal intubation is unsuccessful. Which of the following is the best alternative method for airway management in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cricothyrotomy

In a cannot intubate, cannot ventilate (CICV) situation with stridor, the preferred emergency airway is cricothyrotomy, which provides rapid access to the airway through the cricothyroid membrane.

·     Indication: Failed intubation with impending airway obstruction

·     Site: Cricothyroid membrane (between thyroid and cricoid cartilage)

·     Advantage: Quick, life-saving, minimal dissection compared to tracheostomy

·    Considered a temporary airway until a definitive airway (tracheostomy) is established

Why not other options:

·      Nasotracheal intubation: Difficult/impossible in obstructed airway

·      Bronchoscopy: Time-consuming, not suitable in emergency

·      LMA: May not bypass severe upper airway obstruction

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 70-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department due to sudden onset of right-sided weakness and urinary incontinence that began about 10 hours ago. On examination, there is 4/5 strength in the right upper extremity, 1/5 strength in the right lower extremity, and a Babinski sign on the right side. Sensation is decreased throughout the right foot and leg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left Anterior cerebral artery stroke

The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of frontal and parietal lobes, which control lower limb motor and sensory function and bladder control.

Key features of ACA stroke:

• Contralateral lower limb weakness > upper limb weakness
• Contralateral sensory loss in leg
• Urinary incontinence (medial frontal micturition center involvement)
• Behavioral changes/abulia (frontal lobe)

Differentiation:

B. Lacunar stroke: Pure motor/sensory without cortical signs

C. Left MCA stroke: Face/arm > leg weakness + aphasia/neglect

D. Right ACA stroke: Would affect left side
questions.learning: Left Anterior cerebral artery stroke — The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of frontal and parietal lobes, which control lower limb motor and sensory function and bladder control.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast and fever. On examination of the affected side, there is localized erythema, warmth, point tenderness, fluctuation test is positive. There is mild axillary lymphadenopathy on the affected side and the contralateral breast is normal. Repeated aspirations under antibiotic cover done were unsuccessful. A USG done showed fluid collection. What is the management plan for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Incision and Drainage

The given case scenario points towards a diagnosis of breast abscess. The latest guidelines for the management of breast abscess specify that multiple aspirations under antibiotic cover should be attempted before an incision and drainage are done. This often allows resolution without the need for an incision scar and also allows the patient to continue breastfeeding. But here aspirations have been unsuccessful and thus incision and drainage have to be the next step in the management of this patient.

Mastitis occurs due to the growth of staphylococcus or streptococcus due to breast milk stasis. This occurs secondary to blockage of lactiferous duct or due to incomplete emptying of breast milk or due to retracted nipple. Overgrowth of these bacteria results in the development of breast abscesses.

It is commoner in new mothers at the beginning of lactation who are inexperienced with breastfeeding or during weaning when nipple trauma occurs due to the infant's growing teeth.

Signs and symptoms of this condition involve:

* Fever and malaise

* Localized pain and tenderness

* Redness and swelling of the affected breast

* Fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

The initial treatment should involve providing pain relief with analgesics. The abscess should then be localized preferably under USG guidance and percutaneous aspiration carried out. The pus should be sent for microbiological examination to find the organism and antibiotic sensitivity. Repeated aspirations may be carried out under antibiotics cover if needed.

In some conditions mentioned below, the breast abscess may be unresponsive to repeated aspirations and antibiotic cover. In such cases, incision and drainage are performed. The conditions include:

* Presence of thick pus

* Bacteria resistant to antibiotics

* If just superficial part has been aspirated in the presence of a multiloculated abscess

* A non-healing breast abscess due to tuberculosis of breast or Inflammatory carcinoma of the breast, or an immunocompromised host.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient’s tissue biopsy reveals asteroid bodies on histopathological examination. Which of the following culture medium is most appropriate for isolating the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sabouraud’s dextrose agar

Asteroid bodies on histopathology are classically seen in sporotrichosis, caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii.

·         Asteroid bodies: central yeast surrounded by eosinophilic radiating material (Splendore–Hoeppli phenomenon)

·         Disease: Sporotrichosis (“rose gardener’s disease”)

·         Transmission: traumatic inoculation via thorns, splinters

·   Culture:

o    Sabouraud’s dextrose agar (SDA) is the medium of choice for fungal isolation

o    Shows mold form at 25°C and yeast form at 37°C (dimorphic fungus)

Why not others:

·         Blood agar / Chocolate agar / Nutrient agar: used for bacteria, not fungi

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: You are conducting an experiment on mitochondrial respiration. You add malate/pyruvate and respiration is normal. You add succinate and respiration is normal. When you add another substance in the presence of pyruvate/succinate and malate, respiration is blocked. Which of the following substances is most likely added?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oligomycin

In the experiment conducted on mitochondrial respiration, respiration will be blocked by the addition of oligomycin, an antibiotic, when added in the presence of pyruvate/ succinate and malate. Oligomycin inhibits oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria and hence blocks respiration.

Electron transport chain (ETC)/respiratory chain is the final pathway by which all the electrons derived from the oxidation of carbohydrates, fatty acids, and amino acids are directed towards the final reaction with oxygen, to form water and adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

The chemiosmotic theory states that the flow of electrons through the respiratory chain generates a proton motive force. This force drives the formation of ATP by the process of oxidative phosphorylation.

Complexes of ETC
Inhibitors

Complex I: NADH-CoQ oxidoreductase
Piericidin, amobarbital, rotenone

Complex II: Succinate-CoQ reductase
TTFA (thenoyltrifluoroacetone), carboxin, malonate

Complex III: CoQH2-cytochrome c oxidoreductase
BAL(British anti-lewisite), antimycin A

Complex IV: cytochrome oxidase
Hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, cyanide

Complex V (informally): ATP Synthase
Atractyloside, oligomycin

In the given experiment, malate and pyruvate are electron donors (NADH) at complex I of the ETC, and succinate is the electron donor (FADH2) at complex II. Normal respiration is observed on the addition of substances at both complexes I and II i.e., both oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis from ADP (adenosine diphosphate) take place.

Oligomycin is a competitive inhibitor of the Fo (oligomycin-sensitive) complex of ATP synthase (complex V) and blocks oxidation and phosphorylation by stopping the flow of protons through the ATP synthase enzyme complex. Hence the addition of oligomycin will inhibit complex V and stop respiration.

Other options:

Options A and B: Rotenone (option A) if added, will inhibit complex I. Electron transfer before complex I will be blocked but not after. Hence, normal respiration will occur. Similarly, antimycin A (option B) inhibits complex III, and electron transfer prior to complex III will be blocked and not after. Hence, respiration will not be completely hindered.

Option C: 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) is an uncoupler that dissociates oxidation in the respiratory chain from phosphorylation. Hence, respiration continues without ATP synthesis.
questions.learning: Oligomycin — In the experiment conducted on mitochondrial respiration, respiration will be blocked by the addition of oligomycin, an antibiotic, when added in the presence of pyruvate/ succinate and malate.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female presents with hirsutism, delayed periods & obesity. USG findings are given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome

The given clinical scenario and the ultrasound image given below showing an enlarged ovary with multiple follicles in the periphery(a string of pearls) is indicative of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS).

PCOS is an endocrinopathy seen in women of reproductive age, affecting multiple systems. The Rotterdam criteria are used to diagnose PCOS. The presence of any two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis of PCOS:

* Clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne)

* Menstrual abnormalities (oligo/amenorrhoea), anovulation, infertility

* Polycystic ovaries on ultrasonography.

Sonographic criteria for polycystic ovaries include ≥ 12 small cysts, an increased ovarian volume (> 10 mL) or both.

Management:

* Weight reduction alone is beneficial in mild hirsutism and lifestyle changes (like smoking cessation) are advised in the management of PCOS.

* Oral contraceptive pills (OCP), preferably fourth-generation pills with 30 mcg E2 and 2-3 mg drospirenone are used to treat menstrual abnormalities. It also reduces acne and further hirsutism.

* Anti-androgens are useful in treating hirsutism. OCP with cyproterone acetate is prescribed for PCOS patients with hirsutism.

* Patients with PCOD are more prone to developing insulin resistance which can be controlled with metformin. Acarbose can be used if metformin is contraindicated

* Patients presenting with infertility are treated by inducing ovulation using clomiphene as a first-line drug, along with dexamethasone and letrozole.

Surgical options include laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary. This is done either by laser or by unipolar electrocautery. It restores the endocrine levels and improves fertility.

Surgery is indicated only if,

* Medical therapy fails

* Hyperstimulation occurs

* Infertile women

* Previous pregnancy losses

Other Options:

Option B: Molar Pregnancy will produce a characteristic Snowstorm appearance on ultrasound.

Option C: Enlarged ovaries meeting in the midline having large cysts are suggestive of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

Option D: The image below depicts multiple theca lutein cysts.

Pearl PF1877: Endocrinological changes of PCOD

* Elevated Estrone/E1 levels.

* LH level is raised over 10 IU/mL. FSH level remains normal to low, but FSH/LH ratio falls.

* Testosterone and epi-androstenedione levels rise.

* Testosterone elevated but < 200 ng/dL (normal range 20 - 70 ng/dL)

* Testosterone > 200 ng/dL suggests androgen-secreting ovarian tumor

* DHEA-S values may be normal or slightly elevated

* DHEA >700 ng/mL suggests adrenal tumour

* Serum SHBG is reduced.

* Triglyceride level >150 mg/dL-hyperlipidaemia HDL <50 mg/dL.

* Fasting blood glucose/fasting insulin <4.5 suggests insulin resistance

* Prolactin is mildly raised in 15% cases

* Fasting insulin is more than 10 mIU/L in PCOS in 50–70%cases

* Thyroid function tests may be abnormal (hypothyroidism)

* 17-a-hydroxyprogesterone in the follicular phase >300 ng/dL suggests adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

* Urinary cortisol <50 μg/24 h.

Pearl PF1729: Management of PCOD

Complaint
Management

Irregular periods
OCPs

Obesity
Lifestyle modification

Insulin resistance
Metformin

Hirsutism /acne

Infertility

Note: Letrozole is as effective as Clomiphene in treating infertility in PCOD with fewer side effects. However, it's pending FDA approval and is used off-label.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A lumbar puncture was performed on a patient in the sitting position, and they are now experiencing a severe headache. Which of the following is not a recommended management strategy for a post-lumbar puncture headache?
options: Perform a low-volume blood patch AAns AAns AAns AAns
questions.explanation: A post-lumbar puncture headache is a common complication caused by the persistent leakage of CSF through the dural hole, which lowers intracranial pressure. Recommended management strategies include lying in a supine (flat) position (Option A) to reduce the pressure at the leak site and administering intravenous caffeine (Option B) or theophylline, which causes cerebral vasoconstriction and may reduce the headache. For severe or persistent cases, a low-volume autologous blood patch (Option D) is performed to "plug" the hole. However, restricting water intake (Option C) is NOT recommended; in fact, increasing fluid intake (hydration) is often encouraged to support CSF production, although its effectiveness is debated. Using a smaller, non-cutting (pencil-point) needle during the procedure significantly reduces the incidence of this type of headache. Clinicians must warn patients that the headache typically worsens when upright and improves when lying down
questions.learning: A post-lumbar puncture headache is a common complication caused by the persistent leakage of CSF through the dural hole, which lowers intracranial pressure.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old presents with edema and anasarca. A diagnosis of minimal change disease is made. Which of the following is true about this condition?
options: Light microscopy shows effacement of podocytes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Good response to steroids

The true statement about minimal change disease is that it shows a good response to steroids.

Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. It is more common in males and appears between 2 to 6 years of age.

The causes of MCD are mostly idiopathic. It is usually associated with Hodgkin's lymphoma (due to the increased production of cytokines), respiratory infections, prophylactic immunizations, eczema, and rhinitis.

Clinically, they mostly present with proteinuria. The child presents with a history of edema that is initially noted around the eyes and gradually progresses into generalized edema. Hypertension and hematuria are uncommon.

Levels of the following proteins are increased in nephrotic syndrome:

• Fibrinogen - leads to hypercoagulability.
• Lipoproteins - due to increased synthesis.

Levels of the following proteins are decreased in nephrotic syndrome as a consequence of selective proteinuria:

• Albumin—the protein with the largest proportion of loss in nephrotic syndrome
• Transferrin
• Cholecalciferol-binding protein
• Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG)
• Ferritin
• Coagulation factors
• Antithrombin III

Diagnosis can be made by urinalysis showing proteinuria, ranging from 3+ to 4+ protein on urine dipstick and a spot urine protein/creatinine ratio (PCR) >2. The proteinuria principally contains albumin, hence known as selective proteinuria. Serum albumin levels are <2.5 g/dL and there is an increase in serum cholesterol and triglyceride levels.

Biopsy findings include the following:

• Light microscopy- glomeruli appear normal (hence called "minimal change")
• Immunofluorescence studies- no Ig or complement deposits
• Electron microscopy- diffuse effacement of foot processes of visceral epithelial cells/podocytes

The image given below shows biopsy findings seen in minimal change disease on light microscopy.

The illustration given below shows the effacement of foot processes of podocytes as seen in MCD.

The majority of children will respond to corticosteroid (prednisone/prednisolone) treatment and will achieve complete remission (urine PCR<0.2 or <1+ protein on urine dipstick).
questions.learning: Good response to steroids — The true statement about minimal change disease is that it shows a good response to steroids. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient died from bronchopneumonia following an intracerebral hemorrhage caused by cerebral metastases from a squamous cell carcinoma of the left main bronchus. What should be recorded in the line I (c) of the death certificate?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the left main bronchus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cerebral metastasis

Cerebral metastasis will be filled in the line I (c) of the death certificate, as one of the antecedent causes in the order of the events that took place.

The death certificate will be filled in the order of the events that took place, as follows:

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the ideal number of antenatal visits?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 12-14

The ideal number of antenatal visits is 12-14.

The antenatal visits should ideally be: monthly once up to 28 weeks, once in two weeks between 28-36 weeks, and once weekly visits from 36 weeks onwards.

This translates to a total of 12-15 visits.

The WHO increased the minimum number of antenatal visits from 4 to 8 visits to reduce perinatal mortality.

In the Indian scenario, the earlier minimum of 4 visits were implemented as follows:

• 1st visit: within 12 weeks (preferably as soon as pregnancy is suspected)
• 2nd visit: between 14-26 weeks
• 3rd visit: between 28-34 weeks
• 4th visit: between 36 weeks and term

A booked case is one that has at least 3 antenatal visits with two visits in the third trimester.
questions.learning: 12-14 The ideal number of antenatal visits is 12-14. The antenatal visits should ideally be: monthly once up to 28 weeks, once in two weeks between 28-36 weeks, and once weekly visits from 36 weeks onwards.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug acts on the marked receptor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tiagabine

The marked receptor is GABA Transporter 1 Receptor (GAT-1), and Tiagabine acts on this receptor.

Tiagabine inhibits the neuronal uptake of GABA and prolongs its time in the synaptic cleft, where the GABA molecules can activate GABA receptors.

Other drugs which act on the GABAergic pathway are:

• Activation of GABA A receptors - Barbiturates, Phenobarbitone
• Activation of GABA B receptors - Baclofen
• Prevents the uptake of GABA - Tiagabine
• Prevents the degradation of GABA (inhibits GABA transaminase) - Vigabatrin

Other options:

Option B: Ganaxolone is a recently approved drug for the treatment of seizures associated with CDKL5 deficiency. The exact mechanism of action of Ganaxolone is unknown, but its anticonvulsant effects are thought to result from positive allosteric modulation of the GABA-A receptor in the CNS. It can be used in adults as well as children older than 2 years of age. The most common adverse reactions associated with the drug are somnolence, pyrexia, salivary hypersecretion and seasonal allergy.

Option C: Felbamate is the NMDA receptor antagonist prescribed to this patient. It also potentiates GABA action. It is indicated in refractory primary or secondary generalised seizures and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Felbamate is associated with aplastic anemia and liver failure.

Option D: Stiripentol is a GABA A receptor modulator with GABA-enhancing activity. It is clinically used in conjunction with valproate and clobazam for refractory generalized tonic-clonic seizures with severe myoclonic epilepsy in infants (Dravet syndrome).
questions.learning: Tiagabine — The marked receptor is GABA Transporter 1 Receptor (GAT-1), and Tiagabine acts on this receptor. Tiagabine inhibits the neuronal uptake of GABA and prolongs its time in the synaptic cleft, where the GABA molecules can activate GABA receptors.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy weighing 30 kg is scheduled for tumor resection surgery and will be kept nil per os (NPO). What is the appropriate daily maintenance fluid requirement for this child?
questions.explanation: Maintenance fluid requirements in pediatrics are calculated using the Holliday-Segar formula ( rule for hourly rates or a tiered system for daily volumes). For a child weighing 30 kg: First 10 kg: (100 mL/kg) Next 10 kg: (50 mL/kg) Remaining 10 kg: (20 mL/kg) Total daily volume: Option A (1000 mL) only accounts for the first 10 kg. Options C (2500 mL) and D (3000 mL) are significantly higher and would lead to fluid overload in a 30 kg child. Maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance is critical during the NPO period to prevent dehydration and metabolic disturbances. Standard maintenance fluids for children usually consist of D5NS with potassium supplementation. Therefore, based on the established physiological tiers, 1700 mL is the precise daily requirement for this 7-year-old patient
questions.learning: Maintenance fluid requirements in pediatrics are calculated using the Holliday-Segar formula ( rule for hourly rates or a tiered system for daily volumes).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the primary position of the right eye in right 3rd cranial nerve palsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Downwards and outwards

In oculomotor (3rd cranial nerve) palsy, the lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) muscles remain unopposed because they are not supplied by the oculomotor nerve. As a result, the affected eye assumes a “down and out” position due to the combined actions of:

• Lateral rectus → abducts the eye (outwards)
• Superior oblique → depresses the eye, especially in the adducted position (downwards)

Associated features of complete 3rd nerve palsy include:

• Ptosis due to paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris.
• Diplopia (double vision).
• Mydriasis and loss of accommodation if parasympathetic fibers are involved (pupil-involving 3rd nerve palsy).
questions.learning: Downwards and outwards — In oculomotor (3rd cranial nerve) palsy, the lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) muscles remain unopposed because they are not supplied by the oculomotor nerve.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which bones are cut during/removed during external Dacryocystorhinostomy?
questions.explanation: Note: The question should ideally specify both bones involved. In external DCR, portions of the Lacrimal bone and the Maxillary bone (specifically the frontal process) are removed to create a permanent fistula between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity. Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the standard surgical treatment for nasolacrimal duct obstruction. During the procedure, a bony ostium is created by removing the thin lacrimal bone (Option C) and a portion of the thick frontal process of the maxilla (Option B). This allows tears to bypass the blocked duct and drain directly into the middle meatus of the nose. The Zygomatic bone (Option A) and Frontal bone (Option D) are not part of the lacrimal fossa and are not removed. External DCR involves a skin incision, while endoscopic DCR is performed through the nose without an external scar. Both methods rely on the successful creation of this bony opening. Precise knowledge of this anatomy is essential for ophthalmic and ENT surgeons to ensure a successful outcome and avoid complications like orbital injury or severe bleeding from the angular vessels
questions.learning: Note: — The question should ideally specify both bones involved. In external DCR, portions of the Lacrimal bone and the Maxillary bone (specifically the frontal process) are removed to create a permanent fistula between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 26-year-old male presented with a large, round, firm, painless, right-sided testicular swelling associated with a dragging sensation. The left testis was normal. AFP was around 3000U. What is the next best step in the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High inguinal orchidectomy

The clinical features of a male patient presenting with a large, round, firm, and painless testicular mass with elevated AFP levels are suggestive of a non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT). Among the given options, a high inguinal orchidectomy would be the next best step in the management.

An ultrasound scan (USG) of the testis is mandatory to confirm the diagnosis of a testicular tumor and assess the contralateral testis. Since USG is not given as an option, the next best step in this scenario would be a high inguinal orchidectomy. FNAC and trucut biopsy are contraindicated due to risk of seeding of the scrotrum and upstaging of the cancer.

Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the gold standard treatment for excision of the primary tumor. Sperm cryopreservation should be offered before surgery.

After removal of the affected testis, a metastatic workup is done with CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to stage the disease as follows:

• Stage I: Localized tumor with no lymph node involvement or distant metastasis
• Stage II: Regional lymph node metastasis
• Stage III: Distant metastasis or nodal metastasis with elevated tumor markers

Further management is based on staging with treatment options including active surveillance, combination chemotherapy with bleomycin-etoposide-cisplatin and retroperitoneal lymph node dissection.
questions.learning: High inguinal orchidectomy — The clinical features of a male patient presenting with a large, round, firm, and painless testicular mass with elevated AFP levels are suggestive of a non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40-year-old smoker presents with soreness of tongue since last 2 months. On examination, it is found that the oral hygiene is poor and there is a white plaque over the lateral border of the tongue. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Edge biopsy of the lesion

A persistent white patch (leukoplakia) on the lateral border of the tongue in a middle-aged smoker is considered premalignant until proven otherwise. The lateral border of the tongue is a high-risk site for oral squamous cell carcinoma, and any lesion persisting for more than 2 weeks requires histopathological evaluation by biopsy.

An edge (incisional) biopsy should be performed to confirm the diagnosis and detect epithelial dysplasia or squamous cell carcinoma.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Oral vitamin C supplementation: Has no role in the evaluation or treatment of suspected leukoplakia.
• B. Oral antifungal treatment: Oral candidiasis typically presents as white plaques that can be scraped off. A non-scrapable lesion in a smoker requires biopsy, not empirical antifungal therapy.
• D. Local topical cauterization: Definitive treatment should only be planned after histological diagnosis.
questions.learning: Edge biopsy of the lesion — A persistent white patch (leukoplakia) on the lateral border of the tongue in a middle-aged smoker is considered premalignant until proven otherwise.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following vitamins is wrongly matched with their associated enzymes?
options: Vitamin B9 (Folic acid) : FIGLU excretion/Histidine load test
Vitamin C : Serum methyl malonate level
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin C : Serum methyl malonate level

Option D is wrongly matched as Vitamin B12 is associated with serum methyl malonyl levels and not Vitamin C.

There are two vitamin B12-dependent enzymes:

* Methionine synthase (Homocysteine methyltransferase): Catalyzes the conversion of homocysteine to methionine

* Methylmalonyl CoA mutase: Methylmalonyl CoA, formed as an intermediate in the catabolism of valine, isoleucine, and propionyl CoA is converted to succinyl CoA

The below figure shows B12 serving as a cofactor of methionine synthase. Its deficiency may cause  folate trap.

Other options:

Option A: Thiamine pyrophosphate (Vit B1) is the cofactor of transketolase. Transketolase and transaldolase are involved in the nonoxidative phase of the HMP pathway.

Option B: Riboflavin deficiency is assessed by measurement of the activation of erythrocyte glutathione reductase by FAD added in vitro. Riboflavin provides the reactive moieties of the coenzymes flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD).

Option C: FIGLU is converted to L-Glutamate by the enzyme glutamate formimino transferase. This enzyme uses folate (vitamin B9). In Vitamin B9 deficiency, FIGLU accumulates in the body and is excreted in the urine. The FIGLU excretion test is used to detect folic acid deficiency.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with O negative and husband B positive delivered a baby. Has received anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks. In which of the following conditions will you give anti-D post-delivery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Baby +ve, DCT -ve

Rh Isoimmunization occurs when:

• Rh-negative mother
• Rh-positive fetus

Fetal red blood cells entering maternal circulation stimulate production of anti-D antibodies, which can attack fetal RBCs in future pregnancies.

Rh-positive fetal RBCs enter maternal circulation

↓

Mother forms anti-D antibodies

↓

Antibodies cross placenta in next pregnancy

↓

Fetal hemolysis

↓

Hemolytic disease of the newborn

Anti‑D Immunoglobulin prevents maternal sensitization by destroying fetal Rh-positive cells before the immune system reacts.

Anti-D is given within 72 hours after delivery if:

• Mother is Rh-negative
• Baby is Rh-positive
• Mother is not already sensitized

Thus:

| Baby Rh status | DCT | Anti-D required

| -------------- | --- | ---------------

| Rh negative | Any | ❌ Not required

| Rh positive | DCT negative | ✅ Give Anti-D

| Rh positive | DCT positive | Usually sensitization already present

DCT detects antibodies bound to fetal RBCs.

| DCT result | Meaning

| ---------- | -------

| Negative | No antibodies attached

| Positive | Hemolysis due to antibodies

Doses of Anti-D-

| Situation | Dose

| --------- | ----

| Routine antenatal prophylaxis | 300 µg at 28 weeks

| Post-delivery prophylaxis | 300 µg within 72 hours

| Early pregnancy events | 50–100 µg

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute loss of vision accompanied by pain on eye movement. Examination reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), a normal-appearing optic disc, and central scotoma on visual field testing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The triad of sudden vision loss, pain on eye movements, and a central scotoma in a middle-aged patient is highly characteristic of optic neuritis. The presence of a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) confirms an optic nerve lesion. Crucially, the finding of an intact optic disc on fundoscopy points specifically to retrobulbar neuritis, where the inflammation occurs behind the globe, sparing the disc from visible edema. Optic nerve glioma (Option A) is a slow-growing tumor of childhood causing progressive, painless proptosis. Eale's disease (Option C) is a peripheral retinal vasculitis causing vitreous hemorrhage. Neuroretinitis (Option D) would show visible disc swelling accompanied by a macular star. Optic neuritis is frequently associated with Multiple Sclerosis. Therefore, because the symptoms localize to the nerve without disc changes, it is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The triad of sudden vision loss, pain on eye movements, and a central scotoma in a middle-aged patient is highly characteristic of optic neuritis. The presence of a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) confirms an optic nerve lesion.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a gunshot case, blackening is noted surrounding a firearm entry wound. Blackening occurs mainly due to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Black smoke particles

Blackening around a firearm entry wound is due to deposition of black smoke (soot) particles from the discharge of the weapon.

• Occurs in close-range firing
• Soot consists of carbon particles produced during combustion of gunpowder
• Appears as black discoloration around the entry wound
• Can be wiped off (unlike tattooing)

Differentiation from other findings:

• Tattooing (stippling):

• Due to unburnt gunpowder particles
• Causes abrasions
• Cannot be wiped off

• Burns: Due to flame/heat effect, not primary cause of blackening
questions.learning: Black smoke particles Blackening around a firearm entry wound is due to deposition of black smoke (soot) particles from the discharge of the weapon. • Occurs in close-range firing • Soot consists of carbon particles produced during combustion of gunpowder…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve innervates the muscle responsible for the movement shown below?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a person shrugging their shoulders, an action primarily performed by the trapezius muscle. The spinal accessory nerve (Cranial Nerve XI) provides motor innervation to the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid muscles. Shrugging tests the upper fibers of the trapezius. The long thoracic nerve (Option B) supplies the serratus anterior muscle; damage to this nerve leads to "winging of the scapula". The axillary nerve (Option C) supplies the deltoid and teres minor muscles. The radial nerve (Option D) innervates the triceps brachii and the extensor muscles of the forearm. Clinically, injury to the spinal accessory nerve—often occurring during neck surgeries like lymph node biopsies—leads to shoulder droop and the inability to shrug the shoulder on the affected side. Patients may also experience difficulty in rotating their head to the opposite side due to involvement of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Precise anatomical knowledge of this nerve is essential for both neurologists and surgeons
questions.learning: The image depicts a person shrugging their shoulders, an action primarily performed by the trapezius muscle. The spinal accessory nerve (Cranial Nerve XI) provides motor innervation to the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid muscles.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-day-old neonate was admitted to the NICU after he was observed to have movements as shown in the clip. His APGAR scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. His blood sugar was within the normal range in the first 24 hours. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Focal clonic seizure

The video clip of a 2-day-old neonate exhibiting repetitive, rhythmic movement in unilateral upper and lower limbs suggests a neonatal seizure of focal clonic type.

A focal clonic seizure is characterized by multiple, repetitive, rhythmic contractions of muscle groups of the limbs, face, or trunk, maybe unifocal or multifocal. It may occur synchronously or asynchronously in muscle groups on one side of the body. It may occur simultaneously but asynchronously on both sides. It cannot be suppressed by restraint.

Other options:

Option A: Focal tonic seizures are characterized by sustained posturing of a single limb, sustained asymmetrical posturing of the trunk, and sustained eye deviation. They cannot be provoked by stimulation or suppressed by restraint.

Option C: Spasms are sudden generalized jerks lasting 1-2 sec and are usually associated with a single, very brief, generalized discharge. They may be flexor, extensor, or mixed extensor/flexor and can occur in clusters. They too cannot be provoked by stimulation or suppressed by restraint.

Option D: Subtle seizures include transient eye deviations, nystagmus, blinking, mouthing, abnormal extremity movements (rowing, swimming, cycling, pedalling), fluctuations in heart rate, hypertension episodes, and apnea. They are more common in preterm than in term babies.

Myoclonic seizures are random, single, rapid muscle contractions of the limbs, face, or trunk. They are not repetitive or may recur at a slow rate. They can be generalized, focal, or fragmentary. They can be provoked by stimulation.

Clinically apparent seizures in a neonate should be treated if they last >3 minutes or are brief serial seizures. In all neonates with seizures, hypoglycemia, CNS infection, and hypocalcemia should be ruled out before starting anti-epileptic drug treatment.

Drug toxicity: lidocaine, penicillin

questions.learning: Focal clonic seizure — The video clip of a 2-day-old neonate exhibiting repetitive, rhythmic movement in unilateral upper and lower limbs suggests a neonatal seizure of focal clonic type.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy presented with tremors, slurred speech, hyperammonemia, and elevated levels of homocitrulline and ornithine in his urine. Which of the following transporter defects is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ornithine transporter

The HHH (Hyperornithinemia, Hyperammonemia, and Homocitrullinemia) syndrome is caused by a defect in the ornithine transporter.

HHH syndrome is caused by a defect in the transport system of ornithine from the cytosol into the mitochondria (ORNT1 gene), resulting in the accumulation of ornithine in the cytosol and a deficiency of this amino acid in mitochondria. The accumulation of cytosolic ornithine leads to hyperammonemia and hyperornithinemia. Homocitrulline is formed from the reaction of mitochondrial carbamyl phosphate with lysine. When ornithine is deficient, it leads to homocitrullinuria.

Components of HHH syndrome:

* Hyperammonemia

* Hyperornithinaemia

* Homocitrullinuria

In the urea cycle, the enzyme ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyses the condensation of carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to the accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate, leading to elevated levels of glutamine in the blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid. Infants present with vomiting, irritability, lethargy, hypothermia, and apnoea due to high ammonia levels in the plasma. Mothers also have an aversion to protein-rich foods.

Urea cycle disorders are all characterised by hyperammonemia, encephalopathy, and respiratory alkalosis. This is due to an accumulation of the precursors of urea, namely ammonia and glutamine. Clinical features of urea cycle disorders are common to all and include vomiting, avoidance of high-protein foods, intermittent ataxia, irritability, lethargy, and severe mental retardation. Long-term treatment consists of a protein-restricted diet.

The enzymes involved in the urea cycle with their related disorders are given below:

* Carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase (CPS) 1 deficiency (hyperammonemia type 1) is rare and characterised by severe hyperammonemia.

* Ornithine transporter deficiency (HHH syndrome) is characterised by hyperornithinemia, hyperammonemia, and homocitrullinuria.

* Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency (hyperammonemia type 2) is inherited as an X-linked trait. Characterised by hyperammonemia and elevated glutamine levels in blood and CSF.

* Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency is characterised by increased citrulline, citrullinuria, and hyperammonemia.

* Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency leads to argininosuccinic acidemia and metabolic acidosis. Hyperammonemia is less severe, and argininosuccinate is found in urine and CSF.

* Arginase deficiency is of the mild variety and is characterised by hyperargininaemia and argininuria.

Other options:

Option A: Citrin Transporter (Citrin Deficiency) – A defect in the citrin transporter leads to citrullinemia type 2, which has elevated citrulline levels.

Option C: Cystinuria: A type of aminoaciduria characterised by impaired reabsorption of positively charged amino acids: Cystine, Ornithine, Lysine and Arginine (COLA).

Option D: Deutetrabenazine is a vesicular monoamine transporter-2 (VMAT-2) inhibitor by which it decreases the uptake of monoamines into synaptic vesicles and depletes monoamine stores from nerve terminals. This drug is indicated for use in the presence of chorea associated with Huntington’s disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is suspected to have transudative type of pleural effusion. Which of the following pleural fluid findings would not be seen in this patient?
options: Low specific gravity in pleural fluid
Low cellular content in pleural fluid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. High fibrin in pleural fluid

This patient has a transudative pleural effusion. High fibrin in pleural fluid in a finding noted in exudative type of pleural effusion, not transudative.

Fibrin is a protein involved in the clotting process. High fibrin levels suggest increased vascular permeability and leakage of proteins into the pleural space, indicative of an exudative process rather than a transudative one.

Light’s criteria can be used to differentiate between transudative and exudative pleural effusions. Exudative effusions will meet at least one of the following criteria:

* Pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5

* Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH >0.6

* Pleural fluid LDH is more than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum.

Other options:

Low protein in pleural fluid: Transudative pleural effusions are typically characterized by low protein levels in the pleural fluid, usually less than 3 g/dL. This is due to the passive filtration of fluid across the pleural membrane in conditions such as congestive heart failure or cirrhosis.

Low specific gravity in pleural fluid: Specific gravity measures the concentration of solutes in a fluid compared to water. In transudative pleural effusions, the specific gravity of the pleural fluid is typically low due to its dilute nature.

Low cellular content: Transudative pleural effusions are characterized by a low cellular content, typically with few white blood cells and no malignant cells.

Pearl PF0570: Types of pleural effusion

Transudative Pleural effusion

* Congestive heart failure

* Cirrhosis

* Nephrotic syndrome

* Peritoneal dialysis

* Superior vena cava obstruction

* Myxedema

* Urinothorax

Exudative Pleural effusion

* Neoplastic disease: metastatic disease and mesothelioma

* Infectious disease

* Pulmonary embolization

* GI: Esophageal perforation, pancreatic disease, intraabdominal abscess etc.,

* Collagen vascular disease: SLE, rheumatoid pleuritis, Wegener's, Churg Strauss syndrome etc.,

* Post coronary bypass surgery

* Asbestos exposure

* Sarcoidosis

* Drug-induced pleural disease: nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, bromocriptine, amiodarone etc.,

* Radiation therapy

* Hemothorax

* Chylothorax

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which of the following is the best test for quantitative analysis of an RNA sample?

PCR: Polymerase chain reaction

RTPCR: Reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction
options: RTPCR followed by Real time PCR
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. RTPCR followed by Real time PCR

RTPCR followed by real-time PCR is the best test for quantitative analysis of an RNA sample.

RTPCR (reverse transcriptase PCR) involves the generation of complementary DNA (cDNA) copies of the mRNA using the reverse transcriptase enzyme followed by amplification of the cDNA copies by PCR technique.

Quantification of DNA involves the assessment of the amount/concentration of DNA that is present in a sample when carrying out a technique like PCR. Real-time PCR or quantitative PCR/qPCR involves the quantification of DNA after each cycle of amplification, or, in "real-time" than at the end of the procedure; therefore real-time PCR helps in quantitative analysis of DNA.

When reverse transcriptase PCR and qPCR are combined, they can be used to determine the relative concentrations of a particular mRNA molecule in a cell.

Other options:
Option A: Real-time PCR alone can only be used for the quantification of DNA only.

Option B: RTPCR can convert the RNA into cDNA by reverse transcriptase enzyme and then amplify the cDNA copies by means of PCR but cannot quantify the DNA/RNA.

Option C: PCR-Restriction fragment length polymorphism (PCR-RFLP) is also called cleaved amplified polymorphic sequence (CAPS) assay. Polymorphisms are inherited differences found among individuals in more than 1% of the normal population. PCR-RFLP is a technique in which organisms may be differentiated by variations in their DNA sequence by restriction endonucleases. Typically, gel electrophoresis is used to visualize RFLPs. Thus, DNA but not RNA molecules can be quantified in this process.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which statement correctly explains the mechanism of action of labetalol?
options: Directly acts as arterial vasodilator resulting in indirect effect tachycardia.
Blocks both alpha and beta-adrenergic receptors.
Primarily acts as a vasodilator with little effect on arterioles
Decreases peripheral vascular resistance by directly acting as a relaxant for vascular smooth muscles.
questions.explanation: Labetalol is a unique antihypertensive agent classified as a combined alpha- and beta-adrenergic antagonist. Specifically, it blocks both alpha-1 and non-selective beta ( and ) receptors. The -blockade causes systemic vasodilation, which lowers blood pressure by reducing peripheral vascular resistance. Simultaneously, its -blockade prevents the reflex tachycardia that would normally occur in response to a drop in blood pressure. This dual action makes it highly effective and safe. Option A describes pure vasodilators like hydralazine. Options C and D are inaccurate descriptions of its direct receptor-mediated effects. Labetalol is especially notable for its safety in managing hypertensive emergencies and is a first-line drug for treating hypertension during pregnancy (e.g., pre-eclampsia). It has a ratio of alpha-to-beta blockade of approximately 1:3 for oral dosing and 1:7 for intravenous use. Understanding this combined blockade is essential for utilizing labetalol correctly in clinical scenarios where both rapid pressure reduction and heart rate control are required
questions.learning: Labetalol is a unique antihypertensive agent classified as a combined alpha- and beta-adrenergic antagonist. Specifically, it blocks both alpha-1 and non-selective beta ( and ) receptors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: At what vertebrae level does the indicated structure correspond?
questions.explanation: The image indicates the carina, which is the site of the bifurcation of the trachea into the left and right main bronchi. In a living, upright person, this anatomical landmark typically corresponds to the level of the T4-T5 intervertebral disc. This level also coincides with the sternal angle (Angle of Louis) on the anterior chest wall. It is a critical landmark in thoracic anatomy, marking the boundary between the superior and inferior mediastinum. Options A, B, and C refer to different thoracic levels. It is important to note that the level of the carina can shift slightly during deep inspiration (descending to T6). However, the standard anatomical "textbook" level for the tracheal bifurcation is the T4-T5 disc. Identifying this level is essential for correctly positioning endotracheal tubes during intubation and for interpreting chest radiographs. Consequently, the bifurcation is fixed as a primary reference point at the T4-T5 vertebral junction
